justification: Multiple independent human genetic studies report their own primary evidence of point/truncating CHD8 variants in ASD probands: Neale-type exome trio studies identified recurrent de novo protein-altering CHD8 mutations (PMID 22495309; PMID 22495311, which explicitly names CHD8 a genuine autism risk factor), and targeted resequencing of 2,446 probands found recurrent disruptive de novo CHD8 mutations linked to macrocephalic ASD (PMID 23160955). Independent clinical cohorts further characterize the phenotype of CHD8 protein-truncating variant carriers, with high rates of ASD, macrocephaly and developmental delay (PMID 31001818; PMID 31526516; PMID 41407309). Balanced chromosomal abnormality sequencing also identified single-gene CHD8 disruption in neurodevelopmental cases (PMID 22521361), and CHD8 is routinely treated as a highly penetrant ASD gene in large cohorts (PMID 35982159). These are human, replicated, single-gene-resolution findings across independent probands, satisfying the Established criteria.

Multiple independent human cohorts report de novo ADNP variants in patients with syndromic autism: Helsmoortel et al. (PMID 24531329) described ten unrelated patients with ASD, ID and dysmorphism carrying de novo ADNP mutations, and Vandeweyer et al. (PMID 25169753) reported an additional independent patient with detailed clinical characterization. Independent replication comes from large-scale sequencing (PMID 35982159, where ADNP is treated as a highly penetrant ASD gene identified by exome-wide significance), a Middle Eastern ASD cohort with a de novo ADNP variant (PMID 38572415), a targeted panel study identifying a de novo pathogenic ADNP frameshift (PMID 40731902), and deep phenotyping of 11 youths with ADNP disruptions (PMID 30107084). Supporting mechanistic and mouse haploinsufficiency work (PMIDs 30106381, 25646590) further corroborates causality, and clinical syndrome descriptions (PMID 27054228) confirm ADNP/Helsmoortel–Van der Aa syndrome as an established monogenic cause of ASD. The evidence is single-gene, human, replicated across independent probands, so "Established" is clearly warranted.

Several human studies report intragenic (non-CNV) EHMT1 lesions in independent probands with autism spectrum disorder: PMID 27651234 identified a de novo nonsense EHMT1 mutation (Trp1138Ter) in an autistic patient with normal intellect; PMID 29416845 identified mosaic EHMT1 mutations in multiple apparently unaffected parents who on detailed assessment showed ASD and neurocognitive dysfunction; PMID 28742076 describes an ASD patient carrying a deleterious premature termination codon in EHMT1; PMID 22521361 sequenced balanced chromosomal abnormalities in autism probands and pinpointed EHMT1 disruption. A large clinical cohort (PMID 39746677) with 54% intragenic sequence variants documents ASD in 38% of patients, supporting replication across independent probands rather than only multigene 9q34.3 deletions. The ASD phenotype is largely embedded within syndromic Kleefstra syndrome, and some supporting work is in Drosophila or iPSC models, which tempers certainty slightly and leaves meaningful weight on "Existing".

Multiple independent human studies report point/truncating TCF20 variants in probands with ASD: PMID 25228304 identified a de novo chromosome 22 rearrangement disrupting TCF20 in two affected brothers plus additional de novo and rare inherited TCF20 mutations in ASD cohorts; PMID 36593604 describes two unrelated individuals with pathogenic TCF20 variants and ASD; PMID 40011607 reports two siblings with a novel TCF20 frameshift and autism via paternal germline mosaicism; PMID 27436265 and PMID 30819258 report de novo nonsense/frameshift variants with ASD as a variably penetrant feature; PMID 30739909 delineates 27 additional patients with TCF20 variants and neurobehavioral/autistic features. These are sequence-level, gene-specific human findings in independent probands/families, not merely multigene 22q13 deletions (PMIDs 30216695, 36118903, 38002941), which cannot isolate TCF20. Autism is thus a recognized, though incompletely penetrant, component of TCF20-associated neurodevelopmental disorder, supporting an Established relationship, with some residual weight on Existing because ASD is one feature within a broader ID/NDD syndrome.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo point variants in KDM6B in probands with autism/neurodevelopmental phenotypes: the Qatari ASD cohort identified a de novo KDM6B variant in an ASD case (PMID 38572415), a case report describes a novel de novo pathogenic KDM6B variant with autism spectrum, ADHD and oppositional traits (PMID 38326731), a cohort of 12 unrelated patients with de novo KDM6B alterations and neurodevelopmental disease (PMID 31124279), and a large 85-individual clinical/molecular spectrum study with functional validation of missense/in-frame variants (PMID 37196654). Family-based linkage/WGS work in ASD/ADHD co-occurring families also prioritized KDM6B (PMID 36251081). Supporting mechanistic and mouse work (haploinsufficiency and mosaic knockout producing ASD-like behaviors, PMIDs 35711692, 39223259) and convergent ASD gene-network analyses (PMID 38588587) reinforce biological plausibility but are animal/in vitro and therefore only supportive. Some uncertainty remains because much of the human phenotype is described as a broader NDD syndrome with variable autistic features rather than isolated ASD, so a portion of probability is retained for "Existing".

There is credible human evidence linking DYNC1H1 to ASD, but it falls short of replicated causal demonstration. PMID 40428333 reports a case-control association analysis of DYNC1H1 polymorphisms with ASD occurrence and clinical phenotype, and PMID 42056834 describes a single ASD proband with a de novo likely-pathogenic DYNC1H1 variant (used to generate an iPSC line, so the primary result is a cell line rather than a cohort). PMID 28325891 notes that de novo DYNC1H1 mutations have been reported in ASD, but this is background citation rather than its own ASD evidence; its primary findings concern epileptic encephalopathy. Broader literature firmly establishes DYNC1H1 in neurodevelopmental disorders with intellectual disability, cortical malformation, epilepsy and behavioral phenotypes (PMIDs 38848546, 36175372, 38953796, 26100331, 38114583), which are strongly linked comorbid/precursor phenotypes supporting "Existing." Without at least two independent primary reports of ASD probands with single-gene DYNC1H1 variants, "Established" cannot be assigned.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report de novo and rare inherited POGZ variants in ASD probands with their own primary data: PMID 26942287 collected 25 individuals with disruptive POGZ mutations from large ASD/ID cohorts with statistically significant enrichment (p = 4.19 × 10⁻¹³); PMID 31196716 demonstrated a significant burden of rare missense variants in a Chinese ASD cohort (OR = 3.96) plus 8 de novo variants; PMID 25694107 reported a de novo missense variant in an ASD proband via trio WES; PMID 31782611 described 22 individuals with 21 unique LOF POGZ variants presenting DD/ID with autism; and PMID 30555518 identified POGZ among causative de novo LOF genes in a trio-WES ASD cohort. These are independent probands and cohorts, single-gene point variants (not multigene CNVs), replicated across populations. Functional work in neurons (PMID 27103995) supports mechanism but the human genetic evidence alone satisfies the Established criteria.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo likely gene-disrupting point mutations (not multigenic CNVs) in DYRK1A in ASD probands: Iossifov/O'Roak-type targeted resequencing of 2446 ASD probands identified recurrent de novo DYRK1A mutations (PMID 23160955), and a large resequencing effort in 7162 ASD/DD cases showed statistically significant enrichment of truncating and de novo DYRK1A mutations defining a syndromic ASD/ID phenotype (PMID 25707398). Additional independent case series with unique truncating/missense variants confirm ASD as a core feature (PMIDs 25920557, 25641759, 35285131, 32193494). Deep phenotyping of 29 individuals with DYRK1A LGD variants confirmed ASD diagnosis in 85% (PMID 37497568), and mental-health phenotyping across gene groups adds further human evidence (PMID 38622540). Animal and functional work (PMIDs 28167836, 30831192, 40634533) corroborates mechanism but is not needed for the causal claim.

Multiple independent human studies report truncating ASXL3 variants in probands with autism as part of the phenotype: the Spanish cohort of 22 BRPS patients found ASD in 75% with 19 identified ASXL3 variants (PMID 39833101), the international series of 45 unpublished individuals delineated the ASXL3-related neurobehavioral phenotype (PMID 34436830), and a retrospective psychiatric case series reported ASD in 43% of BRPS patients (PMID 34086428). Independent single-proband reports with de novo ASXL3 variants and autism further replicate the association (PMIDs 27075689, 34247375, 29305346), and an ASD-ascertained cohort using targeted sequencing identified two children with de novo ASXL3 variants (PMID 37007974). These are point/truncating variants in single genes, not multigene CNVs, and come from multiple independent families and centers, supporting a causal role of ASXL3 haploinsufficiency in a syndromic ASD phenotype. Residual probability is placed on "Existing" because ASD is one feature of a broader neurodevelopmental syndrome rather than an isolated autism phenotype.

Multiple independent human studies report single-gene DEAF1 variants in probands with autism spectrum disorder: PMID 26048982 describes a homozygous recessive DEAF1 mutation segregating in a consanguineous Omani family with autism, ID and epilepsy; PMID 35981081 reports 10 individuals with de novo DBD variants whose phenotype includes ASD, with functional validation; PMID 29366832 identified a de novo DEAF1 splice variant in a Chinese ASD trio; PMID 41518091 reports an inherited pathogenic variant with ASD in both proband and mother; PMID 36010237 and PMID 38073621 are additional single-patient reports with de novo missense variants and ASD features. These are independent probands/families with point variants (not multigene CNVs), supported by functional assays showing altered transcriptional activity. The main caveat is that ASD appears as one feature within the broader DEAF1-associated neurodevelopmental disorder/VSVS spectrum rather than as isolated autism, which leaves some weight on "Existing".

Several human studies report de novo STXBP1 variants in individuals with autistic phenotypes: the Chinese ASD cohort sequencing study identified de novo mutations in STXBP1 among ASD probands (PMID 27824329), a case report describes a novel splice-site variant in a child with intellectual disability, epilepsy and ASD (PMID 39359953), an Emirati case series found co-existing ASD/ADHD in most STXBP1 patients (PMID 37908909), and a single de novo p.Arg292Cys variant was identified in a boy with ASD (PMID 34840252). These are independent probands with single-gene variants, supporting an established-level link, though autism in STXBP1 is usually one feature of a broader developmental and epileptic encephalopathy rather than isolated ASD, and large phenotyping cohorts (PMID 35190816) emphasize epilepsy/NDD rather than quantifying ASD causality. Several other listed articles (reviews of SNAREopathies, synaptic vesicle cycling, lncRNA networks) restate the association as background or provide mechanistic/expression support rather than primary genetic evidence. Therefore probability is split mainly between Established and Existing, with a modest allocation to Hypothesized.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report KDM5B variants in probands with autistic features: a retrospective series of 21 individuals with mono- and bi-allelic KDM5B variants in which ASD behaviors were prominent (PMID 39202393), two de novo splice variants in three patients with ID/ASD (PMID 30217758), a de novo variant in a patient with ASD and OCD (PMID 40657596), compound heterozygous variants with DD/ASD-spectrum phenotype (PMID 34573379), and trio WES in ASD families identifying KDM5B (PMID 28720891). Additional supporting human evidence comes from de novo variant enrichment analyses implicating KDM5B in ASD-adjacent phenotypes such as complex motor stereotypies and ADHD (PMIDs 37788244, 38997333), and mouse Kdm5b models show autism-like behaviors (PMID 42160407), reinforcing biological plausibility. Counterbalancing this, penetrance is incomplete—heterozygous protein-truncating variants occur in unaffected individuals and the core syndrome is autosomal recessive DD/ID with ASD as a variable feature (PMIDs 30409806, 35905858)—so the gene–ASD relationship, while replicated, is not unequivocally causal for ASD per se. Points are therefore split nearly evenly between Established and Existing, with little weight on Hypothesized or Novel.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo, truncating, missense, mosaic, and inherited SYNGAP1 point variants in probands with intellectual disability and autism/autistic features: Hamdan et al. reported de novo truncating mutations in non-syndromic ID with autism (PMID 21237447), Carvill/Berryer et al. identified novel missense and truncating de novo mutations with autism and epilepsy (PMID 23161826), a familial cohort delineating SYNGAP1-related disorder with ASD (PMID 40407699), postzygotic mosaic single-nucleotide mutations in ASD probands (PMID 28867142), and long-read genome sequencing identifying a pathogenic SYNGAP1 variant in an unsolved autism family (PMID 40778144). Additional cohorts document autistic traits in >90% of SYNGAP1-DEE patients (PMIDs 38505260, 41856439), and DNM enrichment analyses list SYNGAP1 among NDD/ASD genes (PMID 31785789). These are single-gene point variants in independent human probands, not multigene CNVs, satisfying replication. Mouse and organoid work (PMIDs 23141534, 37946050) provides supporting mechanism but is not needed for the causal call.

Multiple human cohorts report single-gene ANKRD11 loss-of-function sequence variants (not just multigene deletions) in independent probands, with autism spectrum disorder/neurobehavioral phenotypes documented: PMID 25424714 (20 patients from 13 families with ANKRD11 sequence variants, many with ASD or hyperactivity), PMID 35970914 (25 new individuals, mostly truncating variants, 28% with ASD diagnosis), and PMID 36446582 (340 KBG patients with genotype–phenotype analysis). Additional large NDD sequencing cohorts list ANKRD11 among the most frequently mutated genes in patients with ASD/ID (PMID 40019509), and scoping reviews synthesize ASD frequency across ANKRD11 variant carriers (PMID 33179249). Mechanistic support comes from mouse/neuronal studies showing Ankrd11 is a chromatin regulator required for neural development with ASD-like behaviors (PMIDs 25556659, 29274743), which reinforces but does not substitute for the human genetic evidence. Some uncertainty remains because ASD in these cohorts is a variable feature of a broader syndrome (KBG) and early evidence came from 16q24.3 contiguous-gene deletions (PMIDs 19920853, 18252227), which cannot isolate ANKRD11; hence a residual weight on "Existing."

Multiple human genetic studies report point/truncating CHD2 variants in independent ASD probands: Iossifov/Turner-type targeted resequencing of 3,486 ASD probands specifically implicated CHD2 by recurrent de novo point mutations (PMID 25418537); a germline mosaic missense variant (p.Thr645Met) segregated in two siblings with ASD (PMID 28960266); postzygotic mosaic SNVs in CHD2 were found in ASD cases in the Simons Simplex Collection (PMID 28867142); and a customized ASD panel identified a de novo pathogenic frameshift CHD2 p.Thr1108Metfs*8 in an ASD patient (PMID 40731902). Additional clinical case series show de novo CHD2 variants in patients with comorbid ASD (PMID 39503459, 34713950). These are single-gene sequence variants (not multigene CNVs) in independent probands, satisfying replication; supporting mouse and in vitro work (PMIDs 41872520, 37366052) adds mechanistic plausibility but is not needed for the human evidence. A small residual probability is left for "Existing" because ASD is often reported as one feature of a broader CHD2 developmental/epileptic encephalopathy phenotype rather than as an isolated ASD diagnosis.

Multiple human studies with molecularly confirmed SATB2 point/intragenic variants report autism as a frequent feature: PMID 33969926 documents autism in 41% of 49 individuals with SATB2-associated syndrome, PMID 35350986 characterizes autistic behaviours in SAS with cross-syndrome comparison, and PMID 33661512 stratifies SAS patients by autism diagnosis. Independent ascertainment from the ASD side also implicates the gene: PMID 22521361 sequenced balanced chromosomal abnormalities in autism/NDD probands and identified direct single-gene disruption of SATB2, and PMID 40642607 reports a causative SATB2 loss-of-function variant in a CNV-negative ASD child. Mutation-update and syndrome reviews (PMIDs 31021519, 27774744, 24301056) confirm SATB2 haploinsufficiency causes the syndrome in which autism is a recurrent phenotype, though autism is one component of a broad syndromic neurodevelopmental presentation rather than an isolated ASD phenotype, which keeps some probability on "Existing."

Multiple independent human studies report de novo, protein-altering GRIN2B variants in their own ASD probands: O'Roak et al. exome sequencing found a de novo GRIN2B mutation in a sporadic ASD case (21572417), a larger exome study identified additional de novo GRIN2B variants in ASD probands (22495309), targeted resequencing of 2446 probands found recurrent disruptive GRIN2B mutations contributing to sporadic ASD (23160955), an NMDAR gene sequencing study reported a de novo GRIN2B mutation in an ASD patient (22833210), and a synaptic gene sequencing study identified a de novo nonsense GRIN2B variant in an ASD case (24126926). Further support comes from panel testing identifying a de novo likely pathogenic GRIN2B variant in an ASD patient (40731902), a Vietnamese ASD cohort (32193494), and case-control/family association studies of common GRIN2B variants with autism (25656819, 36399225). These are single-gene, point-mutation findings in independent human probands, not multigene CNVs, satisfying replication requirements. Animal/in vitro work (38926089) adds mechanistic support but is not needed for the classification.

Multiple independent human studies report ARID1B point/truncating variants in probands with autism: Halgren et al. (PMID 21801163) mapped a de novo balanced translocation truncating ARID1B in a patient with autism, corpus callosum agenesis and severe speech impairment, referencing a second similar translocation case; Lim et al. (PMID 26637798) found recurrent deleterious single-nucleotide variants in ARID1B among postmortem ASD brains; van der Sluijs et al. (PMID 30349098) characterized 143 ARID1B-variant patients spanning nonsyndromic ID to Coffin-Siris with autistic features, and the CSS registry cohort (PMID 34205270) plus a detailed ASD/CSS case report (PMID 37692302) add further independent probands. Additional human sequencing cohorts (PMIDs 35699097, 39280100, 40019509) and functional/animal work (PMIDs 28695822, 32887689) corroborate the mechanism, and neuroimaging of ARID1B variant carriers (PMID 42156711) documents the ASD phenotypic spectrum. Evidence is thus replicated, gene-specific (not merely multigenic CNVs), and human-based, supporting an Established relationship.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo SCN2A variants in autism probands as their own primary results: Sanders et al. (PMID 22495306) found two independent de novo nonsense variants in unrelated ASD probands, a result highly unlikely by chance; a de novo splice-site variant was functionally characterized in a boy with ASD (PMID 24650168); mosaic/postzygotic damaging SCN2A mutations were identified in ASD probands (PMID 28714951); large-scale exome analysis of 42,607 autism cases lists SCN2A among highly penetrant ASD genes (PMID 35982159); and noncoding plus coding de novo mutations in SCN2A were associated with ASD in >5000 families (PMID 40894881). Deep phenotyping of 81 SCN2A patients included an autism-without-seizures subgroup with severe loss-of-function variants (PMID 38651838), and additional cohorts confirm ASD within the SCN2A phenotypic spectrum (PMIDs 34894057, 32193494). All key evidence is human, single-gene resolution, and replicated across independent probands, supporting an Established relationship.

Primary human genetic evidence exists in multiple independent cohorts: Loveday/Houge-type series reported four de novo missense PPP2R5D variants in seven unrelated probands with intellectual disability, macrocephaly, hypotonia and autism spectrum disorder (PMID 26576547), and an expanded international series with functional characterisation and genotype–phenotype analysis independently confirmed the phenotype including autism (PMID 36216457). Deep-phenotyping natural history cohorts of 42 and ~100 individuals with pathogenic de novo PPP2R5D variants consistently list autism/autistic features as a core manifestation (PMIDs 39169681, 37339871). Additionally, an unbiased gene-burden analysis of whole-exome data in an ASD patient cohort implicated PPP2R5D variants (p.Glu198Lys, p.Arg253Gln) in ASD (PMID 37167322), providing ASD-ascertained rather than only syndrome-ascertained evidence. Some residual probability is left for "Existing" because ASD in PPP2R5D-related disorder is one feature of a broader syndromic NDD rather than isolated ASD, but replication across independent probands in human studies strongly supports "Established".

Several human studies report their own primary results identifying single-nucleotide/frameshift de novo KMT2A variants in probands with autistic phenotypes: PMID 31044088 characterized six individuals with de novo KMT2A variants and described a distinct ASD subtype in five, plus a meta-analysis showing excess de novo LoF/missense; PMID 34948243 identified a pathogenic KMT2A variant by trio WES in an ID/ASD cohort; PMID 37007974 found KMT2A among the most frequent variant genes in a targeted sequencing panel of 160 ASD children; PMID 33387673 reported a novel de novo KMT2A frameshift with broad neurodevelopmental/ASD-related features. Cohort studies of Wiedemann-Steiner syndrome (PMIDs 33783954, 37470210, 35821609) further document autistic traits/ASD diagnoses in a substantial fraction of KMT2A-mutated individuals, supporting replication across independent probands. Points are withheld from full certainty because much of the ASD phenotype is embedded within syndromic WSS rather than isolated ASD, and several supporting items are reviews or animal/in vitro work (PMIDs 26077434, 35444258, 40102613) that only restate the association.

Two independent human genetic studies report their own primary evidence of SHANK3 sequence-level mutations in ASD probands: Durand et al. (PMID 17173049) identified de novo/segregating SHANK3 point mutations (including a frameshift) in autism/Asperger families, and Moessner et al. (PMID 17999366) found a de novo SHANK3 mutation plus deletions in 400 Canadian ASD cases, concluding haploinsufficiency causes a monogenic form of autism. Large-scale exome/genome studies add replication, with SHANK3 among exome-wide significant, highly penetrant ASD genes in 42,607 cases (PMID 35982159) and recurrent identification in Chinese trios and family-based NGS panels (PMIDs 39126614, 41096937). Clinical delineation of SHANK3-related Phelan-McDermid syndrome, explicitly including pathogenic point variants rather than only multigenic 22q13 deletions, further supports causality in humans (PMID 37003575). Mouse and iPSC work (e.g., PMID 40089604) provides mechanistic corroboration but is not needed for the human causal claim.

Multiple independent human studies report point mutations (not just multigene CNVs) in FOXP1 in probands with autism: PMID 20950788 identified a de novo nonsense variant (p.R525X) with functional validation in a patient with ID and autism; PMID 21572417 found a de novo FOXP1 mutation in a sporadic ASD trio exome study; PMID 25853299 reported a de novo frameshift (p.V423Hfs*37) in a child with ASD and severe language impairment with functional confirmation; PMID 30385778 described a recurrent missense p.R525Q in three additional patients with ASD features. Prospective phenotyping of FOXP1 syndrome cohorts (PMID 29090079) and a scoping review (PMID 40101508) confirm ASD diagnosis in a substantial proportion of mutation carriers, and large-scale sequencing studies list FOXP1 among highly penetrant autism risk genes (PMID 35982159). Animal/cellular work (PMIDs 30124790, 26494785) provides supporting mechanism but is not needed given replicated human proband evidence. This constitutes strong, replicated causal evidence in independent probands.

Several human studies report gene-specific (intragenic, exon-disrupting) NRXN1 lesions in independent ASD probands, which isolate NRXN1 rather than a multigenic CNV region: PMID 22617343 (24 patients with intragenic NRXN1 deletions, 56% with ASD), PMID 23533028 (25 new individuals with NRXN1 exonic deletions, 65% ASD), and PMID 20468056 (12 clinically ascertained exonic deletion carriers plus 3 additional ASD families with segregation). Sequence-level evidence also exists: PMID 21424692 identified truncating NRXN1/NRXN2 mutations in ASD probands with functional validation, and PMID 28289584 found NRXN1 missense variants in nonsyndromic ASD cases. Unbiased population-based data (PMID 39695155) show a ~3-fold increased autism risk for exon-disrupting NRXN1 deletions, supporting replication beyond ascertainment bias. Counterweight for "Existing" comes from incomplete penetrance, variable expressivity, additional modifier CNVs, and the pleiotropic phenotype spectrum emphasized in reviews (PMIDs 30873608, 30031152), which complicate a strictly causal designation.

Direct human evidence of PTEN point mutations in ASD probands is present in the list: PMID 17427195 screened 88 patients with ASD and macrocephaly and identified a de novo missense mutation (D326N) in a boy with autism; PMID 16894538 reports a patient with Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome, autism and a PTEN mutation; PMID 34489750 characterizes a sizeable independent clinical cohort of 38 children with germline PTEN mutations and ASD; and PMID 39994410 reports de novo PTEN mutations in patients with ventriculomegaly/hydrocephalus linked to ASD. These are single-gene sequence variants (not multigene CNVs) in independent probands, satisfying replication across separate clinical studies. Supporting functional/genotype–phenotype work (PMIDs 29706350, 21828076, 32350270, 26827793) shows ASD-associated germline variants are typically hypomorphic relative to PHTS-associated ones, reinforcing a specific causal mechanism. Only a small residual probability is assigned to "Existing" in case one judges the human proband series to be modest in size.

Multiple human studies report single-nucleotide/frameshift TLK2 variants (not multigene CNVs) in patients whose phenotype includes autism spectrum disorder: the large multicenter cohort of 40 individuals with de novo/inherited loss-of-function TLK2 variants defining MRD57 with prominent behavioral/neurodevelopmental abnormalities (PMID 29861108), a de novo TLK2 case with explicit ASD diagnosis (PMID 39538191), and an independent young adult with de novo p.Arg123Ter and diagnosed ASD (PMID 41931014), plus additional independent probands with neuropsychiatric phenotypes (PMIDs 39296544, 34821460, 31558842). Functional work supports haploinsufficiency/impaired kinase activity as the mechanism (PMIDs 33323470, 29955062), and reviews describe TLK2-related NDD as including ASD (PMID 31302748). Thus the gene is causally linked to a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder in which ASD is a recurrent feature, replicated across independent probands, supporting Established. Some weight remains on Existing because ASD is a variable component of the broader MRD57 syndrome rather than the primary, systematically ascertained phenotype in most reports.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo/likely gene-disrupting single-gene variants in NAA15 in probands with neurodevelopmental disorder including autism spectrum disorder. Cheng et al. (PMID 29656860) identified 25 distinct LGD NAA15 variants in 38 individuals from 33 unrelated families with ASD among the clinical features; Stessman et al. (PMID 28191889) found an excess of de novo/private disruptive NAA15 mutations in a large NDD/autism cohort with clinical follow-up; Lyon et al. (PMID 37130971) phenotyped 66 NAA15 cases including ASD; and a Chinese ASD targeted-sequencing cohort added further variants (PMID 39825710). These are independent probands with point/truncating variants (not multigene CNVs), satisfying replication. A small residual probability is left for "Existing" since ASD is one manifestation within a broader NAA15-related neurodevelopmental syndrome rather than an isolated ASD phenotype.

CDK13 is firmly established as a cause of a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder (CHDFIDD/CDK13-related disorder) with intellectual disability, developmental delay and behavioral problems, and several human studies report autism specifically among variant carriers: a deep phenotyping cohort of 41 individuals found autism in 7 (PMID 36599938), a case report describes ASD in a boy with a CDK13 variant (PMID 35651941), and a WES study of ASD probands identified a CDK13 variant as contributory (PMID 40558542). De novo mutation analyses across NDD trios also list CDK13 as a significantly enriched gene in cohorts that include ASD probands (PMID 31785789). However, ASD in these reports is a variable, secondary feature of a broader syndromic phenotype rather than the primary replicated phenotype, and mouse/cardiac work (PMID 39556044) is not human ASD evidence. This places the relationship at the boundary between well-supported "Existing" and "Established," with slightly more weight to Existing.

TCF4 haploinsufficiency causes Pitt-Hopkins syndrome, repeatedly described as a syndromic form of autism spectrum disorder, and multiple human studies report their own patient-level variant data: PMID 29318938 presents 23 patients with molecularly confirmed TCF4 variants, many meeting ASD criteria, including point/small variants that implicate TCF4 specifically; PMID 22712893 systematically characterizes ASD manifestations in 10 PTHS individuals; PMID 22521361 sequenced balanced chromosomal abnormalities in autism/NDD probands and identified TCF4 disruption; PMID 25356899 reports de novo pathogenic TCF4 mutations in probands with moderate/severe ID; and PMID 36448207 is an independent human case-control association of a TCF4 polymorphism with ASD. Supporting reviews (22670138, 23640545, 33414364) summarize >100 patients with private TCF4 mutations, indicating broad replication across independent probands. Some uncertainty remains because much of the ASD framing is via the syndromic PTHS phenotype rather than idiopathic ASD, and several supportive works are functional/animal (37770578, 29228394, 37573005), so a portion of probability is retained for Existing/Hypothesized.

Human genetic evidence directly implicates CTCF in neurodevelopmental disorders: the large-scale targeted sequencing study (PMID 33004838) found significant de novo/ultra-rare disruptive variant burden in CTCF across thousands of NDD and autism trios and provided genotype–phenotype correlations, and CTCF-related disorder (MRD21) is a recognized monogenic NDD whose phenotypic spectrum includes autism (PMIDs 38662876, 37324587, 35456389). However, most of these sources describe CTCF variants as causing a broad NDD/intellectual disability phenotype in which autism is one variable feature, and the catalog/review papers are compilations rather than primary replication of an autism-specific causal link; independent primary proband series with ASD as the defining outcome are not clearly evidenced here. Considerable additional support is mechanistic or model-based (conditional Ctcf knockouts causing social deficits, MGE interneuron defects, CTCF R567W mouse/organoid models, protocadherin regulation), which supports Hypothesized rather than human causal evidence (PMIDs 35379308, 30377227, 38951485, 39185186). Weighting these, "Existing" is the most defensible category with substantial probability for "Established" given the strong human NDD variant burden data.

WAC loss-of-function variants cause DeSanto-Shinawi syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder in which autism spectrum disorder is repeatedly listed as part of the phenotypic spectrum, and WAC was originally identified partly in ID/autism screening cohorts (PMID 26264232). Patient-level evidence linking sequence-level WAC variants to ASD comes chiefly from PMID 33387902, where two of four children with heterozygous truncating WAC variants had ASD diagnoses, supported by cohorts of individuals with de novo WAC variants in whom ASD is described within the spectrum (PMIDs 35018708, 32214004, 41700448). Several other reports involve multigene 10p11–p12 deletions (PMIDs 35766809, 27119754, 35266333), which cannot isolate WAC and therefore do not count toward replication of an ASD-specific causal claim. Most remaining papers emphasize intellectual disability, dysmorphism, hypotonia and behavioral problems, restating ASD as background rather than reporting it as their primary phenotypic result. This supports credible but not fully definitive, independently replicated ASD-specific evidence, so "Existing" is the most likely category with substantial probability for "Established."

Multiple independent human genetic studies report de novo/disruptive KMT5B variants in probands with autism and related neurodevelopmental phenotypes: Stessman et al. (PMID 28191889) identified KMT5B via targeted sequencing of >11,730 NDD/ASD cases with clinical follow-up defining syndromic and nonsyndromic disease; a large Chinese ASD cohort study curated 39 KMT5B variants and performed genotype–phenotype correlation showing ASD, ID and macrocephaly (PMID 35331928); deep phenotyping of 43 patients confirmed autism as a core feature (PMID 36897941); and statistical de novo burden analysis independently implicated SUV420H1/KMT5B in ASD (PMID 26235986). Additional independent case reports and cohorts (PMIDs 35433545, 41409306, 37927187, 29276005, 41153391) replicate the association in unrelated families with single-gene point variants, not merely CNVs. Functional work in organoids and mice (PMID 35110736) supports mechanism but is not needed for the human causal evidence. The residual probability for "Existing" reflects that ASD is one feature within a broader KMT5B-related neurodevelopmental syndrome rather than an isolated ASD phenotype.

MEF2C haploinsufficiency syndrome is a recognized syndromic form of autism/ID, and several human studies report patient-level variants: PMID 34055696 describes seven independent probands with MEF2C point mutations (six novel, mostly de novo), several with autistic features; PMID 30763456 reports rare MEF2C variants in a Chinese ASD sequencing cohort with genotype–phenotype correlation; PMID 39349966 uses hiPSC-derived neurons/organoids from patients carrying MHS-specific MEF2C mutations diagnosed with ASD/ID. Additional support comes from small/intragenic deletions restricted to MEF2C in probands with ASD, epilepsy and severe ID (PMIDs 20412115, 20333642, 22031302), though multigene CNVs alone are less discriminating. Some points remain on "Existing" because much of the strongest mechanistic work is in mouse or isogenic iPSC models (PMIDs 32418612, 41125877) and several human papers restate the association as background rather than generating new proband-level evidence.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo point/truncating AHDC1 variants in probands who meet criteria for autism spectrum disorder: the phenotypic spectrum study of 20 XGS patients used a modified autism screening tool and found significant overlap with ASD (PMID 29696776); the original seven-patient de novo truncating variant series listed autism among neurological features (PMID 27148574); a Brazilian cohort of 16 patients with 12 novel AHDC1 variants reported ASD in nearly all (PMID 40501103); an Italian multicenter cohort of 15 patients with heterozygous AHDC1 variants documented ASD (PMID 42059486); and individual cases with molecularly confirmed variants describe ASD directly (PMIDs 34073322, 40046197). These are independent cohorts with sequence-level (non-CNV) variants, satisfying replication. The main uncertainty is that ASD is a variable comorbid feature of the syndromic Xia-Gibbs phenotype rather than an isolated autism phenotype, which leaves meaningful weight on "Existing"; CNV-only reports (PMIDs 30615951, 39359946) do not contribute.

Two provided articles report primary human genetic evidence with variants ascertained in autism probands: Chen et al. (PMID 35917186) analyzed 46 GIGYF1 likely gene-disruptive variants (de novo and inherited, including a recurrent frameshift) across large ASD cohorts, ranking GIGYF1 among the top mutated high-confidence ASD risk genes; and the de novo variant study of 41,367 trios (PMID 41646820) independently found exome-wide significant enrichment of GIGYF1 DNVs in males with autism. These are single-gene sequence variants, not multigenic CNVs, and derive from independent cohorts/analyses, supporting an Established rating. Supporting functional/animal work (Gigyf1 conditional KO mice with social deficits, zebrafish/mouse ablation, IGF-1R recycling mechanism; PMIDs 36924980, 36189799) strengthens biological plausibility but is non-human and would only support "Hypothesized" on its own. Other listed studies (type 2 diabetes, obesity, grip strength, cognition, LOY) implicate GIGYF1 in other human traits and are peripheral, so some residual probability remains for "Existing" if one judges the ASD replication insufficiently independent.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo, gene-disruptive point variants in ASH1L in ASD/NDD probands with primary data: the Chinese ASD cohort found recurrent de novo LGD mutations in ASH1L among 1,543 probands (PMID 27824329), targeted sequencing of >11,730 NDD cases identified ASH1L as a risk gene with clinical follow-up defining a new syndromic/nonsyndromic form (PMID 28191889), and independent case reports describe de novo loss-of-function or missense variants in patients with ID/autistic features (PMIDs 29753921, 28394464, 41291913, 38674358). These are single-nucleotide/frameshift variants, not multigene CNVs, and come from separate cohorts and clinics, satisfying replication in independent probands. Supporting functional work in Drosophila and mice (PMIDs 32609087, 31673123) and convergent neuronal differentiation assays (PMID 32887689) reinforce plausibility but are not required for the human evidence. A small residual probability is left for "Existing" because the core phenotype in several reports is intellectual disability/NDD with variable autism penetrance rather than isolated ASD.

Two independent human genetic studies report their own primary data linking EBF3 sequence variants to autism: PMID 29162653 identified seven unrelated individuals with de novo frameshift, nonsense, splice, and missense EBF3 variants with an increased frequency of autism, and PMID 34256850 analysed whole-genome sequencing in 2671 autism families (discovery plus replication) and implicated both coding and noncoding (enhancer hs737) EBF3 variants in HADDS and simplex autism. PMID 35340043 adds an integrated phenotype–genotype cohort in which heterozygous loss-of-function and ZNF-domain missense EBF3 variants segregate with autism spectrum/neurodevelopmental phenotypes and severity subtypes. Other papers (28017370, 28017372, 28017373, 34050706, 36937983) firmly establish EBF3 haploinsufficiency as causal for a syndromic NDD (HADDS) with autistic features, a phenotype strongly overlapping ASD, though autism is a variable component rather than the core diagnosis. CNV/translocation reports (33335013, 34999443) do not isolate EBF3 and were not counted. The residual uncertainty reflects that ASD is a partially penetrant feature within a broader syndrome, which some would rate as "Existing" rather than fully established for ASD per se.

Multiple human studies report de novo DLG4 variants (mostly protein-truncating) in patients with DLG4-related synaptopathy/SHINE syndrome, in which autism spectrum disorder is a recurrent phenotypic feature: the large multicenter cohort of 53 patients (PMID 33597769), a Japanese proband with a novel frameshift variant diagnosed with ASD and ADHD (PMID 38182567), and an adolescent with a de novo DLG4 variant previously diagnosed with pervasive developmental disorder/ASD (PMID 40444229). Additional human genetic work includes rare missense variant resequencing in ASD/schizophrenia cohorts (PMID 27271353) and earlier evidence linking human DLG4 variation to autism-relevant phenotypes (PMID 20952458). Supporting biology comes from model organisms (C. elegans knock-in of ASD-associated DLG4 variants, PMID 31220273; 41210176) and human brain proteomics showing DLG4 as a hub in ASD cortex (PMID 31511657), which strengthen but do not by themselves establish causality. Because ASD generally appears as part of a broader neurodevelopmental syndrome rather than isolated autism, some probability remains on "Existing," but independent probands with single-gene variants and ASD support "Established."

Multiple independent human cohorts report de novo/inherited single-nucleotide SLC6A1 variants in probands whose phenotype includes autism spectrum disorder: the 172-individual genotype–phenotype curation (PMID 37647852), the 116-patient aggregate cohort (PMID 33241211), the neurodevelopmental phenotype series (PMID 34006619), a case with epilepsy plus formally diagnosed ASD with functional validation (PMID 32398021), an intrafamilial variability series (PMID 37502687), and two French/GenIDA series of 14+14 patients showing autistic features (PMID 39889538). These represent independent probands and families with point variants, not multigene CNVs, and functional assays consistently show loss-of-function/haploinsufficiency (PMID 38781976), supporting causality. Some residual uncertainty remains because ASD in SLC6A1-NDD is usually one feature of a broader epilepsy/developmental-delay syndrome rather than isolated autism, which is why a portion of probability is retained for "Existing."

Multiple human studies report point/loss-of-function variants in HNRNPU in individuals with neurodevelopmental phenotypes that include autism: the ASD postzygotic mutation study identified damaging HNRNPU mutations in ASD probands (PMID 28714951), large-scale targeted sequencing of NDD/autism trios established HNRNPU as a significant risk gene with genotype–phenotype correlation (PMID 33004838), and clinical cohorts of de novo HNRNPU variants describe autistic features among the core phenotype (PMIDs 35138025, 39976380, 33874999), with an individual case of a pathogenic missense variant in a patient diagnosed with ASD (PMID 38846959). However, the dominant, best-replicated phenotype for HNRNPU is developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with severe intellectual disability, and autism is generally a comorbid/secondary feature rather than the primary evidenced outcome; some supporting reports involve multigene 1q44 CNVs (PMIDs 24885232, 29307321) which cannot isolate HNRNPU. Functional and mouse/methylome work (PMIDs 35864088, 41674383, 37120726) supports a plausible mechanism but is not itself variant–phenotype evidence in humans. The evidence therefore sits between Established and Existing, with points split nearly evenly.

Direct human variant-level evidence linking MED13L to autism features is present but thin in this set: PMID 29593475 reports a single proband with a de novo nonsynonymous MED13L change (p.Cys63Arg) and an autism-like phenotype, and PMID 42463903 (large Chinese ASD whole-genome cohort integrated with >40,000 ASD cases) includes MED13L among identified ASD risk genes, though its abstract frames MED13L mainly in a single-cell expression context. The remaining MED13L literature (PMIDs 25758992, 29511999, 29959045, 32646507, 40500968, 41465117) robustly establishes MED13L syndrome — intellectual disability, speech impairment, hypotonia, dysmorphism and behavioral difficulties — a neurodevelopmental phenotype strongly linked to, but not equivalent to, an ASD diagnosis; several of these note autism/behavioral comorbidity as background rather than as their primary result. Other papers (25626716 multigene CNV linkage, 37086723 craniosynostosis, 29740699 MED13, 29158550 pooled exome) cite MED13L only incidentally or for non-ASD phenotypes. Because I cannot cite two independent studies whose own results demonstrate single-gene MED13L variants causing diagnosed ASD in multiple probands, Existing is the most defensible category, with meaningful probability retained for Established given MED13L's status as a recognized ASD risk gene.

Multiple independent human studies report intragenic (non-CNV) de novo loss-of-function SETD5 variants in probands with a neurodevelopmental disorder in which autism/autistic behaviors are a recurrent feature: Grozeva et al. (PMID 24680889) identified seven de novo nonsense/frameshift SETD5 variants with prominent autistic and ritualized behaviors; the multicenter cohort of 28 previously unreported patients, 26 with single-nucleotide variants, documented autism among the core neuropsychiatric phenotypes (PMID 39603091); the National Brain Gene Registry cohort of 13 individuals with 11 unique pathogenic SNV/frameshift variants adds deep phenotyping (PMID 40265665); and further phenotypic series (PMIDs 42468298, 32793091, 25138099) and a systematic review of 42 mutation carriers reporting ~24% autistic features (PMID 29484850) provide replication. These are human proband-based studies with variants that isolate SETD5 itself rather than multigene 3p25.3 deletions, satisfying the criteria for replicated causal evidence, although ASD is one component of a broader ID/NDD syndrome rather than an isolated ASD phenotype, which leaves some probability on "Existing". Mouse model data (PMID 36685966) supports biological plausibility but is not needed for the higher categories.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo, single-gene TBR1 variants in probands with autism spectrum disorder: PMID 23160955 identified recurrent de novo disruptive mutations in TBR1 among 2446 ASD probands (own resequencing results), PMID 32005960 reported 25 new individuals with de novo TBR1 variants showing ID with autistic traits in 76%, PMID 32948248 described a de novo frameshift in a patient with ASD without ID, PMID 29288087 provided a detailed ASD case with a TBR1 variant, and further independent cases come from PMID 38448025, PMID 40004448 and PMID 34625926 (IDDAS pedigree). These are independent probands/families with point mutations, not multigene deletions, so the microdeletion reports (PMIDs 23112752, 24508274) are not required. Functional work (PMIDs 25232744, 30250039, 36579832, 27325115) supports pathogenic mechanisms of these patient-derived variants, reinforcing rather than substituting for the clinical evidence. The evidence therefore clearly meets the "Established" threshold.

Multiple independent human studies report MARK2 variants in ASD probands with primary evidence: PMID 35982159 identified MARK2 at exome-wide significance among 42,607 autism cases (de novo/inherited coding variants); PMID 39419027 describes a cohort of 31 individuals with mostly loss-of-function MARK2 variants presenting with ASD/NDD plus functional validation; PMID 41918168 expands the affected cohort including a familial case with variant-level functional classification; and PMID 40542891 reports an independent de novo frameshift in a child with ASD, epilepsy and developmental delay. Replication across ancestries is provided by the GALA consortium (PMIDs 39830258, 41912808), which found MARK2 among genome-wide significant autism genes in Latin American cohorts. Supporting mechanistic and animal data (Mark2+/- mice with ASD-like behavior, PMIDs 39419027, 39436150) reinforce biological plausibility but are not needed for the human causal claim. A small residual probability is assigned to "Existing" in case some reviewers consider the single-gene clinical cohorts insufficiently independent.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo loss-of-function CUL3 variants in ASD probands: a Chinese ASD cohort identified recurrent de novo LGD mutations in CUL3 (PMID 27824329), a Japanese patient with a novel stop-gain variant (PMID 33097317), a Chinese patient with a nonsense variant and ASD/epilepsy (PMID 37026922), a Brazilian trio cohort with a de novo LOF variant (PMID 31696658), and large case series defining CUL3-related neurodevelopmental disorder with autism/seizures (NEDAUS) in dozens of new individuals with pathogenic single-nucleotide/indel variants (PMIDs 39301775, 39501558). These are single-gene variants (not multigenic CNVs) in independent probands, satisfying replication. Animal and cellular models (mouse, Drosophila, C. elegans) provide converging mechanistic support but are not required here. Therefore the association is Established, with a small residual probability that some might regard the ASD phenotype as part of a broader NDD syndrome (Existing).

Multiple independent human studies report de novo single-nucleotide/loss-of-function MYT1L variants in patients with autism and neurodevelopmental disorder, not merely multigenic CNVs. Specifically, PMID 27824329 reports recurrent de novo likely gene-disrupting MYT1L mutations in a Chinese ASD cohort; PMID 38136944 describes a novel de novo missense variant (p.His516Gln) in a proband with complex ASD; PMID 41210245 reports a de novo missense variant causing MRD39 with ASD; PMID 34748075 assembles 40 new patients with pathogenic MYT1L variants showing developmental delay, ID and behavioral/autistic features; and PMID 35741772 identifies MYT1L as a top gene in ASD panel sequencing with shared clinical features. Additional cohort/registry data (PMIDs 38632549, 41409659, 38572415) and systematic review (PMID 32267091) corroborate replication across independent probands and populations. This constitutes strong, replicated human genetic evidence for a causal MYT1L–ASD relationship, though ASD is one feature of a broader MYT1L-related neurodevelopmental syndrome.

Multiple independent human studies report intragenic, single-gene-resolution AUTS2 variants (frameshift, nonsense, in-frame and truncating translocation breakpoints) in probands with autism/autistic features: PMID 34573342 describes five new patients with loss-of-function sequence variants where ASD/autistic features were present in 80%; PMID 25205402 reports two unrelated males with a 2-bp deletion and a single-exon deletion; PMID 31788251 reports a de novo nonsense variant in a child with autism; PMID 20635338 reports a de novo translocation truncating AUTS2 in a patient with autism; PMID 34273950 reports a multigenerational family with a frameshift variant. Larger cohort descriptions (PMID 27075013, 40317680) confirm autistic traits in ~50% of AUTS2 syndrome patients, and de novo variant burden analyses in large trio cohorts identify AUTS2 as exome-wide significant (PMID 41646820). This constitutes replicated human evidence across independent probands and families, not merely CNVs spanning multiple genes. Functional zebrafish/mouse work (PMID 23349641) provides supporting mechanism but is not required for the classification.

Direct human evidence with sequence-level (non-CNV) variants exists in multiple independent cohorts: PMID 39448799 reports 42 newly ascertained plus 35 previously reported individuals with 60 unique BCL11A point/frameshift/nonsense/splice variants, listing autism spectrum disorder among the most prevalent features of BCL11A-IDD (Dias-Logan syndrome); PMID 28891213 explicitly reports novel BCL11A mutations in patients with autism and intellectual disability; PMID 35856171 adds three children with de novo missense/nonsense variants and ASD-overlapping phenotypes, and PMID 32903878 and 39187446 describe additional de novo truncating variants in the same ASD-associated syndromic spectrum. Multigene 2p15-p16.1 deletion reports (PMIDs 25938782, 28573701, 37937284) are supportive but cannot isolate BCL11A. Functional/ChIP-seq convergence work (PMID 38850535) and reviews (38392344, 32322190) further corroborate BCL11A as an ASD-associated transcriptional regulator. Some residual probability is assigned to "Existing" because ASD is a variable feature within a broader intellectual disability syndrome rather than an isolated, consistently replicated ASD phenotype.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo/loss-of-function KMT2C variants in probands with a neurodevelopmental phenotype that prominently includes autism: PMID 29069077 describes five patients with de novo KMT2C LoF mutations and ID/ASD overlapping Kleefstra syndrome; PMID 39013459 delineates 98 individuals with rare KMT2C variants (81 pathogenic/likely pathogenic) defining a distinct NDD with behavioral/psychiatric features and a DNA methylation signature; PMID 35324822 reports a de novo missense variant in a child with childhood autism plus a review of 10 similar patients; PMID 41914216 adds three further patients; PMID 29276005 firmly associates KMT2C haploinsufficiency with dominant developmental disorders. Additional supporting human genetic data come from mosaic LGD variants in ASD probands (PMID 27632392) and ASD cohort sequencing (PMIDs 35190550, 41420732, 34356069). Animal work (Kmt2c mice, PMIDs 38528071, 37538398) corroborates causality but is not required here. Some uncertainty remains because the core phenotype is described as a broader KMT2C-related NDD/Kleefstra syndrome 2 rather than isolated ASD, which supports a small allocation to "Existing".

EP300 is one of the two causal genes for Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome (RSTS2) and the allelic Menke-Hennekam syndrome, and several primary reports describe independent human probands carrying single-nucleotide/small de novo EP300 variants who have autism spectrum disorder: a Swedish RTS cohort with a de novo EP300 frameshift in a patient with autism (PMID 26788536), two unrelated patients with de novo EP300 exon-20-skipping variants presenting with ASD (PMID 39603792), a de novo missense/delins variant in an adolescent with intellectual disability and ASD (PMID 42569773), and MKHK cohorts with EP300 exon 30/31 variants showing developmental delay and autism (PMID 38553851, 40167301). These are point variants (not multigene CNVs) in independent probands, supporting a causal, syndromic contribution to ASD. Some uncertainty remains because ASD is reported as one variable feature within a broader syndrome rather than as an isolated primary outcome, and the strongest sources are case reports/series rather than ASD-focused genetic studies, hence substantial weight also on "Existing".

Multiple independent human cohort studies report markedly elevated ASD prevalence and characterized ASD phenotypes in individuals with NF1 mutations: PMID 25475362 (n=36 children with NF1, ADOS-2/SRS profiling), PMID 33519543 (n=48 NF1+ASD compared with other RASopathies), and PMID 24101678 (systematic assessment of autism traits across RASopathies), with a systematic review confirming "ample evidence" for NF1 (PMID 38581124). Independently, whole-genome sequencing of Chinese ASD trios lists NF1 among well-known ASD risk genes with damaging variants in probands (PMID 39126614). Supporting human imaging (PMID 31128207) and older locus-association studies (PMID 15389774, 10581497) are weaker or inconsistent, but the syndromic cohort evidence in independent probands is replicated. Animal-model and organoid work (Nf1+/- mice, CRLF3 organoids) adds mechanism but is not required for the human evidence. Some residual probability is assigned to "Existing" because several cohort studies characterize ASD phenotype in clinically diagnosed NF1 rather than reporting molecularly confirmed variant-level data.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo, single-nucleotide/frameshift (not multigene CNV) variants in BRSK2 in probands with autism and neurodevelopmental disorder: PMID 30879638 (nine unrelated probands via GeneMatcher, mostly de novo LoF, with autism and DD/ID), PMID 31452935 (SPARK exome cohort where BRSK2 reached genome-wide significance as an ASD risk gene), PMID 42509346 (52 additional heterozygous cases with functional Drosophila modeling), and PMID 37961520/38519481 (two de novo pdSNVs in BRSK2 among 116 ASD families). Independent case reports add further probands (PMID 37671287; PMID 35754711, which also includes a de novo nonsense variant proband, and PMID 41423339 with functional iPSC evidence for the frameshift). These represent replicated, independent probands with variant-level evidence in humans, supported by convergent zebrafish and Drosophila functional models. Several other listed papers (heroin dependence GWAS, cancer, MS, glomerulonephritis, LKB1 biochemistry) are unrelated to the ASD association and do not detract from this evidence.

Several primary human studies report de novo/loss-of-function CTNNB1 variants in patients whose phenotype includes autistic features: the Spanish CTNNB1 syndrome cohort (PMID 40240530) with 25 genetically confirmed patients of whom ~60% met ASD criteria; the large 404-individual genotype-phenotype cohort (PMID 36083290) and the 127-participant standardized phenotyping study (PMID 40684264); and the Simons Simplex Collection mosaic-mutation analysis (PMID 28867142), which identified CTNNB1 postzygotic mutations in ASD probands. Earlier resequencing work also lists CTNNB1 as a recurrently disrupted gene in ASD/ID (PMID 24387789), and systematic reviews confirm autism features across many independent CTNNB1 probands (PMIDs 39976812, 33179249). These are independent human cohorts with single-gene point variants rather than multigene CNVs, supporting an Established relationship, though the phenotype is usually a broader NDD syndrome with autistic features rather than isolated ASD, which leaves some weight on Existing. Mouse and organoid data (PMIDs 27131348, 39395167) provide converging mechanistic support but are not required for the human evidence.

Multiple independent human cohorts report pathogenic TSC2 variants in probands who also meet criteria for autism spectrum disorder: the Turkish NGS cohort (PMID 39722056) found ASD in 6/22 TSC patients, all carrying TSC2 mutations; the TSC cohort study searching for ASD risk markers (PMID 26631248) assessed ASD prevalence and genotype-related risk; a systematic review of 2,666 patients (PMID 32849171) reported that 85.6% of TSC patients with autism carried TSC2 variants; a candidate-gene association study directly tested TSC2 variants in autistic disorder (PMID 14627686); and a family-based NGS study of ASD families identified TSC2 variants among high-confidence risk genes (PMID 41096937). These are point/sequence variants in a single gene, not multigene CNVs, and come from independent patient series, supporting replication in humans. Some weight remains for "Existing" because several sources are reviews restating known association, and ASD in TSC is a syndromic comorbidity with variable penetrance rather than a fully specific TSC2 phenotype; mouse Tsc1/Tsc2 social-deficit models (PMID 36732866, 26303409) provide supporting biology only.

ZEB2 is unequivocally causal for Mowat-Wilson syndrome, a human neurodevelopmental disorder whose phenotype includes intellectual disability, epilepsy and behavioral features often described as autistic-like (PMID 34199024, 17958891, 39941075). However, none of the listed articles report primary, replicated cohorts of ASD probands in whom point mutations in ZEB2 were identified as the cause of autism itself; the closest human evidence is a small CNV/variant study of 14 probands with autism, ID and self-injurious behavior in which ZEB2 disruption was implicated (PMID 26933844), and CNV-based findings cannot isolate ZEB2 from neighboring genes. The syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype (a recognized ASD-associated syndrome and precursor context) plus this single human report supports "Existing" rather than "Established". Mechanistic/animal work on Zeb2 in neurogenesis, GABAergic transmission and neural crest (PMID 26193487, 30266271, 34356053) provides additional biological plausibility, supporting a residual "Hypothesized" weight.

CNOT3 is the causative gene for "intellectual developmental disorder with speech delay, autism, and dysmorphic facies" (IDDSADF, OMIM #618672), where autism is a defining feature of the syndrome. Multiple independent human cohorts report de novo or inherited point/truncating variants in unrelated probands with autism spectrum features: PMID 31201375 (16 probands with de novo CNOT3 variants and behavioural/neurodevelopmental phenotypes), PMID 40562808 (51 patients from 42 families, with ASD and attention deficits in over half), PMID 36802310 (three unrelated Chinese patients with novel frameshift/splice variants), PMID 32720325 (two unrelated families with autosomal dominant transmission), and PMID 42117603 (two Japanese cases). These are single-gene sequence variants, not multigene CNVs, and are replicated across independent populations, satisfying the criteria for Established. A small residual probability is retained for Existing, since ASD is one variable feature within a broader syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than an isolated ASD diagnosis.

GATAD2B is firmly established as a cause of a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder (GAND/MRD18) with intellectual disability, speech impairment, hypotonia and macrocephaly (PMIDs 23644463, 31949314, 32688057, 25356899), and severe NDD/ID is a recognized context in which autistic features occur; one ASD-focused WES cohort detected a GATAD2B variant among children with ASD (PMID 40642607), and behavioural phenotyping with ADOS has been performed in GATAD2B-related syndrome patients (PMID 28498556). However, the largest clinical series explicitly notes autistic behaviour is uncommon in GAND (PMID 32688057), and no study demonstrates replicated, ASD-specific causation in independent probands, so "Established" is not supported. Supporting biology (NuRD complex, cortical patterning defects in Gatad2b mutant mice, PMIDs 38238293, 31737996) is animal/functional and contributes to the "Hypothesized" weight rather than human evidence. On balance, the evidence best fits "Existing": credible but limited human data linking GATAD2B variants to autistic phenotypes within a broader NDD presentation.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo point variants (nonsense, frameshift, splice, missense) in TRIP12 in probands with autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability. PMID 25418537 identified recurrent de novo TRIP12 mutations in simplex autism probands from a large resequencing cohort; PMID 27848077 reported seven novel TRIP12 mutation-positive individuals of whom 8/11 had ASD; PMID 28251352 documented four inactivating SNVs (mostly de novo) with ID with or without ASD; PMID 32424948 described two further unrelated de novo cases with ASD; and PMID 36747006 delineated 38 individuals with 35 TRIP12 variants, about half with autistic features. These are independent probands with single-gene-resolution variants, supported by methylation episignature evidence (PMID 36430143) and zebrafish functional work, so the causal relationship is replicated and established, with residual uncertainty only because ASD is a variable feature of the broader Clark-Baraitser neurodevelopmental phenotype.

No article in this list reports BRAF variants in ASD probands with its own case-level data; therefore "Established" cannot be supported. The closest human variant evidence is the French exome cohort (PMID 41168819), which identified a pathogenic/likely pathogenic BRAF variant in a child with a severe specific learning disorder — a neurodevelopmental phenotype, but the cohort explicitly excluded ASD and intellectual disability, so it supports at most a limited/adjacent association. The remaining support is mechanistic: upregulated Ras/Raf/ERK1/2 signaling in the BTBR mouse model of autism with B-Raf hyperphosphorylation (PMID 21595826), tuberin/Rheb regulation of B-Raf in TSC, a disorder featuring autism (PMIDs 15150271, 16382052), RAS/MAPK pathway involvement in NF1-associated ASD traits (PMID 30963251), and rodent multi-omics listing BRAF among ASD-relevant genes (PMID 40907684) — all animal or in vitro, i.e., hypothesized. The BRAF mentions in the CSF liquid-biopsy, PHF21A/BHC80, and FXS R-loop papers are incidental or refer to somatic oncogenic/other-gene contexts. Given BRAF's well-known role in the RASopathies (a recognized ASD risk context) but the absence of direct human ASD genetic evidence here, weight is split between Existing and Hypothesized.

Multiple independent human cohorts and case reports demonstrate de novo germline DNMT3A variants in probands with autism spectrum disorder: the 55-patient TBRS cohort found ASD in 51% of individuals with de novo DNMT3A variants (PMID 29900417), a French series of 24 patients further characterized the neurobehavioral phenotype (PMID 38937076), and independent single-proband reports describe novel DNMT3A variants with severe ID and ASD (PMIDs 32435502, 41384217). In addition, whole-genome sequencing of ASD trios identified a damaging de novo DNMT3A mutation in an idiopathic ASD case with aberrant methylation (PMID 27525107), and a candidate-gene association study reported DNMT3A rs2289195 association with ASD (PMID 30786140). Mouse and stem-cell models (PMIDs 33238114, 37952155, 40667376) provide converging mechanistic support but are not the basis of the human evidence. Residual probability is assigned to "Existing" because ASD is a variable feature of a broader syndromic overgrowth/ID disorder rather than an isolated DNMT3A phenotype.

The only report with a GABRA1 variant in a patient explicitly diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder is the single case with a loss-of-function p.(Arg112Gln) variant treated with vinpocetine (PMID 37434477); a GABAA-receptor cohort/genotype–phenotype study (PMID 35718920) describes neurodevelopmental phenotypes broadly but does not establish GABRA1–ASD causation in independent probands. Candidate-gene association studies of GABA receptor subunits in autism cohorts found no significant association for GABRA1 itself (PMIDs 24249596, 16080114), with signals instead at GABRA4/GABRB1/GABRB3. Human post-mortem work shows reduced GABRA1 expression in autism brain regions (PMID 18821008), which is supportive biological/expression evidence rather than variant-level causal evidence, and rodent/MIA studies (PMIDs 29391390, 38950841) are non-human. Most other papers concern epileptic encephalopathies, Dravet syndrome, or JME and merely mention autism as background, so they are citations rather than evidence. This pattern fits "Existing" (limited, non-definitive human evidence) with substantial weight also on "Hypothesized".

De novo PPP3CA variants are firmly established as causing developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE91) and a distinct GoF congenital anomaly syndrome in human patients (PMIDs 28942967, 29432562, 33963760, 40548073). Autism spectrum disorder specifically is reported as a clinical feature within this spectrum, most explicitly in the truncating/missense genotype–phenotype comparison where ASD was a more frequent feature among patients with loss-of-function missense variants (PMID 33963760), and the broader phenotype expansion papers describe severe neurodevelopmental impairment (PMIDs 39305655, 39707491). However, only one report substantively documents ASD as its own result; most others describe epilepsy, intellectual disability, and dysmorphism, with ASD not systematically ascertained, so replicated ASD-specific proband evidence is insufficient for "Established". Supporting biological plausibility comes from synaptic roles of calcineurin (PMID 31357244, AMPAR/PSD complexes in 41127817), but these are mechanistic rather than ASD genetic evidence. Papers about HDAC inhibitors in myeloma, anorexia GWAS, endurance traits, and zebrafish NPC are peripheral or non-ASD.

Several independent human studies report MBD5-specific (not merely multigene CNV) lesions in patients with autistic phenotypes: Talkowski et al. (PMID 21981781) identified 14 alterations, including translocations and small deletions, disrupting MBD5 alone with intellectual disability, epilepsy and autistic features, plus an ASD-associated conserved missense variant (p.Gly79Glu); Cukier et al. (PMID 23055267) sequenced MBD family genes in 287 ASD probands and found ASD-specific MBD5 coding variants segregating in multiplex families; sequencing of balanced chromosomal abnormalities in autism cases also singled out MBD5 as a disrupted locus (PMID 22521361). Additional point-mutation reports (frameshift, nonsense, splice-site) in independent probands/families with autistic behaviors support replication (PMIDs 33427406, 35385942, 33374027, 28807762), and de novo mutation enrichment analyses in NDD trios list MBD5 among significant genes (PMID 31785789). Functional/cellular work (NPC transcriptomics, SH-SY5Y knockouts, circadian pathways) adds mechanistic support but is not needed for the human genetic case. Some residual probability is assigned to "Existing" because much of the ASD phenotype is embedded within a broader MAND/ID-epilepsy syndrome rather than isolated ASD.

There is credible human genetic evidence linking NR3C2 to ASD: a single family in which three affected brothers carried a maternally inherited stop-gain variant (p.Q919X) in NR3C2 (PMID 32064789), and a whole-genome sequencing study of multiplex families implicating recurrent structural deletions of the NR3C2 promoter, supported by zebrafish nr3c2 loss-of-function causing sleep and social deficits (PMID 31398340). A further WGS study reports enrichment of noncoding regulatory disruptions near ASD genes including NR3C2, but largely restates prior association as background (PMID 26749308), and an expression-mapping study lists NR3C2 among high-confidence ASD genes without new variant data (PMID 42499009). This does not meet the bar for Established, since only one study reports a coding variant in a single family, while the other rests on promoter/structural variants and an animal model; the remaining articles concern pseudohypoaldosteronism, hypertension, PCOS, or suicide/depression and are unrelated to ASD. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with residual probability for "Established" (given replication across two independent ASD cohorts) and "Hypothesized" (if the coding-variant family is deemed insufficient).

Several human studies report SCN1A point variants in ASD probands within their own results: O'Roak et al. exome sequencing of sporadic ASD trios identified a severe de novo SCN1A mutation (PMID 21572417) and a follow-up screen of 1,703 probands found additional de novo protein-altering SCN1A mutations (PMID 22495309); deep sequencing of postmortem ASD brains found recurrent deleterious SCN1A mutations enriched over controls (PMID 26637798). Additional cohorts support the link, including SCN1A as the most frequent gene in Chinese children with co-occurring epilepsy and ASD (PMID 31139143), targeted sequencing in NDD/ID-EP cohorts (PMID 38081334), and familial/consanguineous WGS studies (PMID 35190550, 34368859). Counterbalancing this, much of the ASD phenotype arises secondary to Dravet syndrome/DEE, and the earliest candidate-gene study of familial autism found only variants of uncertain significance (PMID 12610651), so some weight remains on "Existing." Animal-model and mechanistic reviews (PMIDs 30838929, 33971653, 41162233) support biological plausibility but are not primary human genetic evidence.

The strongest evidence is a single cohort study (PMID 31353024) reporting 15 individuals from 12 unrelated families with heterozygous pathogenic DLL1 sequence variants, in which autism spectrum disorder was one of the most common features — this is credible human variant-level evidence, but it is one report and cannot alone constitute replication. The other supporting human papers are terminal 6q26-q27 deletion series (PMIDs 36935482, 34894355, 35707784), which are multigene copy number changes and therefore cannot isolate DLL1, and they largely cite the DLL1 variant work as background. Independent supportive human evidence comes from placental methylome studies reporting replicated differential methylation at DLL1 in prospective autism cohorts (PMIDs 28018572, 41120033), which is epigenetic/association rather than variant-based. Remaining articles concern Notch biology in skeleton, cancer, immunity, or non-ASD skeletal phenotypes and contribute only mechanistic plausibility. Overall, evidence is credible but not yet replicated at the variant level, so "Existing" is the best fit.

Human evidence linking SRCAP variants to ASD exists but is limited: a single case report of a child with SRCAP-related Floating-Harbor syndrome who also met ASD criteria (PMID 41777507), and a case with co-occurring de novo SHANK3 and SRCAP frameshift variants where the SHANK3 variant confounds attribution (PMID 41282476). The largest human cohort of truncating non-FLHS SRCAP variants (PMID 33909990, 33 individuals) describes developmental delay with behavioral and psychiatric problems, a neurodevelopmental phenotype strongly overlapping ASD, supporting "Existing" but not explicitly replicating ASD diagnoses across independent probands. The strongest mechanistic support is a mouse model (Srcap+/- mice with autistic-like behaviors via Satb2/H2A.Z; PMID 38733588), which is animal work and therefore counts toward "Hypothesized," alongside chromatin-remodeling/H2A.Z biology relevant to neurodevelopment (PMIDs 41278978, 27208210). Because I cannot cite at least two independent human studies whose own results demonstrate SRCAP variants causing ASD specifically, "Established" is not warranted, and most probability rests on "Existing."

Multiple human studies report point/frameshift de novo variants in TBL1XR1 in independent ASD probands from their own data: PMID 23160955 found recurrent disruptive de novo mutations in TBL1XR1 among 2446 ASD probands (estimating contribution to ~1% of sporadic ASD together with other genes); PMID 25102098 reported a de novo missense variant (p.Gly70Asp) in a girl with West syndrome and autistic features; PMID 32524419 reported a novel de novo frameshift (p.T130Sfs*14) in a patient with ASD; PMID 33527360 reported a de novo missense variant with autism plus Pierpont-overlapping features; and PMID 40778144 identified a pathogenic TBL1XR1 variant in a previously unsolved autism family via long-read sequencing. A large trio cohort analysis (PMID 41646820) further found TBL1XR1 exome-wide significant for de novo variant enrichment in females with autism, supporting statistical replication. Copy-number cases (PMIDs 28574232, 24891185, 25425123) are supportive but not counted as gene-specific evidence. Some residual probability is assigned to Existing because ASD is often one feature within a broader TBL1XR1 neurodevelopmental/Pierpont phenotype rather than an isolated ASD diagnosis.

The literature robustly establishes IRF2BPL as a cause of a severe neurodevelopmental/neurodegenerative spectrum (NEDAMSS, DEE, progressive myoclonus epilepsy, dystonia), but autism per se is only mentioned in passing as background (e.g., PMID 39843638 states pathogenic variants "have been reported to cause ... autistic spectrum disorder") rather than demonstrated in the studies' own results. No article in this set reports ASD-diagnosed probands with IRF2BPL variants as a primary finding, and the psychiatric review (PMID 39031186) describes catatonia, affective and psychotic symptoms plus "developmental disorders" in a minority of cases without dedicated ASD phenotyping. Because IRF2BPL variants clearly cause global developmental delay/intellectual disability with regression and loss of speech—phenotypes strongly linked to and often comorbid with ASD in humans—the evidence best fits "Existing" rather than "Established," which would require at least two independent human studies reporting ASD probands in their own results. Some probability remains for "Hypothesized" (biological plausibility via WNT-signaling and neuronal maintenance, supported by fly models in PMID 30057031 and zebrafish in PMID 38481258) and a small residual for "Novel."

Multiple independent human genetic studies report ZNF292 point/loss-of-function variants in ASD probands with their own primary data: PMID 27824329 identified recurrent de novo likely gene-disrupting ZNF292 mutations in a Chinese ASD cohort, and PMID 31723249 delineated a cohort of individuals with de novo and inherited ZNF292 variants causing a neurodevelopmental disorder with prominent autism spectrum features. Additional independent replication comes from the expanded ACGC cohort (PMID 30564305), a consanguineous ASD family WGS study (PMID 35190550), a Pakistani ASD cohort (PMID 38649688), and a Turkish ASD cohort (PMID 41420732), all reporting ZNF292 variants in ASD-affected individuals. Human stem-cell functional work (PMID 40257863) provides supportive mechanistic evidence but is not needed for the genetic case. The only caveats are that some reports are single VUS-level findings or multigene deletions (PMID 29904178), which do not count, but the point-variant evidence in independent probands is sufficient for Established.

The strongest direct evidence is the trio-WES study (PMID 34948243), which reported a pathogenic ACTB variant among a cohort of syndromic ID/ASD patients — a single human study, insufficient for "Established". The 7p22.1 microduplication case with autism features (PMID 25893121) is a multigene CNV and cannot single out ACTB, and the 7p22.1 refinement paper (PMID 27866048) likewise concerns contiguous-gene duplications. The remaining literature ties ACTB variants to Baraitser-Winter cerebrofrontofacial syndrome, loss-of-function neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability, syndromic thrombocytopenia, and Becker's nevus (PMIDs 29220674, 27625340, 30315159, 31898838, 41062261, 29158550) — these establish a robust neurodevelopmental/ID phenotype (a phenotype strongly linked to and frequently comorbid with ASD) but rarely document autism itself as the assessed outcome. Therefore evidence supports at least "Existing" (human variant-level data in ID/ASD probands and ASD-associated neurodevelopmental syndromes), with insufficient replicated ASD-specific proband data for "Established".

The primary evidence is PMID 31616000, which reports 20 patients with likely gene-disrupting TANC2 variants presenting with autism, intellectual disability, and language/motor delay across multiple independent probands and families — a strong, single-gene-resolved human dataset.
