Additional independent human reports with point/truncating variants include PMID 39344613 (two children with TANC2 variants and neurodevelopmental disorder), PMID 42397682 (expanded electroclinical spectrum of TANC2-related disorder, described as intellectual developmental disorder with autistic features and language delay), PMID 40110879 and PMID 34861844 (de novo/truncating variants with DEE and Lennox-Gastaut phenotypes within the same NDD spectrum). Supporting mechanistic work (zebrafish knockout with autism-like behavior, PMID 36534563; postsynaptic scaffold/KIF1A interaction, PMID 30021165; Tanc2 mouse models, PMID 34964047) reinforces biological plausibility but is non-human. The microdeletion case (PMID 33160097) does not count as gene-specific evidence; nonetheless, replication of single-gene disruptive variants in independent probands supports Established, with residual weight to Existing because the autism phenotype is embedded in a broader NDD/epilepsy spectrum largely anchored on one large cohort.

Most of the corpus concerns 17p11.2 deletions/duplications (Smith-Magenis and Potocki-Lupski syndromes), where autistic features are common but the multigene CNV cannot isolate RAI1 from neighboring genes (PMID 20981775, 17357070, 17334992, 20188345). Single-gene, sequence-level human evidence exists but is sparse: one de novo RAI1 missense variant (p.R1147Q) in a patient with autism and atypical SMS with functional validation (PMID 29794985), a multiplex Indian family with exome-identified RAI1 (and FLII) variants in siblings with autism/SMS (PMID 39634244), and a regulatory enhancer SNP (rs4925102) showing allele-specific RAI1 expression plus case-control and near-significant TDT association with ASD (PMID 38674394). This constitutes credible but limited and only partially independent human evidence—the family study implicates two genes, and the association study is modest—so replication of unambiguous RAI1-specific causation for ASD is not firmly demonstrated. Reviews (PMID 40437981, 21629438, 35205380) largely restate the association as background rather than provide new probands. Therefore "Existing" is most probable, with a substantial minority weight on "Established."

The only article directly linking AP2S1 to autism is the zebrafish study (PMID 38550987), which describes ap2s1 as an "autism-linked" gene as background but generates its own evidence in a vertebrate animal model of habituation and behavioral selection, not in human patients — this supports Hypothesized. No paper in this list reports autism-affected human probands or families with AP2S1 variants, so Established cannot be supported. Human AP2S1 variant studies here (PMIDs 29325022, 41501259) concern familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia type 3; one case notes persistent neurodevelopmental difficulties, which gives weak, indirect human support for a neurodevelopmental phenotype (some weight to Existing). Other reports are murine loss-of-function models (PMID 29479578), calcium-signaling reviews (PMID 41597215), or unrelated virology (PMID 40156834), which contribute biological plausibility at best. Overall the evidence is biologically suggestive but not demonstrated in human autism cohorts.

Multiple human studies report single-nucleotide/frameshift MED13 variants in independent probands where ASD is part of the phenotype: the GeneMatcher cohort of 13 individuals with mostly de novo MED13 protein-altering variants (PMID 29740699) listed autism spectrum disorder among recurrent features; a de novo frameshift variant (c.4880del) in a girl evaluated for ASD (PMID 38528425); a de novo missense variant in a Kabuki-like patient within the ASD/ADHD-associated MED13 spectrum (PMID 33258286); and a de novo MED13 variant identified in an ASD cohort from Qatar (PMID 38572415). An additional single-case report describes a heterozygous MED13 variant of uncertain significance in a child with ASD (PMID 38854223), which is supportive but weaker. Thus the causal link is to a MED13-related neurodevelopmental disorder in which ASD is a frequent but variable component, so the evidence sits between Established and Existing, with de novo point variants in multiple independent probands favoring Established. No CNV-only evidence was required to reach this conclusion, and animal/in vitro data (e.g., Med13l mice, mitochondrial fibroblast studies) were not counted.

Human variant-level evidence linking TAOK1 to autism comes from PMID 37656623, which reports a de novo frameshift variant in TAOK1 in a Chinese ASD cohort (with supporting mouse haploinsufficiency work), and from the large sex-stratified de novo variant analyses of >41,000 autism trios (PMIDs 41646820, 42032772) in which TAOK1 reached exome-wide significance in females with autism—though these two trio reports appear to be the same dataset/author and thus may not constitute truly independent replication. The remaining human reports (PMIDs 31230721, 33565190, 35091509, 38443934) firmly establish TAOK1 de novo/truncating variants as causal for a neurodevelopmental disorder with behavioral abnormalities, a phenotype strongly overlapping but not strictly equivalent to ASD. Functional and model work (PMIDs 36595571, 40552535) supports plausible mechanism (membrane remodeling, neuronal maturation, ciliary/NPC biology) but is not itself human genetic evidence for ASD. Given credible human proband-level ASD evidence from at least one dedicated cohort plus a large trio-based statistical association, the case sits between Established and Existing, leaning slightly to Established.

The literature robustly establishes CLTC as a cause of a human neurodevelopmental disorder (intellectual developmental disorder 56) with de novo missense, frameshift, in-frame and splice variants in multiple independent probands (PMIDs 26822784, 31776469, 34230591, 37196051, 29100083), but none of these abstracts report autism spectrum disorder as the studied outcome — they describe developmental delay, ID, epilepsy, "behavioral problems," parkinsonism and brain malformations. ASD is therefore supported only indirectly, via the strongly ASD-linked ID/NDD phenotype and clathrin-mediated synaptic vesicle recycling biology, which fits "Existing" at best rather than "Established" for ASD specifically. The only abstract explicitly about autism (PMID 25343687) concerns NCS-1 R102Q, a different gene, and the Zbtb18/NAFLD and integrin αvβ6 papers are non-neuronal, non-ASD contexts. A COS exome study (PMID 36645932) implicates CLTC in a psychiatric phenotype, adding modest weight. Hence points concentrate on Existing with substantial mass on Hypothesized.

Direct human genetic evidence with patient variants is present in multiple independent reports: Sands et al. (PMID 31177578) described a cohort of individuals with de novo KCNQ3 gain-of-function variants presenting with autism and developmental disability; Gilling et al. (PMID 23596459) reported a de novo translocation truncating KCNQ3 in a boy with childhood autism plus three unrelated individuals carrying p.P574S with functional validation; Wang et al. (PMID 32580997) identified a de novo KCNQ3 frameshift in a child with autism traits; and additional independent case reports (PMIDs 42255468, 42024975) and large-scale targeted sequencing of NDD cohorts (PMID 33004838) provide replication across probands. These are human, single-gene (not CNV-based) findings in independent probands, supported by convergent electrophysiological mechanism studies. Points are retained for "Existing" because much of the ASD evidence comes from small case series and mixed NDD phenotypes rather than large, ASD-specific replication cohorts.

No article in this list reports its own cohort of ASD probands carrying single-gene RORB variants; the strongest human genetic data (PMID 27352968, 38165337, 32162308, 39897619, 38088023) concern generalized/photosensitive epilepsy, eyelid myoclonia, and intellectual disability, with ASD mentioned only as background or as a feature of multigenic 9q21.13 microdeletions (PMID 24355400, 30102487, 40692708), which cannot isolate RORB. The mouse allelic-series paper (PMID 37300435) restates ASD susceptibility as known background and provides only animal-model behavioral/UPR data, which supports Hypothesized rather than human evidence. The Mendelian randomization study (PMID 38671846) tested autism but found RORB significant only for schizophrenia, and the orphan GPCR review (PMID 40538218) is a narrative synthesis implicating RORβ in ASD without primary variant data. Thus the balance favors "Existing" (autistic behaviour within RORB-related neurodevelopmental phenotypes and deletion syndromes) with substantial weight on "Hypothesized" given the largely indirect, background-level nature of the ASD link.

Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in SON cause Zhu-Tokita-Takenouchi-Kim (ZTTK) syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder whose described neurological spectrum explicitly includes autism spectrum disorder (PMID 36387043, two unrelated probands with novel de novo SON variants; PMID 34521999, 52 individuals with SON variants and broad HPO-coded neurodevelopmental phenotypes). Additional human evidence comes from a diagnostic gene-panel study of adolescents/adults with ID/ASD in which a pathogenic SON single-nucleotide variant was identified (PMID 34363551), and from a craniosynostosis trio-exome study reporting genome-wide-significant damaging de novo variants in SON and noting overlap of these risk genes with autism (PMID 37086723). Thus direct human variant-level evidence exists in independent probands, though ASD is reported as one variable feature within a broader syndrome rather than as the primary phenotype in dedicated ASD cohorts, which tempers a full "Established" call. Functional/mechanistic work (splicing regulator, nuclear speckle core, zebrafish models: PMIDs 24789761, 33095160, 33630943) supports biological plausibility but is not human phenotype evidence.

Two independent primary human studies report de novo, single-gene CIC variants in probands whose phenotype includes autism spectrum disorder: PMID 28288114 identified five individuals with de novo heterozygous truncating CIC mutations sharing intellectual disability, ADHD and ASD, and PMID 35165976 reported additional novel CIC variants including a de novo CIC-L frameshift in an individual with speech delay, ID and ASD, with functional validation of loss of repressor activity. A subsequent review (PMID 39596625) summarizes the broader CIC-related neurodevelopmental disorder cohort in which ASD is a recurrent feature, supporting replication across probands. The SLC25A1/CIC autism paper (PMID 35203088) uses "CIC" as the citrate carrier acronym and is dismissed as a homonym, and the numerous glioma/oligodendroglioma papers are cancer-focused and irrelevant to ASD; the multigene 19q13.2 deletion report (PMID 34117072) cannot isolate CIC. Some residual probability is assigned to Existing because ASD appears as one feature within a broader syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than as isolated ASD.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report sequence-level (not merely CNV) SHANK2 variants in ASD probands: Berkel et al. (PMID 20473310) identified a de novo nonsense mutation plus rare inherited variants by sequencing 396 ASD cases versus 659 controls; Leblond et al. (PMID 22346768) independently sequenced SHANK2 in 455 additional patients and found significant enrichment of deleterious variants (OR 2.37) with functional validation; the SHANK meta-analysis/screen (PMID 25188300) found truncating SHANK2 mutations in ~0.17% of ASD cases across thousands of patients. Further independent clinical cohorts and case series (PMIDs 40307697, 32987185, 38075274, 36450866) describe de novo protein-truncating and missense SHANK2 variants in patients with ASD/neurodevelopmental disorder, and a case-control association study (PMID 29934968) supports common-variant association. Human iPSC-derived neuron work (PMID 30911184) provides mechanistic support in patient-derived cells. The evidence is replicated across independent probands and families in humans, supporting an Established relationship, with residual probability for "Existing" given the variable penetrance and broader NDD phenotype.

Recurrent germline gain-of-function point variants in SMAD4 (p.Ile500Val/Thr/Met, p.Arg496Cys) cause Myhre syndrome, in which autism/ASD-like behaviour is a recognized neurodevelopmental manifestation. Independent human cohorts and probands document this: a molecularly confirmed p.Arg496Cys patient with standardized-instrument–confirmed High Functioning ASD (PMID 30968316), the 47-patient MGH deep-phenotyping natural history cohort (PMID 38779990), the 105-patient international registry reporting autism (PMID 41216670), seven Brazilian patients including one with an ASD diagnosis (PMID 39810609), and additional case reports (PMIDs 36373990, 35386616). These are single-gene point variants in multiple unrelated probands, supporting a causal, syndromic gene–phenotype relationship rather than a copy-number or purely background citation. Some weight remains on "Existing" because much ASD documentation is descriptive/self-reported within syndrome series rather than from dedicated ASD-focused genetic studies; human iPSC assembloid CRISPR screening (PMID 37758944) adds supportive mechanistic evidence for interneuron development.

Only one article reports its own patient-level evidence directly linking a DNM1 variant to autism: PMID 37132416, a single de novo p.(Leu665Pro) GED-domain variant in a man with autism, intellectual disability, and mild epilepsy. The remaining DNM1 literature centers on developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, severe intellectual disability, and refractory seizures (PMIDs 28667181, 37248033, 34172529, 36413998, 42006794), with autism mentioned only as a variable comorbidity or as background in reviews of synaptic vesicle cycling disorders (PMID 32738165). Because a single human proband cannot support replication, and multi-gene DNM-database/statistical papers (PMIDs 25849321, 29754769) merely aggregate de novo mutation data without singling out DNM1 as an ASD risk gene, the evidence best fits "Existing"—one credible human report plus association with a severe NDD phenotype commonly accompanied by autistic features. Some probability remains for "Hypothesized" since much of the mechanistic support (synaptic vesicle fission, GABAergic dysfunction, mouse fitful model) is biological rather than ASD-specific genetic evidence.

SMARCA2 is unequivocally causal for Nicolaides-Baraitser syndrome (PMID 26468571, 25169058, 38721580), a BAF-complex neurodevelopmental disorder with ID, seizures and behavioral abnormalities, but these cohort reports characterize ID/NCBRS rather than demonstrating ASD as the phenotype in independent probands. The strongest direct human evidence linking SMARCA2 to ASD is the Japanese case-control targeted sequencing study, which found significant enrichment of rare missense/pathogenic-predicted variants in BAF genes (SMARCA2 among the four sequenced) in ASD patients (PMID 35699097) — credible but limited, gene-set-level and unreplicated for SMARCA2 alone. Other papers (PMID 28824374, 25954173, 24140580, 25169878) restate BAF/nBAF involvement in ASD as background, which constitutes citation rather than primary evidence, and the iPSC heat-shock expression work (PMID 24736721) and organoid screen (PMID 37704762) provide mechanistic/in vitro support only. Therefore "Existing" is the best fit, with residual probability on "Established" (given syndromic autistic features in NCBRS) and "Hypothesized."

Multiple independent human clinical studies report intragenic SOX5 single-nucleotide variants and gene-disrupting rearrangements in patients whose phenotype includes autism spectrum disorder or autistic features: the Spanish/literature cohort of 111 LAMSHF patients (PMID 37702321) explicitly lists ASD among the recurrent features, the 16-patient cohort with truncating/missense SNVs describes autistic behavioral phenotypes (PMID 36861937), the expanded clinical/genetic spectrum study includes point mutations (PMID 31578471), a de novo balanced translocation truncating SOX5 intron 4 produced autistic features (PMID 29477873), and an individual de novo LAMSHF case with formally diagnosed ASD is reported (PMID 41531626). These are independent probands with variants that pinpoint SOX5 rather than multigene deletions, supporting a causal role, although ASD is a variable rather than obligate feature of Lamb-Shaffer syndrome, which tempers full confidence. Additional supportive human data include SOX5 dysregulation in post-mortem ASD cortex (PMID 27919067) and its inclusion among ASD-implicated neocortical transcription factors (PMID 24290386), plus its listing as a de novo intellectual disability gene (PMID 27479843). I therefore split weight mainly between Established and Existing.

Independent human reports describe de novo SYNCRIP variants in patients with neurodevelopmental disorder that includes autistic features: PMID 34157790 presents three new individuals with novel de novo variants (autistic features in two, ID in all), and PMID 33874999 clinically characterizes patients with rare deleterious HNRNP-family variants including SYNCRIP with shared NDD/ASD phenotypes; PMID 27479843 (de novo mutation meta-analysis of 2,104 trios) statistically implicates SYNCRIP in ID, and a GeneReviews-style entry (PMID 42160654) codifies a SYNCRIP-related neurodevelopmental disorder. This supports at least Existing and plausibly Established, though ASD is a variable feature within a broader ID/NDD phenotype rather than the core, replicated diagnosis, and the 6q deletion cohort (PMID 29904178) is multigenic and cannot isolate SYNCRIP. Additional support comes from human genome-sequencing of ASD probands (PMID 30504930) and mechanistic neuronal/cortical studies (PMIDs 33030396, 39776340) showing SYNCRIP regulates neurogenesis and that pathogenic human mutations impair its function, which underpins biological plausibility. Points therefore concentrate on Established/Existing with a small residual for Hypothesized.

The provided literature robustly establishes PUF60 haploinsufficiency as a cause of Verheij syndrome/PUF60-related neurodevelopmental disorder, with de novo single-nucleotide and frameshift variants in multiple independent human probands (PMIDs 27804958, 28327570, 36367278, 37303278, 38396730, 28990276). However, none of these abstracts report a formal autism spectrum disorder diagnosis; they describe developmental delay, intellectual disability, and "behavioral" or "social-emotional" difficulties (PMID 38396730), which are recognized correlates/comorbid features of ASD rather than direct ASD ascertainment. Because the phenotype is a broad neurodevelopmental disorder strongly linked to, but not explicitly diagnosed as, ASD in these reports, "Existing" is the best fit, with meaningful weight on "Hypothesized" given the indirect, non-ASD-specific phenotyping. "Established" cannot be supported since no two independent studies here document ASD itself in probands with PUF60 point variants, and CNV-based reports (24140112, 26437074) cannot isolate PUF60 from neighboring genes.

Several human studies report single-gene (non-CNV) PHF21A variants in patients whose phenotype includes autism/autistic features: PMID 31649809 describes seven unrelated individuals with PHF21A disruption and "neurobehavioral problems including autism"; PMID 30487643 reports three de novo truncating variants with ASD recognized in one case; PMID 38572415 identifies a de novo PHF21A variant in an ASD proband from a Middle Eastern cohort; and PMID 37904995 references an autism-associated missense variant (c.1285G>A), further characterized functionally in PMID 40622422. These are independent probands with gene-specific variants, supporting more than a single-report association. However, ASD is a variable, secondary feature of the broader PHF21A/IDDBCS syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than a consistently replicated primary outcome, and much of the mechanistic work is in vitro or zebrafish, so full "Established" status for ASD specifically is arguable. Points are therefore split mainly between Established and Existing, with little weight for Hypothesized or Novel.

Multiple human cohort studies report truncating, splice and missense CAMTA1 variants causing a neurodevelopmental syndrome (CECBA) with developmental delay, intellectual disability and prominent behavioral problems (PMID 38044714, 33131045, 32157189, 33677721), and a clinical cohort of progressive myoclonus ataxia including a CAMTA1 case documents autism spectrum disorder in 27% of patients (PMID 38844245), though ASD there is not gene-specific. Biological plausibility is strong: CAMTA1 is a calmodulin-binding activity-dependent transcription factor required for long-term memory and neuronal excitability in mice (PMID 27194798) and central to nervous system function (PMID 35949142). However, no paper in this list presents ASD as a systematically ascertained, replicated primary outcome of point variants in independent CAMTA1 probands; autism is reported within a broader "behavioral problems" category, so replicated causal evidence specifically for ASD is not demonstrated. Therefore "Existing" is the most likely correct label, with residual probability on "Established" (given several independent SNV cohorts with neurobehavioral phenotypes) and on "Hypothesized" (if ASD co-mentions are considered incidental to the ataxia/ID phenotype).

The only human genetic evidence is a single family case report of a 350 kb 20q11.21 microduplication segregating with ASD/autistic traits and mood disorders (PMID: 38076678), which includes TM9SF4 among several genes; a multigenic CNV in one family cannot establish causality for this specific gene, so "Established" is excluded. However, it is a credible human report that also cites prior implication of TM9SF4 in ASD risk, which best fits "Existing" as limited, non-definitive evidence. The CRISPR screen paper (PMID: 36661306) is an in vitro study of epithelial polarity and apical transport with no ASD relevance, contributing at most weak biological plausibility. Some probability remains for "Hypothesized" (if the CNV is judged too diffuse to count as gene-level association) and a smaller amount for "Novel" given the incidental nature of the co-mentions.

POU3F3 de novo variants cause Snijders Blok–Fisher syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder in which autism/autistic features are a recurrent component. Primary human evidence with patient variants includes PMID 37165752 (28 individuals from 26 families, mostly de novo variants, with autism explicitly reported and enriched among truncating variants, plus in silico structural support) and PMID 33645921 (novel de novo missense variant with autistic features), with the founding cohort PMID 31303265 establishing pathogenicity of 19 heterozygous disruptions through functional assays, though it emphasizes DD/ID and speech impairment rather than ASD per se. Additional single cases (PMID 37593446, 40472468, 42578133, 41491245) replicate the gene–syndrome link but focus on other features. Because ASD is described as a feature within a well-delineated monogenic syndrome supported by multiple independent probands, "Established" is plausible, but since only one large cohort explicitly quantifies autism, substantial probability remains on "Existing". Animal/in vitro work (PMIDs 39878593, 32958671, 27003440) supports biological plausibility only.

ZBTB20 single-nucleotide de novo missense variants unambiguously cause Primrose syndrome (PMIDs 25017102, 27061120, 29681083, 29737001, 30637921, 32266967), a neurodevelopmental syndrome whose phenotype includes intellectual disability, behavioral abnormalities and autistic traits/autism, so the gene is best described as a syndromic-ASD gene rather than a classic idiopathic ASD gene. Direct, per-proband ASD documentation attributable to a point variant is less consistently reported: several Primrose series list "autistic traits" or "behavioral issues" as background/phenotypic descriptors, and one clinical panel study identified a pathogenic ZBTB20 variant in an adult ID/ASD cohort (PMID 34363551). Additional supportive human data come from 3q13.31 microdeletions in ASD patients (PMIDs 23032108, 23878096, 25062845), but these are multigenic CNVs and cannot isolate ZBTB20. Functional work in rat neurons showing autism-risk ZBTB20 variants alter spine morphology (PMID 30281617) and the Zbtb20+/- mouse displaying ASD-like behaviors (PMID 41729076) are non-human and support mechanism only. Overall the evidence sits between Existing and Established, with a lean toward Existing because ASD itself is a variable feature rather than the replicated, variant-anchored endpoint.

Human genetic evidence comes from at least two independent primary studies: the Chinese ACGC targeted-sequencing cohort reported recurrent de novo likely gene-disrupting mutations in WDFY3 among the most prevalent ASD risk genes (PMID 27824329), replicated/expanded in ACGC phase II (PMID 30564305), and an independent international series of 13 probands with mostly de novo truncating/missense WDFY3 variants showed significant de novo enrichment with autism spectrum disorder/ADHD among the overlapping phenotypes (PMID 31327001). Additional single-patient reports support haploinsufficiency causing neurodevelopmental disorders with macrocephaly (PMID 39614649), and extensive mouse/Drosophila work provides convergent mechanistic support (PMIDs 25198012, 35733184, 32609087, 30054502). The main caveat is that the core clinical phenotype is neurodevelopmental delay/ID with altered brain size, with ASD as a frequent but not obligate feature, which leaves some probability for "Existing." Overall the replicated de novo variant evidence in independent ASD probands favors Established.

The strongest primary human evidence is PMID 28051072, which reports a novel homozygous GRIN1 missense variant (p.Asp227His) in two consanguineous sibs with severe intellectual disability and autistic features, and notes a previously published second family with p.Arg217Trp and a similar phenotype — but that second family is only cited, not reported here. PMID 41420732 adds a GRIN1 variant of uncertain significance in an ASD cohort (1.6% of cases), which supports but does not establish causality. Other papers (38836461, 32712275, 31429998, 39535073, 40994429) list autism among GRIN1-associated neurodevelopmental phenotypes as background while their own results are functional/in vitro characterizations, so they count as citation rather than independent proband evidence; notably PMID 22833210 found no truncating GRIN1 variants in ASD cases. Because only one study in this list reports its own ASD-relevant GRIN1 probands (a single family), the evidence best fits "Existing," with residual probability for "Established" given the broader GRIN1-NDD literature including autism features.

Human genetic evidence links TCF12 to neurodevelopmental disorders: the large-scale targeted sequencing study (PMID 33004838) identified TCF12 among genes with significant de novo/ultra-rare disruptive mutation burden in >16,000 NDD cases including thousands of autism trios, and provided genotype–phenotype correlations for TCF12. The Chinese ASD whole-genome study (PMID 42463903) lists TCF12 among ASD risk genes, though its own primary novel findings center on other genes. Clinical cohorts of TCF12 pathogenic-variant carriers with craniosynostosis report elevated social communication difficulties (~42%) and one case with regression of language and social communication (PMIDs 33904513, 42098324), supporting an ASD-related phenotype but not a definitive, replicated ASD-causal role. Other listed papers concern craniosynostosis, Kallmann syndrome, oligodendroglioma, or mouse suture/oligodendrocyte biology (PMIDs 34878091, 32266943), which are biologically suggestive but not ASD-specific human evidence. Because ASD-specific proband-level replication is limited (one large NDD burden study plus supportive cohort/list-level data), "Existing" is most likely, with meaningful probability for "Established."

De novo variants in CSNK2A1 cause Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome (OCNDS), a human autosomal dominant disorder in which autism spectrum disorder is a recurrent phenotypic feature. Human patient-based evidence with identified variants includes the original de novo missense/splice cohort (PMID 27048600), the Chinese case plus systematic review reporting autism in 8 of 28 characterized patients (PMID 31060130), further independent probands and phenotype expansions (PMIDs 34038195, 38444259, 39497417, 30655572, 40677894), and inherited familial cases (PMID 37491870). These are independent probands/families with single-gene point variants, supporting a causal syndromic link in which ASD is a frequent component. Uncertainty remains as to whether ASD is a core, consistently replicated outcome versus a variable behavioral feature of the broader neurodevelopmental syndrome, so substantial weight is retained for "Existing"; network/omics work (PMID 42330854) is supportive but not primary genetic evidence.

Primary human genetic evidence comes from Lim et al. (PMID 25284784), where clustering of de novo frameshift indels in unrelated ASD probands identified KMT2E (MLL5) as an ASD-associated gene, and from O'Donnell-Luria et al. (PMID 31079897), which reported 38 individuals in 36 families with mostly de novo truncating KMT2E variants, one-quarter of whom met criteria for autism (autism more frequent in males). These two independent single-gene (non-CNV) studies satisfy replication. Further independent cohorts add support: a second multinational ODLURO cohort explicitly listing ASD susceptibility (PMID 34321323), a novel patient cohort with loss-of-function variants (PMID 39709003), and deep behavioral phenotyping showing two-thirds of ODLURO participants in the moderate-to-severe range on the SRS-2 (PMID 41137515). Remaining uncertainty reflects that autism is one variable feature within a broader neurodevelopmental syndrome rather than an isolated ASD phenotype, which supports some probability for "Existing".

Most of the retrieved Noonan syndrome/RASopathy papers use "ASD" as an acronym for atrial septal defect (e.g., PMID 23918763, 40332000), a homonym that must be dismissed, and the remainder simply describe PTPN11 mutation spectra and cardiac/growth phenotypes without autism outcomes. The one directly relevant human study (PMID 41074228) measures autism spectrum disorder-related traits and correlates them with genotype within PTPN11 in Noonan syndrome/NSML, providing credible but single-report, trait-level evidence rather than replicated causal demonstration. PMID 34746237 implicates PTPN11 in an ASD peripheral-blood ceRNA/expression network, which is human but expression-based rather than variant-based, supporting a biological/pathway rationale. No two independent studies report PTPN11 variants causing autism in separate probands or families, so Established cannot be supported; the RAS-MAPK pathway's known role in neurodevelopment keeps some weight on Hypothesized.

Direct human genetic evidence comes from PMID 33658631, which reports de novo and inherited deleterious RFX3 (and other RFX family) variants in multiple independent probands with ASD, ID, and ADHD, and is supported by independent single-patient reports: PMID 37717291 (RFX3 mutation with infantile epileptic spasms syndrome and ASD) and PMID 40200712 (long-read sequencing identifying RFX3 haploinsufficiency in an adolescent with autism and ID). These are sequence-level variants in distinct probands, satisfying replication rather than multigene deletions. Mechanistic human iPSC/organoid work (PMID 40060598), interneuron development studies (PMID 38827400), and post-mortem cortical multi-omics implicating RFX3 networks in autism (PMID 41959023) provide convergent biological support. Residual probability is assigned to "Existing" since the case-level replication is still relatively small and partly from single case reports.

Direct human variant-level evidence exists: PMID 34813034 reports seven novel de novo/missense SMARCA4 variants in eight Chinese pediatric probands, seven of whom had autistic or likely autistic features rather than typical Coffin-Siris syndrome; PMID 28714951 identified damaging postzygotic mosaic SMARCA4 mutations in ASD probands from a large trio cohort; and PMID 33799280 describes an individual with ASD carrying a de novo germline SMARCA4 missense mutation (p.Arg1203Cys). PMID 35699097 adds a Japanese case–control burden analysis of rare missense variants across BAF genes including SMARCA4, though the signal is gene-set rather than SMARCA4-specific. Supporting mechanistic and background work (BAF/nBAF complex in neurodevelopment, Brg1 mouse synapse and hydrocephalus studies, organoid CRISPR screens) is non-human or in vitro and only supports Hypothesized. Because the strongest single-gene proband series is essentially one cohort plus a single case report and a mosaic-mutation screen, the evidence sits between clearly Existing and near-Established, with SMARCA4 also frequently cited as a high-confidence ASD gene; a copy-number deletion spanning SMARCA4 (PMID 37076741) does not count as gene-specific evidence.

Two human reports provide direct variant-level evidence linking TUBB2A to autistic phenotypes: PMID 33776625 describes three patients with a novel de novo p.Gly98Arg TUBB2A variant, some of whom carried a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder, and PMID 34363551 identified a pathogenic single-nucleotide TUBB2A variant in an adult ascertained through an ID/ASD gene panel. Most other papers (PMIDs 24702957, 32571897, 32203252, 28840640, 41872443) firmly establish TUBB2A as a cause of tubulinopathy with global developmental delay, epilepsy, and cortical malformations—neurodevelopmental phenotypes strongly linked to ASD but not ASD itself. ASD is thus reported as an occasional accompanying feature rather than a replicated, systematically assessed primary phenotype, and the mechanistic work (microtubule/heterodimer assays, iPSC lines) is in vitro. This supports "Existing" as the best fit, with some probability for "Established" given multiple independent probands and for "Hypothesized" given the strong neurodevelopmental biology.

The ZMYM3 papers (PMIDs 41958272, 40896224) concern a different gene and are excluded from consideration for ZMYM2. For ZMYM2 itself, multiple human reports describe heterozygous de novo loss-of-function variants causing NECRC syndrome, whose phenotype explicitly includes a variety of neurodevelopmental disorders, motor stereotypies, Rett-like features, and an expanding neuropsychiatric spectrum (PMIDs 32891193, 40112685, 37383123, 42053849) — phenotypes strongly overlapping with, but not explicitly reported as, autism spectrum disorder. Supporting biology includes ZMYM2's interaction with FOXP1/FOXP2 cortical transcription factors implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders (PMID 29365100), chromatin/CoREST corepressor function, and behavioral abnormalities (anxiety, aggression) in Zmym2 mutant mice (PMID 40313719), which are non-human and thus support only a hypothesized mechanism. Because no cited study reports ZMYM2 variants in probands with a formal ASD diagnosis in independent replicated cohorts, "Established" is not supported; the human syndromic NDD variant evidence makes "Existing" the most likely category, with substantial probability remaining for "Hypothesized."

PMID 33658631 provides primary human evidence: de novo and inherited deleterious variants in RFX family genes, including RFX7, in patients with ASD, ID, and ADHD, with multiple probands. Subsequent human reports (PMIDs 36334883, 39007708) describe additional individuals with de novo RFX7 variants, but their own probands present chiefly with global developmental delay, ID, microcephaly and malformations, referencing ASD mainly as prior background rather than demonstrating it themselves. Thus only one study clearly documents ASD in RFX7 variant carriers, falling short of the two-independent-paper standard for Established, though the phenotype spectrum (neurodevelopmental/neurobehavioural disease) is strongly linked to ASD. Functional work (PMID 36864036) supports RFX7 regulation of neuronal genes, reinforcing biological plausibility; PMID 35986039 (Rfx7 motif in T1D) and PMID 18673564 are peripheral. Overall, evidence best fits Existing, with meaningful probability for Established.

FOXP2 is unambiguously causal for childhood apraxia of speech/verbal dyspraxia (PMIDs 27336128, 38366112, 17033973), and several human studies report ASD-relevant genetic findings: a family-based association in Chinese trios (15108192), an intronic allele excess and polyglutamine deletion in Japanese patients (15737702), variant analyses in Turkish ASD cohorts including a likely pathogenic FOXP2 variant (34526837, 41420732), and symptom-severity association (28081867). However, multiple well-powered mutation-screening and association studies were negative (11894222, 12116195, 12655497, 15998549, 23277129), and the reported ASD cases with FOXP2 loss largely involve deletions/UPD spanning additional genes, so no two independent studies convincingly demonstrate FOXP2 point variants causing ASD in separate probands. This mixture of positive but non-replicated human association data, plus a strongly related speech/language phenotype frequently comorbid with ASD, best fits "Existing." Some probability remains for "Hypothesized" since much of the FOXP2–ASD link is inferred from locus proximity (7q31), transcriptional targets such as CNTNAP2, and expression data rather than validated ASD-causing variants.

Witteveen et al. (PMID 27399968) reported dominant point/loss-of-function SIN3A variants in independent probands whose phenotype explicitly included mild intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder, and this is supported by their own patient data rather than background citation. Independent replication comes from the 28-patient SIN3A-haploinsufficiency cohort (PMID 33437032), where 27 novel truncating/missense variants were identified and ASD was diagnosed in several patients, and from a deep neurobehavioral phenotyping study of five WITKOS individuals showing ASD/ADHD features and social dysfunction (PMID 32783353). Additional single-patient sequencing reports (PMIDs 31427378, 36158056, 38528912) and the episignature study (PMID 36399132) further corroborate SIN3A single-gene causation of the neurodevelopmental syndrome, though these focus less on ASD specifically. Points are withheld from full certainty because ASD is a variably penetrant feature within a broader syndromic ID phenotype rather than a consistently replicated primary outcome, and because contiguous 15q24 deletion evidence (PMID 22216833) cannot isolate SIN3A. Mouse/Drosophila/zebrafish data (PMIDs 18773074, 38464057) provide supportive biology only.

Direct human variant-level evidence comes from PMID 33596411, which reports 34 independent individuals with truncating SPEN variants defining Radio-Tartaglia syndrome, with autism spectrum disorder explicitly part of the clinical profile, and from the GALA sequencing studies (PMIDs 39830258 and 41912808), where SPEN reached genome-wide significance as an autism-associated gene in >15,000 Latin American individuals. PMID 33004838 independently confirms de novo/ultra-rare disruptive mutation burden in SPEN across large NDD/autism cohorts with genotype–phenotype correlation. Additional single-patient reports (PMIDs 39431794, 40529391) describe de novo or rare SPEN variants with developmental delay and autistic behavior, adding supporting but weaker evidence. Remaining papers concern 1p36 contiguous deletions (which cannot isolate SPEN), Xist/chromatin biology, or Drosophila metabolism, and serve only as mechanistic or background context. The convergence of a large multi-proband cohort plus replicated statistical association in autism case sequencing supports an established relationship, though some uncertainty remains as ASD is one feature within a broader NDD syndrome.

Several human studies report their own patient-level data linking single-nucleotide KCNQ2 variants to autism/autistic features: PMID 35780567 describes KCNQ2 R144W/Q/G gain-of-function variants in patients with neurodevelopmental disability, language impairment and autistic features; PMID 33754465 reports four unrelated probands with likely pathogenic KCNQ2 variants showing ID with prominent autistic features; PMID 35269516 links de novo selectivity-filter variants to encephalopathy with autistic spectrum manifestations; and PMID 39175503 studies patients with KCNQ2/KCNQ3 gain-of-function variants and autism treated with donepezil. Additional independent probands come from single-case reports (PMIDs 35645364 de novo variant with ASD, 38108335 inherited c.402delC with autism) and from ASD-cohort sequencing (PMID 23849776). This constitutes replication in independent human probands, supporting Established, though much of the evidence is case reports/small series in which autism is a feature of a broader DEE/NDD phenotype rather than isolated ASD, which keeps substantial weight on Existing. Purely mechanistic/heterologous-expression papers (e.g., 32580997, 33794528) alone would only support Hypothesized.

SETD1A is unambiguously established for schizophrenia and a broader neurodevelopmental syndrome (PMID 26974950, 32346159), and autism-relevant features (developmental delay, ID, behavioural/psychiatric problems, speech delay) are part of that phenotype, but direct ASD-proband evidence is thinner. The strongest primary ASD-specific data come from a small WES cohort of 22 Bulgarian ASD individuals reporting novel SETD1A variants (PMID 40558542), and from de novo variant analyses showing shared disruptive coding/regulatory variants across ASD, schizophrenia and developmental disorders (PMIDs 26938441, 34504065) — though in those studies SETD1A's signal was principally in schizophrenia. Other papers cite ASD only as background, network inference, or in vitro/model-organism work (PMIDs 42523465, 31197650, 34803610), which supports Hypothesized-level biology rather than causal human genetic proof for ASD. Because I cannot cite two independent primary studies demonstrating SETD1A variants causing ASD in separate probands/families, Established is capped and Existing is the most probable category.

De novo/heterozygous QRICH1 variants cause Ververi-Brady syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder in which autism spectrum disorder is an explicitly reported feature. Two independent human cohorts report ASD in their own probands: PMID 28692176 (3 unrelated children with de novo LoF variants, one with autism) and PMID 34859529 (38 individuals, ASD in 29%), with additional support for social-behavioral deficits in PMID 33009816 and behavioral phenotypes in PMID 33738978. This satisfies replication across independent probands with single-gene (not CNV) variants, so Established is plausible; however, ASD is described as one variable feature of a broader syndromic ID phenotype rather than the primary studied outcome, and no ASD-specific association study exists, keeping substantial weight on Existing. Functional work (e.g., PMID 30281152 chondrocyte knockdown, PMID 40355839 cardiac ER stress) is supportive biology but not ASD-specific, so Hypothesized retains little weight, and Novel is essentially excluded.

Two independent human cohort studies report de novo/heterozygous SPTBN1 variants in unrelated probands with a neurodevelopmental syndrome that explicitly includes autistic features: Cousin et al. (PMID 34211179, 29 individuals with developmental delay, ID and autistic features) and PMID 33847457 (7 unrelated individuals, autistic features in 4/6), both with functional support and single-gene resolution (not CNVs). Additional independent human reports and cohorts (PMID 35190550 identifying SPTBN1 rare variants in an ASD familial cohort; PMID 41420732 listing SPTBN1 VUS in ASD patients; PMID 39162370, 40869952, 41862830 expanding the phenotypic spectrum) reinforce replication. The main caveat is that autism presents as one feature within a broader syndromic NDD (DDISBA) rather than isolated idiopathic ASD, which slightly tempers full confidence and leaves meaningful weight on "Existing". Animal/in vitro and cancer-related SPTBN1 papers (e.g., PMID 39217614, 40311681, 37921259) are irrelevant to the ASD link.

Multiple human studies with molecularly confirmed intragenic NSD1 variants report autism spectrum phenotypes among probands: a Chinese cohort of 23 molecularly confirmed Sotos patients in which 21.7% showed ASD, including two novel point mutations (PMID 40693312); a single-center cohort of 25 molecularly confirmed Sotos patients with a behavioral phenotype including ASD (PMID 40558479); a case report of a de novo NSD1 point variant in a child with ASD and congenital heart disease (PMID 37212006); and a Sotos case with a novel de novo NSD1 variant and mild autism (PMID 38459438). Behavioral phenotyping of Sotos syndrome shows a high proportion meeting ASD cut-offs (PMID 26418839), and reviews of neuropsychiatric features reinforce this (PMID 38673476). Counter-evidence exists: targeted NSD1 screening in idiopathic ASD with macrocephaly did not establish NSD1 as a common non-syndromic ASD gene (PMID 18001468), and much of the ASD link is syndromic rather than isolated, which tempers full confidence. Supporting mechanistic work places NSD1 among chromatin-modifier ASD genes with shared transcriptional signatures and ciliary/neural progenitor effects (PMIDs 36104286, 40552535), but these are in vitro. Overall the evidence is strong and replicated in humans for syndromic ASD, so Established is most likely, with Existing a substantial alternative.

Multiple independent human reports describe single-gene KCNB1 variants in probands with autism spectrum disorder: PMID 29264390 characterized a de novo KCNB1 variant in a proband with autism, intellectual disability, and epilepsy; PMID 39135902 reported a sibling pair (and an autistic obligate carrier father) with a KCNB1 p.S114R variant and ASD, with supporting electrophysiology; PMID 31696658 identified a pathogenic de novo KCNB1 missense variant in a Brazilian ASD cohort. Additional human evidence includes a candidate-gene association study of KCNB1 polymorphisms with ASD susceptibility (PMID 36756634), cross-disorder GWAS implicating KCNB1 across five psychiatric disorders including ASD (PMID 32606422), and cohort phenotyping showing autism/behavioral comorbidity within KCNB1 encephalopathy (PMIDs 34915430, 32954514). These are independent probands with point variants rather than multigene CNVs, supporting Established, though much of the ASD phenotype is embedded within a broader developmental/epileptic encephalopathy spectrum rather than isolated ASD, which keeps substantial weight on Existing.

Human genetic evidence clearly links de novo loss-of-function variants in PRR12 to a neurodevelopmental/neuro-ocular syndrome (PMIDs 29556724, 33824499, 26163108, 38798311, 41357555), with intellectual disability, developmental delay and neuropsychiatric features. Autism specifically is reported as a variable behavioral feature in the three-proband series of PMID 29556724, and broader neuropsychiatric/behavioral phenotypes appear in the haploinsufficiency cohort (PMID 33824499), but ASD is not consistently or systematically documented as the core phenotype across independent probands, and one cohort explicitly notes absence of neuropsychiatric disorders (PMID 33314030). Thus the ASD link rests largely on syndromic co-occurrence rather than replicated ASD-specific causal evidence, supporting "Existing" over "Established". Zebrafish expression data (PMID 38674426) provide only supportive biological plausibility (brain regions implicated in autism), which is animal-model evidence and counts toward "Hypothesized". PMID 32597225 is an incidental co-occurring variant report and adds little.

Multiple human reports describe single-gene ANK2 variants in independent ASD probands: PMID 40035441 reports clinical/genetic characterization of patients with ANK2-associated ASD and epilepsy plus a literature review, PMID 37088467 details a patient with autism carrying a novel ANK2 mutation, and PMID 39978592 describes a familial heterozygous missense variant (p.Arg987Trp) segregating with ASD/subthreshold autistic traits; PMID 30755392 additionally identified a novel candidate ANK2 variant in a child with developmental delay and autism. These are point/LoF variants that isolate ANK2 rather than multigene CNVs (the duplication rearrangement in PMID 39472019 would not count). Supporting mechanistic work in mice and human iPSC neurons (PMIDs 35313230, 38290518, 37195288, 36604605) shows plausible neurodevelopmental mechanisms (dendritic NaV1.2 scaffolding, AIS plasticity, neuronal migration), reinforcing but not by itself establishing causality. Because much of the strongest replication comes from large exome studies cited only as background here, and the direct human reports are mostly small case reports, substantial probability remains on "Existing."

Multiple human studies report de novo single-nucleotide/indel variants in GRIA2 in independent probands presenting with autism spectrum disorder among other neurodevelopmental features. The key primary evidence includes PMID 31300657 (28 unrelated patients with heterozygous de novo GRIA2 variants, phenotypes including ASD, with functional validation), PMID 35534222 (de novo missense p.Lys530Met in a patient with ASD, GDD and epileptic encephalopathy), PMID 36329391 (novel GRIA2 variant in atypical ASD), and PMID 38572415 (de novo GRIA2 variant identified in a Middle Eastern ASD cohort). Additional independent case reports (PMID 32948840, 34899870, 40391499) support GRIA2-related neurodevelopmental disorder in which autistic behaviors are a recurrent feature, and an ASD patient-derived iPSC line carrying a GRIA2 mutation exists (PMID 35134694). The main residual uncertainty is that ASD is one component of a broader GRIA2 neurodevelopmental syndrome (NEDLIB/DEE) rather than an isolated ASD phenotype, which keeps meaningful weight on "Existing"; the deletion case (PMID 22669415) spans GLRB and cannot single out GRIA2.

Direct human genetic evidence exists but is limited: PMID 35217385 reports two patients with de novo GRIN2A pathogenic variants presenting with autism, intellectual disability and focal epilepsy, while explicitly noting that autism in GRIN2A-related disorders is "questionable"; PMID 32722525 found recurring GRIN2A variants (classified as VUS) in a regressive-autism cohort; PMID 15830322 reported single-marker and replicated SNP association at GRIN2A in autism families/trios. Other cited GRIN2A studies (PMIDs 30544257, 27683935, 31807283) delineate the GRIN2A phenotype as predominantly epilepsy-aphasia spectrum with speech disorder, contrasting GRIN2B as the neurodevelopmental/autism-associated paralog, and PMID 22326929 found significant association only for GRIN2B. Several remaining papers (schizophrenia exome/GWAS, epilepsy and EDC reviews) mention autism only as background overlap and constitute citation rather than primary evidence. Because independent, replicated proband-level causal evidence for ASD specifically is thin—largely one small case report plus VUS-level and older association findings—Existing is the best fit, with residual probability for Established.

Human genetic evidence directly links PACS1 to ASD: the GALA consortium sequencing study of >15,000 Latin American individuals identified PACS1 as a genome-wide significant (FDR<0.05) autism-associated gene from de novo/deleterious coding variants (PMIDs 39830258 and its published version 41912808), and an independent trio-WES cohort of ID/ASD patients reported a pathogenic PACS1 variant among diagnosed cases (PMID 34948243). Additional independent probands with PACS1 point variants show autistic traits as part of the phenotype, including systematic longitudinal, multimodal characterization of five children with PACS1-NDD showing autistic traits comparable to autistic cohorts (PMID 42392841), a novel missense variant case with autistic features (PMID 36415352), and clinical delineation series describing autism-spectrum characteristics (PMIDs 34517877, 41882293). These are single-gene missense variants (predominantly p.Arg203Trp), not multigene CNVs, and derive from independent probands, supporting replication. Some uncertainty remains because the two GALA reports represent one dataset and much of the remaining evidence concerns a syndromic NDD in which autistic traits are one feature, so points are also allocated to Existing.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo single-nucleotide/indel variants in SETD1B in probands whose phenotype explicitly includes autism spectrum disorder or autistic behavior: PMID 29322246 (two unrelated individuals with de novo missense variants, autistic behavior), PMID 31440728 (de novo p.Val129Gly with formal ASD diagnosis), and PMID 31110234 (de novo frameshift with autistic behavior). Further replication comes from a large cohort delineating the SETD1B-related syndrome with autistic features (PMID 34345025), a family with an inherited in-frame deletion segregating with ASD and schizoaffective disorder without ID/seizures (PMID 39169470), and identification of SETD1B among pathogenic findings in an ASD exome cohort (PMID 39632905). These are point variants in independent probands, so the evidence is not dependent on multigenic 12q24.31 deletions (PMID 27106595), which cannot isolate the gene. Some residual probability is retained for "Existing" because ASD is generally reported as one feature of a broader syndromic neurodevelopmental/epilepsy phenotype rather than as isolated ASD.

De novo loss-of-function and missense variants in WDR26 are robustly established as causing Skraban-Deardorff syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability, developmental delay, seizures and prominent behavioral abnormalities including autistic-like features (PMIDs 28686853, 33675273, 33506510, 35627197, 40826479). However, none of these human cohort reports use ASD itself as the primary ascertained phenotype or systematically diagnose autism in multiple independent probands; ASD-related behaviors are described as part of a broader syndromic NDD phenotype, which qualifies as a strongly linked subtype/risk phenotype rather than replicated direct ASD causation. The only paper explicitly reporting autism (PMID 33678339) involves a multigenic 1q41-q42 microdeletion, which cannot isolate WDR26. Additional support is non-human/in vitro: Wdr26+/- mice show social dysfunction and learning deficits (PMID 42138082), and CTLH E3 complex/chromatin studies provide mechanistic plausibility (PMIDs 38575527, 39837355). Therefore "Existing" is the best fit, with meaningful probability mass on "Hypothesized" (animal/functional data) and some on "Established" given the strong syndromic human variant evidence with autistic features.

None of the provided articles reports an association between CSNK1E variants and Autism Spectrum Disorder itself; there is no ASD cohort, proband, or family study, so Established is untenable. The strongest human genetic data are a de novo loss-of-function splice variant in CSNK1E in West syndrome/epileptic encephalopathy (PMID 30488659) and a CGG repeat expansion/methylation change in progressive myoclonic epilepsy and developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (PMID 40751262); these are neurodevelopmental phenotypes frequently comorbid with, but not equivalent to, ASD, and the same paper only notes that CSNK1E interactors are shared across neuropsychiatric disorders. Other human work links CSNK1E to bipolar disorder, schizophrenia protein levels, stimulant/opioid response and mood disorders (PMIDs 30445897, 27236410, 18228528, 16237383), supporting broad neuropsychiatric relevance rather than ASD specifically. Mouse studies of Csnk1e affecting sleep architecture, anxiety/fear behaviours and psychostimulant sensitivity (PMIDs 24744456, 34514665, 22089318) provide biologically plausible, animal-based support, which fits Hypothesized. Accordingly most weight goes to Hypothesized, with meaningful weight to Existing based on the human neurodevelopmental epilepsy variants.

Multiple independent human cohort and case studies report de novo point/frameshift/nonsense variants in NR2F1 (not just multigene deletions) in patients presenting with autism spectrum disorder diagnoses or autistic features as part of Bosch-Boonstra-Schaaf optic atrophy syndrome. Primary-evidence papers with their own probands include PMID 26986877 (20 new cases), PMID 32275123 (18 new cases plus 9 previously reported, explicitly documenting ASD diagnoses/features), PMID 39972940 (47 individuals with autistic features and genotype-phenotype analysis), PMID 31729143 (de novo nonsense variant p.Gln28* in a patient formally diagnosed with ASD), and PMID 28963436 (novel missense DBD/LBD variants with repetitive behaviors). Supporting mechanistic work in human ESCs carrying the patient-derived NR2F1-R112K variant and corresponding mice (PMID 32320667) demonstrates excitatory/inhibitory imbalance, a recognized ASD mechanism, while enhancer work (PMID 39312666) links de novo ASD variants to Nr2f1 regulatory elements. The main uncertainty is that ASD here is a variably penetrant feature of a broader syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder rather than isolated autism, which keeps meaningful weight on "Existing."

None of the provided articles report VEZF1 variants in individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder, nor any association study, family, or proband linking the gene to ASD. The literature is dominated by VEZF1's role in vascular/lymphatic development, endothelin-1 regulation, cardiac structure and dilated cardiomyopathy (PMID 36657711), hematoendothelial lineage specification, and cancer biology — none of which are ASD phenotypes. The only tangentially neurodevelopmental items are prenatal alcohol exposure studies where Vezf1 is downregulated by miR-150-5p in brain microvasculature and altered in ethanol-exposed human brain endothelial cells (PMIDs 36109176, 41668336), plus Vezf1's control of Dnmt3b and genomic DNA methylation in mouse ES cells (PMID 18676812); these give only a weak, indirect mechanistic rationale (epigenetic/neurovascular contributions to neurodevelopmental impairment) rather than ASD-specific evidence. This falls short of even hypothesized-level direct relevance in most respects, so the bulk of probability goes to Novel with a modest allocation to Hypothesized.

The only human genetic evidence (PMID 40936200) reports de novo truncating ZNF865 variants in 18 patients with a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay, hypotonia, dysmorphism and intellectual disability; autism spectrum disorder is not explicitly reported in the abstract, though ID/NDD is a phenotype strongly linked to and frequently comorbid with ASD, supporting "Existing" as the most likely category. No article demonstrates variants specifically causing ASD in independent probands, so "Established" cannot be supported (the single cohort paper does not name ASD, and there is no independent replication for the ASD phenotype). The CRISPR study (PMID 39521313) is in vitro/tissue engineering work on cell cycle and protein processing in stem cells, which provides no ASD-relevant neurobiology and cannot elevate the human categories. Some probability remains for "Hypothesized" (gene biology as a C2H2 poly-zinc-finger transcription factor in a class enriched for NDD/ASD genes) and for "Novel" if the reported phenotype excludes autism entirely.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report TRIO point variants in patients with ASD phenotypes: Sadybekov et al. identified a de novo missense mutation hotspot in the TRIO GEF1 domain in ASD probands from exome-sequencing cohorts (PMID 28928363), and Barbosa et al. described an international cohort of 24 individuals with pathogenic TRIO missense/nonsense variants presenting with developmental delay, ID and neurobehavioral/ASD phenotypes (PMID 32109419). Additional independent human evidence includes a family-based association study of common TRIO variants in 427 Chinese Han autism trios (PMID 41438617), a diagnostic exome cohort reporting a pathogenic TRIO variant in a neurodevelopmental phenotype (PMID 41168819), and the GeneReviews summary of TRIO-related neurodevelopmental disorder (PMID 28796471). Functional and animal work (PMIDs 34353896, 40488445, 39300136, 38566250) provides convergent mechanistic support via TRIO–RAC1 signaling at glutamatergic synapses but is supportive rather than primary. Because the ASD phenotype is often embedded within a broader NDD/ID spectrum rather than isolated ASD, some probability remains on "Existing."

The GALA consortium sequencing study of >15,000 Latin American individuals identified YWHAG among 35 genome-wide significant autism-associated genes, explicitly labeling it an "emerging" ASD gene (PMID 41912808; the preprint PMID 39830258 is the same cohort, not independent replication). Independently, clinical cohorts of de novo heterozygous YWHAG missense variants in DEE-56 report autism spectrum disorder in a substantial fraction of probands (3/7 in PMID 31926053; additional neurodevelopmental/autistic features in PMIDs 38491959, 39413657, 33393734, 41886798), supporting human variant-level evidence with individual probands. Thus the two strongest lines are a statistically significant human sequencing association plus multiple case series with de novo point variants and ASD phenotypes, which approaches but does not fully meet replicated, definitive causal proof of ASD specifically (much of the literature frames ASD as a comorbidity of the epileptic encephalopathy phenotype). Deletion reports at distal 7q11.23 (PMIDs 21109226, 23756441) involve multiple genes (HIP1, YWHAG) and cannot isolate YWHAG. Weighting therefore favors Existing with substantial probability for Established.

Many listed papers concern TCF4 (transcription factor 4/ITF2, Pitt-Hopkins syndrome), a distinct gene from TCF7L2 despite the historical "TCF-4" alias, and were dismissed. Genuine TCF7L2 evidence in humans includes PMID 34003604, which reports 11 individuals with de novo truncating and missense TCF7L2 variants and a syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype including autism and ADHD, and PMID 42417140, which characterizes an independent, larger cohort of patients with mono-allelic pLOF TCF7L2 variants (TCF7L2-related neurodevelopmental disorder). Additional human support comes from an East African ASD familial cohort with potentially pathogenic TCF7L2 variants (PMID 37492102) and diagnostic case reports (PMID 36553572). Mouse work (PMID 36782064) shows patient-derived TCF7L2 mutations disrupt vocalization and transcriptional repression, providing mechanistic but non-human support. Because autism appears as a variable comorbid feature of a broader syndromic NDD rather than a consistently replicated primary ASD phenotype, points are split between Established and Existing with a slight lean to Existing.

None of the provided articles studies Autism Spectrum Disorder; there are no human genetic association or proband/family studies linking ATAT1 variants to ASD, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. The literature is dominated by cell-biological work on ATAT1-mediated α-tubulin K40 acetylation in cancer, mitochondria, lysosomes, cilia, cardiomyopathy, and Alzheimer models. Weak indirect neurobiological plausibility exists: ATAT1/MEC-17 modulates KIF1A/UNC-104-dependent axonal synaptic vesicle transport (PMID 41452330), MFN2-dependent mitochondrial motility in axons (PMIDs 38883841, 36993604), and the canine GWAS notes Atat1 near behavior-associated variants with reported anxiety-related behavior in mice (PMID 37147374) — animal/in vitro only, supporting at most a Hypothesized relationship. Given that even these connections are tangential to ASD, Novel remains the most probable classification with Hypothesized a plausible alternative.

De novo missense variants in FBXW11 are established in humans as causing a diverse neurodevelopmental syndrome (NEDJED) with brain, eye, jaw, and digit anomalies (PMID 31402090, seven probands; PMID 40178747, a second case report), but neither abstract explicitly documents autism spectrum disorder as a core phenotype — only neurodevelopmental delay, which is a broadly related but not ASD-specific outcome. Thus no article demonstrates in its own human results that FBXW11 variants cause ASD, precluding "Established." The strongest ASD-specific link is the murine study showing Fbxw11 disruption regulates neurofibromin degradation and corrects social learning deficits and impulsivity in Nf1+/- mice (PMID 40590220), which is animal work and therefore supports "Hypothesized." Remaining papers concern unrelated biology (RVFV NSs degradation, SCF ubiquitin variant inhibitors, PTENα/β, Alzheimer's neuroinflammation, γδT17 cells, growth GWAS) and provide only pathway-level relevance. The balance therefore lies between Existing (human NDD phenotype overlapping ASD-risk conditions) and Hypothesized (strong ASD-relevant animal/mechanistic data).

Heterozygous SKI point mutations cause Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome, a human disorder with developmental delay, intellectual disability and behavioral dysregulation (PMID 39600231, 37697026, 35810425, 33416497), but none of these papers reports autism diagnoses in probands, so no article demonstrates a causal SKI–ASD link with patient variants; the 1p36 deletions containing SKI (PMID 23892090, 26345236) are multigenic CNVs and cannot implicate SKI specifically. The strongest mechanistic support is biological: SKI forms the AWS complex with the prominent ASD risk factor AUTS2 and WDR68 to control neuronal lineage choice via BMP/SMAD signaling (PMID 36258139), and SKI is listed among autism risk genes targeted by ASD-dysregulated miRNAs in a bioinformatic review (PMID 34744804). This pathway-level and neurodevelopmental evidence supports "Hypothesized" most strongly, with meaningful weight on "Existing" because SKI variants do cause a human neurodevelopmental phenotype (ID/DD) that is a recognized ASD-associated context. "Established" is essentially excluded since no two independent human studies report ASD probands with SKI point variants.

Multiple human studies report point/frameshift variants in CREBBP in patients with autism or autistic features: a de novo CREBBP variant in an ASD proband from the Qatari ASD cohort (38572415), a de novo CREBBP frameshift in a girl with RSTS whose autism was confirmed by ADOS/ADI-R (25768348), and large MKHK cohorts with missense/in-frame variants in exons 30–31 where autism is a recurrent feature (38553851, 37353886). Additional RSTS series link CREBBP mutations and deletions to autistic features and note lower IQ/autistic traits with large deletions (18792986, 23315884, 34271530), and a candidate-gene association study found nominal single-marker association at CREBBP in autism families (15830322). However, most evidence is syndromic (RSTS/MKHK) where ASD is one of many features, and the copy-number/duplication reports (24035902, 39472019) cannot isolate CREBBP; thus points are split between Established and Existing, with little support for a purely biological/hypothetical or null relationship.

De novo heterozygous EEF1A2 missense variants cause a neurodevelopmental syndrome in which autistic behavior is a recurrent core feature. Primary human evidence with autism in the authors' own probands includes PMID 24697219 (two unrelated patients with de novo p.Asp252His and p.Glu122Lys showing severe ID, absent speech, epilepsy and autistic behavior) and PMID 30377530 (a patient with an EEF1A2 variant, epilepsy, ID and autism), with further supporting cohorts describing autism within the EEF1A2 phenotype spectrum (PMIDs 27441201, 32196822, 38355961, 33307280). A suggestive but non-genome-wide-significant autism GWAS signal at EEF1A2 (PMID 31647196) adds weak independent support. Uncertainty remains because autism is reported as one feature of a broader developmental and epileptic encephalopathy rather than as an isolated, systematically ascertained ASD diagnosis, which keeps substantial probability on "Existing"; supportive animal/in vitro work (PMIDs 28378778, 27976757) alone would only justify "Hypothesized".

NSD2 haploinsufficiency causes Rauch-Steindl syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder in which autism and global developmental delay are reported features (PMID 42221011 describes a proband with a de novo intragenic NSD2 exon 6–22 deletion presenting with autism; PMID 33941880 reports a cohort with LoF and missense NSD2 variants and a distinct developmental phenotype). Other reports (PMID 30345613, 38353053) describe de novo truncating NSD2 variants in developmental delay and cite, as background only, recurrent de novo LoF variants in autism cohorts—background citations do not constitute independent evidence. Notably, one "ASD" mention (PMID 41593547) refers to atrial septal defect, a homonym, and several papers (cancer/enzymology: 26411517, 34555356, 38965384, 25942451) are not phenotype-relevant. Because only one included paper explicitly documents autism in a patient with an unambiguous single-gene NSD2 variant, replicated proband-level autism evidence within this list is insufficient for Established, though the syndromic neurodevelopmental link is strong.

Human evidence is substantial: PMID 38815585 reports 25 individuals with heterozygous de novo MSL2 variants presenting a neurodevelopmental syndrome in which autism spectrum disorder is an observed behavioral phenotype, with a supporting episignature and iPSC functional data; PMID 38702431 independently describes three novel protein-truncating MSL2 variants in syndromic NDD/ASD probands and reviews additional de novo PTVs from ASD/DD cohorts; PMID 33860439 identified two de novo frameshift MSL2 variants in NDD patients; and PMID 37280359 nominates MSL2 as an ASD candidate gene from de novo variant analysis in a Brazilian ASD cohort. These constitute multiple independent probands with single-gene (not CNV) variants, supporting causation for an MSL2-related NDD in which ASD is a frequent but partial feature. Mouse conditional knockout data (PMID 42168661) showing autism-like social deficits and impaired neurogenesis strengthen biological plausibility but are animal-based. Because ASD is one component of a broader syndromic phenotype rather than the primary replicated outcome, probability is split roughly evenly between Established and Existing.

Human evidence directly implicating NBEA disruption in autism includes a de novo balanced translocation disrupting the neurobeachin gene in a patient with idiopathic autism (PMID 12746398), the positional cloning/LDCV secretion study describing autism patients with NBEA haploinsufficiency (PMID 20071347), and a de novo truncating NBEA variant in a child with epileptic encephalopathy and prominent autistic features (PMID 34609286). Large de novo variant cohorts establish NBEA as a neurodevelopmental disorder gene whose spectrum includes intellectual disability and ASD (PMIDs 30269351, 41113443), which supports a causal role, though the primary phenotype in most probands is early-onset generalized epilepsy/NDD rather than isolated ASD. Deletion cases (PMIDs 12826745, 32507666, 34716974) involve multi-gene CNVs and therefore cannot isolate NBEA. Several remaining papers are functional/model-organism, machine-learning prediction, or restate the ASD candidacy as background rather than providing new proband-level ASD evidence. Given at least two single-gene, patient-level reports but a phenotype that is often NDD-with-autistic-features rather than replicated primary ASD, probability is split between Established and Existing with a slight lean to Existing.

De novo missense variants in ARF3 are convincingly linked in humans to a neurodevelopmental "Golgipathy" with developmental delay/intellectual disability, microcephaly, epilepsy and brain malformations (PMID 34346499, 36369169, 41507605, 38712921), and one genome-sequencing study reported a likely pathogenic ARF3 missense variant in a child with idiopathic speech delay (PMID 40225914). However, none of these reports explicitly describes autism spectrum disorder as a phenotype; the human evidence supports a broader NDD/ID phenotype that is only indirectly related to ASD, so "Established" for ASD is not supported. Points are therefore split between "Existing" (human variants causing an NDD phenotype overlapping ASD-associated developmental and speech impairments) and "Hypothesized" (Golgi trafficking/vesicle biology and zebrafish/Drosophila models provide mechanistic plausibility rather than direct ASD genetic evidence, e.g., PMID 36456556). Several listed papers concern plant ARF3 (auxin response factor) or unrelated ARF biochemistry and are homonym/irrelevant. A residual probability for "Novel" reflects the complete absence of any explicit ASD ascertainment or association.

No article in this set reports PTPRS variants identified in autism probands or families; the human genetic studies present concern Alzheimer's disease (rs10415488), CADASIL-like small-vessel disease, nonsyndromic cleft palate, and deafness locus mapping, none of which are ASD or a recognized ASD precursor. The autism links are purely mechanistic/biological: PTPσ is a presynaptic LAR-RPTP hub that trans-synaptically binds ASD-implicated partners (SALM5/LRFN5, TrkC/NTRK3, Slitrks) and organizes excitatory synapse assembly, with mouse knock-in disruption of the TrkC–PTPσ complex producing impaired social responses and avoidance behavior. These are in vitro, rodent, or review-level pathway data, which support Hypothesized rather than Existing. A small residual probability is left for Existing in case unlisted human association data exist, and a small one for Novel since most ASD mentions are generic background statements about synaptic adhesion molecules.

Several human studies report intragenic (non-CNV) FOXG1 variants in independent probands with autistic features/ASD: PMID 40819013 identified a novel de novo FOXG1 nonsense variant (p.Ser280Ter) in an Iranian family ascertained for ASD; PMID 41136907 systematically phenotyped 101 individuals with pathogenic FOXG1 variants and reported ASD features especially in missense carriers; PMID 31316448 identified FOXG1 mutations (including a novel one) by exome sequencing in three patients with autistic behaviors; PMID 24836831 described 23 subjects with deletions or intragenic FOXG1 mutations having absent speech with autistic features. These constitute replicated human proband-level evidence, though the autism phenotype is generally a feature of the broader FOXG1/Rett-like syndrome rather than idiopathic ASD, which keeps meaningful probability on "Existing." Reviews (PMIDs 32158381, 31824897) additionally frame FOXG1 as implicated in ASD, but count only as background rather than primary evidence.

Multiple independent human studies report pathogenic sequence-level variants in TNRC6B in probands with neurodevelopmental phenotypes that prominently include autism: PMID 32152250 delineates a cohort of patients with truncating TNRC6B variants (including cases originally ascertained in autism cohorts) presenting DD/ID with autism and ADHD; PMID 37348364 reports an independent proband with epilepsy and ASD attributed to a pathogenic TNRC6B variant; PMID 38404251 and PMID 39115759 add further independent probands with novel/splice-altering variants causing the TNRC6B-related disorder with behavioural abnormalities. Additional support comes from de novo/LoF TNRC6B variants in speech and language disorder cohorts (PMIDs 29463886, 38300321), which are closely allied neurodevelopmental phenotypes. Reports based on 22q13.1 deletions (PMID 42074582) or combined Xq28 deletion (PMID 41147347) are contributory but cannot isolate TNRC6B; papers on Ago2 hydroxylation, HCV replication, miRNA SNV frequencies, and MDD exome screening are not autism-causal evidence. Overall the replicated point-mutation evidence in independent human probands supports Established, with residual probability on Existing since autism is one facet of a broader DD/ID syndrome rather than a specifically replicated primary outcome.

No article in this set reports BRD4 variants in ASD probands; the human genetic evidence involving BRD4 concerns Cornelia de Lange spectrum/disorders of transcriptional regulation (PMIDs 37377026, 38735830), where BRD4 is listed as a rare cause of a CdLS-like neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than of ASD per se, and these are largely cohort/review contexts. The ASD-specific genetic findings here belong to BICRA (PMIDs 33232675, 39246911), a distinct gene that merely interacts with BRD4, so they cannot be credited to BRD4. The strongest autism-relevant BRD4 evidence is mechanistic and murine: Brd4 is an FMRP target whose inhibition rescues Fragile X phenotypes (PMID 28823556), plus zebrafish chd8–brd4 interplay (PMID 41226840), which supports a Hypothesized relationship. Remaining BRD4 papers (cancer, fibrosis, degraders, kidney disease) are unrelated to ASD. Hence Hypothesized is most likely, with some probability for Existing given the CdLS-spectrum human variants that overlap ASD-associated neurodevelopmental phenotypes.

Only one article in this set provides human genetic evidence: PMID 35916866 reports de novo ZMYND8 variants in patients with an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder, a phenotype spectrum that commonly encompasses autistic features and is a recognized context for ASD risk. This is a single publication rather than replicated independent clinical studies, so it does not meet the bar for "Established" (no second independent variant-level study is present in this list). The remaining articles (PMIDs 34764296, 36153585, 26655721, 32832624, 28055972) concern ZMYND8's chromatin-reader, super-enhancer, DNA-damage, immune, and cancer biology in vitro or in tumor datasets, which supports mechanistic plausibility (chromatin regulation is a well-known ASD pathway) but not direct ASD association. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with residual probability on "Hypothesized" if the NDD cohort does not explicitly document ASD diagnoses.

The core, replicated human evidence for HIVEP2 concerns de novo loss-of-function variants causing intellectual disability/developmental delay (MRD43) with behavioral abnormalities (PMIDs 26153216, 27003583, 31602191, 31207095, 36588750, 34704275), a neurodevelopmental phenotype strongly linked to but not equivalent to Autism Spectrum Disorder; autistic features are described only inconsistently within these ID cohorts. One human genetic association study reports HIVEP2 common variants nominally associated with ASD in a large case-control sample (PMID 35052433), providing limited, non-definitive direct evidence for ASD. No paper in this list demonstrates, in its own results, HIVEP2 variants segregating with a primary ASD diagnosis in two or more independent probands, so Established is not supportable.
