Additional support is biological/animal (Hivep2-knockout mice with immature dentate gyrus, hyperactivity and memory deficits; NF-κB regulation), which underpins a Hypothesized fallback rather than a human causal claim.

Direct human evidence exists: Laumonnier et al. (PMID 16946189) mapped a de novo balanced translocation disrupting KCNMA1 in a proband with autism and intellectual disability, with demonstrated functional BKCa haploinsufficiency; a de novo KCNMA1 variant was reported in an ASD/head-circumference cohort (PMID 31674007); and KCNMA1 was identified as a credible autism-associated gene in a family pedigree WES study (PMID 34368859), with a common variant also implicated in ASD-language modeling (PMID 40483526). However, these are single or few probands with variable evidence quality, and much of the remaining literature (potassium channel reviews, KCNMA1-channelopathy series) cites autism only as an occasional accompanying feature of a broader dyskinesia/epilepsy/developmental disorder rather than providing independent replication of an ASD-specific causal role. Functional/animal work (PMID 35819138, 35095492) supports plausible biology but is not human genetic proof of ASD causation. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with a modest chance that the accumulated human probands qualify as "Established."

Neither provided article mentions Autism Spectrum Disorder or any neurodevelopmental phenotype. One paper concerns a triterpenoid inducing ROS and Sp transcription factor repressors (ZBTB4/10/34) in rhabdomyosarcoma cells, and the other characterizes ZBTB34 as a hepatocellular carcinoma-associated nuclear protein with a monopartite NLS. There are no human genetic variant studies, probands, families, or association analyses linking ZBTB34 to autism, and no brain/neurodevelopmental biology that would provide a plausible mechanistic hypothesis. The evidence base is therefore entirely oncological and incidental to the phenotype, supporting a Novel classification.

The strongest link is PMID 40161581, which identifies PBX1 as a convergent downstream target of three autism risk genes (CTNNB1, PTEN, DVL3) in isogenic human iPSC-derived neural progenitor cells, with PBX1a overexpression rescuing aberrant NPC proliferation — this is mechanistic/functional evidence in a human cellular model, not identification of PBX1 variants in ASD probands. All other PBX1 clinical reports describe germline variants causing CAKUTHED (renal/urinary anomalies with hearing loss, abnormal ears, developmental delay), DSD, glaucoma, oligomeganephronia, or congenital heart disease (PMIDs 37571997, 36318887, 34797033, 33098248, 36833200, 42230622), with developmental delay/intellectual disability but no reported ASD diagnoses. No two independent human studies report PBX1 variants causing ASD, so Established is excluded; the neurodevelopmental phenotype and NPC proliferation biology give a modest allowance for Existing. The bulk of probability therefore falls on Hypothesized, since the biology (neurogenesis, ASD-gene convergence) is directly relevant but variant-level ASD evidence is absent.

SOX11 de novo point variants cause a distinct neurodevelopmental disorder (IDDMOH/CSS9), and at least one cohort explicitly reports autism/ADHD in 5 of 7 probands with de novo SOX11 variants (PMID 39333428), while a dedicated behavioural characterisation of SOX11 syndrome (PMID 37924570) and adult CSS cohorts (PMID 38117302) document prominent behavioural/neurodevelopmental anomalies. The 2p25.2 deletion case with autism (PMID 18992374) is a multigene CNV and therefore cannot single out SOX11. Reviews and registry studies (PMIDs 34205270, 30123105) restate the SOX11–neurodevelopmental link but do not independently establish ASD causation. Because replicated, ASD-specific evidence from sequence-level variants in independent probands is limited essentially to one cohort plus one behavioural report, "Existing" is most appropriate, with meaningful residual probability for "Established" given the strong ID/neurodevelopmental phenotype that is a recognized ASD-linked context.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo, single-gene (SNV/indel) pathogenic variants in USP7 causing Hao-Fountain syndrome, in which autism spectrum disorder is a prominent, recurrent feature: Hao et al. (PMID 26365382) identified de novo heterozygous loss-of-function USP7 mutations in individuals with intellectual disability and ASD; Fountain et al. (PMID 30679821) described further pathogenic USP7 variants with ASD among the phenotypes; PMID 36466803 expanded the mutation spectrum with additional probands including autism; and PMID 38126281 phenotyped 18 HAFOUS participants with ASD and derived a DNAm episignature. These are point variants in independent probands, so the evidence is not dependent on multigene CNVs (e.g., the 16p13.2 de novo duplications in PMID 21658581, which cannot isolate USP7). Supporting mechanistic and mouse work (PMIDs 35800757, 39862434, 39919828) shows USP7 loss/overexpression produces autistic-like behaviors and altered neuronal connectivity, reinforcing biological plausibility. Some residual probability is assigned to "Existing" because ASD is one feature within a broader syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than an isolated ASD association.

De novo heterozygous CNOT1 variants are definitively causal for Vissers-Bodmer syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder in which autistic features are a recognized component (PMID 32553196, cohort of 39 probands with behavioral problems; PMID 38434094, three unrelated Chinese probands presenting with developmental delay, intellectual disability and/or autism; additional single-proband reports PMID 37818768, 37507849, 41155467). These are human studies with independent probands and point/frameshift variants, which supports a strong link; the Drosophila work showing impaired genetic interaction with ASD genes (ASH1L, DYRK1A, SHANK3) adds mechanistic plausibility but is non-human. However, the primary and consistently reported phenotype is syndromic global developmental delay/ID with autistic features as a variable manifestation, rather than ASD as the defined outcome measure, so the evidence for ASD per se is strong but somewhat indirect. Other listed papers (HPE/pancreatic agenesis, CCR4-NOT biochemistry, CLL miRNA SNPs, mood disorders) are not ASD-relevant. Accordingly, probability is concentrated between Existing and Established.

Multiple human genetic studies report association between GABRB3 variants and autism: linkage disequilibrium with the 155CA-2 microsatellite (PMID 9545402), replication by TDT in 80 families (PMID 11920158), Korean trio studies (PMIDs 17230033, 19430570), a rare maternally transmitted signal peptide variant P11S with functional receptor consequences (PMID 19935738), and association with Asperger syndrome and autism endophenotypes (PMID 24321478). However, the evidence is inconsistent: two meta-analyses (PMIDs 29725984, 30074174) found no significant association for rs2081648, rs1426217, rs4906902 or rs20317, and other candidate-gene studies were negative (PMIDs 37019319, 24999380), while epileptic encephalopathy de novo mutations (PMID 23934111) and mouse models (PMID 27293187) support biological plausibility rather than a causal ASD link. Because no two independent studies convincingly demonstrate causal single-gene variants in ASD probands (the strongest, PMID 19935738, is a single rare-variant transmission report, and 15q11-13 duplications span several genes), Established cannot be supported. The weight of evidence therefore falls on "Existing," with some residual probability for merely hypothesized/biological support.

Multiple human studies report point/loss-of-function SETBP1 variants in probands with neurodevelopmental phenotypes that include autism spectrum disorder: the SETBP1-HD/RD cohort study (PMID 38923504) documents ASD diagnoses across 22 SETBP1-HD and 5 SETBP1-RD individuals with molecularly confirmed variants, and the exome-wide association study in Arab-ancestry boys with autism identified SETBP1 among susceptible genes (PMID 32996047). Additional human variant-level evidence comes from deep phenotyping of 18 individuals with non-degron missense variants (PMID 41073373) and gene-panel sequencing noting a de novo SETBP1 variant previously reported in an ASD subject (PMID 33391157); the CNV/SNV morbidity map (PMID 25217958) resequenced SETBP1 in autism cases but its ASD signal was for ZMYND11. However, much of the core evidence frames ASD as a comorbid feature within a broader ID/speech-disorder syndrome rather than as a primary replicated ASD-causal association, and several supporting reports (PMIDs 38674362, 33867525) are CNV-based or restate background. Hence probability is split roughly evenly between Established and Existing, with little support for purely hypothesized or novel status.

None of the provided articles reports YLPM1 variants in autism spectrum disorder probands or families, so Established is untenable (no PMIDs demonstrate ASD-causal variants). The strongest human genetic evidence is a pan-biobank rare coding variant analysis reporting YLPM1 for "psychiatric disease" broadly (PMID 39210047) and cross-ancestry obesity work linking YLPM1 to brain expression and "altered mental status" (PMIDs 39484254, 41168175), which are related but not ASD-specific phenotypes. A single-cell eQTL/MR study prioritizes YLPM1 for schizophrenia and depression with virtual knockout implicating neurodevelopmental and synaptic signaling pathways (PMID 42372879), providing a plausible biological rationale for a neurodevelopmental role without direct ASD variant evidence. Remaining papers concern clonal hematopoiesis and cardiomyocyte miRNA biology and are irrelevant to ASD. Overall this best fits Hypothesized, with some weight to Existing given human psychiatric/neurodevelopmental associations, and residual weight to Novel because ASD itself is never assessed.

Two independent human reports provide primary evidence: PMID 30735662 identified de novo PPP2CA variants in a cohort of individuals with syndromic intellectual disability (Houge-Janssens syndrome type 3), and PMID 36531959 reported a novel de novo missense variant (p.Cys196Arg) in a patient with developmental delay, autistic behaviors and seizures, with biochemical validation of pathogenicity. Reviews (PMIDs 40555839, 34241636) confirm that autistic features are a recurrent component of the PPP2CA-related HJS phenotype, and cross-gene PP2A studies (PMID 39978342) place PPP2CA within a spectrum including behavioral/autistic problems. The main caveat is that autism is described as one feature of a broader neurodevelopmental syndrome rather than isolated ASD, and the number of ASD-specific probands is modest, which keeps substantial weight on "Existing." Several other listed papers concern lupus, gastric cancer, medulloblastoma, spermatogenesis, or in vitro/mouse mechanism and do not bear on ASD causality in humans.

The strongest human evidence is PMID 22105621, a QTL/targeted family-based association study in AGRE and AGP autism cohorts reporting association of a KCND3 intronic haplotype with nonverbal communication deficits in ASD (p=0.001, with a nearby block p=0.008 in the replication sample); this is a single, modest, sub-genome-wide association to an ASD endophenotype rather than replicated causal variant evidence, so it supports "Existing" but not "Established". Other KCND3 human reports describe neurodevelopmental disorders, intellectual disability, epilepsy and SCA19/22 (PMIDs 32823520, 28895081, 32921676, 32655623, 41188451), which are neurodevelopmental phenotypes broadly overlapping ASD risk but not ASD diagnoses per se. Additional support is biological/background only: Kv4.2/Kv4.3 channels with DPP6/DPP10 auxiliary subunits are "implicated in autism spectrum disorders" (PMID 23440961), and mouse Kcnd3 models show cognitive/behavioural deficits (PMID 41554439), which underpins the Hypothesized allocation. No article demonstrates KCND3 variants causing autism in two or more independent probands/families, so Established receives minimal weight.

No article in this set reports a cohort of ASD-diagnosed probands carrying TUBB3 variants, so Established cannot be supported (no two independent human studies with ASD-diagnosed carriers). However, human TUBB3 missense variants (E410K, G71R, G98S, M323V) cause tubulinopathies with intellectual disability, developmental delay, absent speech, and explicitly "intellectual and social disabilities" and behavioral impairments (PMIDs 30272120, 20074521, 26639658, 32573066), phenotypes that overlap and co-occur with autism spectrum features, supporting a limited/indirect Existing-level link. The two ASD-focused articles (33083014, 39788508) concern polygenic scores/gene sets and gene–environment interaction and do not provide clear TUBB3-specific ASD evidence. Much of the mechanistic support (microtubule dynamics, axon guidance, knock-in mouse models, yeast tubulin modeling; PMIDs 20074521, 33064843, 36943622) is biological rather than clinical genetic evidence for ASD, so substantial weight also goes to Hypothesized. Small residual probability for Novel since ASD itself is essentially never the reported diagnosis in these reports.

H1-4 (HIST1H1E) frameshift variants cause Rahman syndrome, a human neurodevelopmental disorder in which autism spectrum disorder is a recurrently described feature. Direct patient-level evidence includes PMID 29704315, reporting a de novo c.435dupC frameshift identified by exome sequencing in a boy with autism and intellectual disability with functional support for haploinsufficiency, and PMID 34788807, which identified additional independent C- and N-terminal H1-4 variants in patients whose phenotype spectrum includes ASD, plus neuronal functional characterization. Additional independent probands/cohorts (PMID 37605493 case report and genotype–phenotype review; PMID 28475857 overgrowth-ID cohort; PMID 31447100 larger RMNS cohort; PMID 33270410 GeneReviews) confirm de novo single-gene variants with a consistent neurodevelopmental phenotype, though several describe ASD as one component of a broader syndrome rather than as the primary studied outcome. Because ASD is a syndromic feature rather than the isolated replicated endpoint in most reports, points are split between Established and Existing; purely in vitro/chromatin biophysics and mouse papers (42173878, 33299181, 39829799) only support mechanism.

The strongest human evidence is a Brazilian three-generation whole-exome study (PMID 37280359) that identified de novo variants and explicitly nominated ZNF536 as an ASD candidate gene, which qualifies as at least one credible human genetic report. A second human report (PMID 41290998) concerns a "19q12 ASD" patient with ZNF536 and TSHZ3 deficiency, but this is a contiguous multi-gene 19q12 lesion and cannot single out ZNF536, so it cannot count toward replication. Remaining supportive data are non-human or non-ASD: zebrafish znf536 knockouts showing social/anxiety and cerebellar phenotypes (PMIDs 38331943, 30929901) and in vitro neuronal differentiation work (PMID 19398580), which support biological plausibility rather than human causality; other papers concern schizophrenia, creativity, sexual orientation, ADHD/obesity, or cancer. Therefore evidence is limited but real, favoring "Existing", with substantial weight on "Hypothesized" given the reliance on animal/functional models.

The only direct human genetic evidence is Zhou et al. (PMID 35982159), a large two-stage rare-variant analysis of 42,607 autism cases in which SCAF1 reached exome-wide significance as a new moderate-risk gene, with LoF carriers phenotypically characterized. This is a single (albeit very large and statistically rigorous) study rather than replicated findings across independent clinical reports, so the criterion of at least two independent proband/family studies for "Established" is not met. Several other SCAF1-labeled papers (PMIDs 31023583, 27997587, 28790391, 38769295) refer to COX7A2L/SCAFI, the mitochondrial supercomplex assembly factor, a homonymous acronym unrelated to autism, and PMID 39698826/29787824 concern SCAF1's RNAPII/splicing biology without autism phenotypes. The remaining ADNP/EB1/microtubule papers are irrelevant to SCAF1. Thus the evidence best fits "Existing," with residual probability for "Established" given the strength and size of the single genetic study.

None of the provided articles reports REV3L variants in autism spectrum disorder cohorts or probands; there is no ASD-specific genetic evidence, so Established is essentially excluded. The strongest human data are de novo REV3L mutations in Möbius syndrome (PMID 26068067, with follow-up cohorts PMIDs 39202332, 38356699 failing to find further REV3L hits) and a homozygous REV3L variant in a child with developmental delay, hypotrophy and dysmorphism (PMID 33474647) — neurodevelopmental phenotypes that overlap with, and in the case of Möbius syndrome are epidemiologically enriched for, autistic features, which supports at most an indirect "Existing"-type link. Supporting biology is largely mechanistic/animal: Rev3l loss causes embryonic lethality and impaired hindbrain/facial motor nucleus development in mice (PMIDs 11050393, 26068067), and translesion synthesis defects affect stem-cell and genome stability (PMID 25655219), which is relevant brain-development biology but not ASD-specific. Remaining papers concern cancer susceptibility, smoking behaviour, diabetes metabolites and protein biochemistry, which are incidental to ASD, keeping substantial probability on Novel.

No articles were provided linking EMC7 to Autism Spectrum Disorder, so there is no evidence of any causal variants, association studies, or even biologically suggestive functional/expression data. EMC7 encodes a subunit of the ER membrane protein complex involved in membrane protein biogenesis, which is broadly relevant to neuronal biology, but no literature here connects it to autism. Without any cited study in humans or model systems tied to ASD, the relationship must be considered Novel. A small residual probability is retained for Hypothesized given the general plausibility of ER membrane complex genes in neurodevelopment.

Multiple human studies convincingly establish that de novo PPP2R1A variants cause Houge-Janssens syndrome type 2, a neurodevelopmental disorder with developmental delay, intellectual disability, epilepsy, hypotonia and behavioral problems (PMIDs 41465181, 37945024, 37761890, 36209351, 35593790) — a phenotype spectrum that is a well-recognized substrate/risk context for autism, supporting "Existing." However, none of the cited primary PPP2R1A reports document autism spectrum disorder as a systematically ascertained outcome in two or more independent probands; "autistic features" in PP2A-opathies are mentioned mainly as background in papers whose own results concern PPP2CA or PPP2R5C/PPP2R5D (PMIDs 36531959, 39978342, 40282429). Thus replication specifically for ASD is lacking, precluding "Established." Some weight remains for "Hypothesized," since mechanistic/animal work (Ppp2r1a haploinsufficiency altering excitatory/inhibitory balance and endocannabinoid signaling, PMID 40839403) provides biologically plausible but non-human support for ASD-relevant synaptic pathology.

The strongest direct human evidence is PMID 39540616, a natural-history analysis of 59 patients with heterozygous DHDDS variants (including five previously unreported cases) in which 19% presented with autism spectrum disorder, explicitly recommending clinical attention to ASD. PMID 38844245 also reports ASD in 27% of a progressive myoclonus ataxia cohort in which DHDDS was one of the causal genes, but ASD is not attributed specifically to DHDDS probands, so it functions as supportive rather than replicating evidence. Other reports (34382076, 34275143, 41110374, 37356182) establish DHDDS variants as causing a neurodevelopmental/epileptic encephalopathy phenotype with developmental delay and behavioral/psychiatric disturbance—a context strongly linked to ASD—but do not independently document autism as a discrete phenotype. Mouse and cell-based work (40894730, 40003936, 42282162) supports plausible neurodevelopmental mechanisms but is non-human. Because I cannot cite two independent human studies whose own results specifically attribute ASD to DHDDS variants in distinct probands, Established is unlikely and Existing is the best-supported category.

De novo FBXO11 variants (point mutations, frameshifts, splice and missense) are firmly established as causing a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder (IDDFBA) in humans, with autism spectrum disorder explicitly reported as a frequent behavioral feature: PMID 30679813 describes 24 individuals with de novo FBXO11 variants in whom ASD/ADHD/anxiety were observed in most, and PMID 30057029 reports 20 further independent individuals with de novo single-gene variants and behavioral problems (17/20). Independent support comes from PMID 31838722, a trio-based whole-exome study of Chinese ASD probands that identified a de novo harmful FBXO11 SNV and lists FBXO11 as a reported ASD candidate gene, plus additional cohorts (PMIDs 34505148, 38740982, 29796876) confirming behavioral/neurodevelopmental phenotypes. Functional work in iPSC-derived neurons and Drosophila (PMID 40114442) supports haploinsufficiency as the mechanism affecting neuronal migration and differentiation. The main uncertainty is that ASD is described as one variable behavioral component of a broader ID syndrome rather than as an isolated, precisely quantified ASD diagnosis in all cohorts, so points are split between Established and Existing.

One human WES study of children with ASD directly implicates EP400, listing it among the most frequently recurrent genes across probands (PMID 42589554), though the cohort is tiny (n=25) and the recurrence finding is not established as causal. Stronger human genetic evidence exists for a closely related phenotype: compound heterozygous and de novo EP400 variants in 12 unrelated individuals with epilepsy and neurodevelopmental disorders, supported by Drosophila and zebrafish models (PMID 39708813), and a familial missense variant segregating with schizophrenia plus mouse behavioral phenotypes (PMID 33602898). NDD/epilepsy are well-recognized comorbid/overlapping neurodevelopmental phenotypes for ASD, supporting "Existing" rather than "Established," since no two independent studies report ASD-specific causal variants in probands. Supporting biological plausibility comes from EP400's role as the catalytic ATPase of the TIP60/NuA4 chromatin remodeling complex, with roles in neural crest development, Schwann cell differentiation, and paralog SRCAP being an NDD gene (PMIDs 37024457, 31142747, 41144712). Remaining probability is assigned to Hypothesized given that much of the mechanistic evidence is non-human or in vitro.

No article in this set reports its own cohort of ASD probands with KCNA2 variants; the primary human genetic papers describe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, intellectual disability, ataxia and spastic paraplegia (PMIDs 25751627, 27543892, 28806589, 31905474, 32903602, 33624935), so the "Established" bar of two independent ASD-proband reports is not met. However, a comprehensive review explicitly lists autism spectrum disorder among KCNA2-related neurological phenotypes alongside epilepsy, ID and ADHD (PMID 38517617), and the human phenotypes actually documented (DEE, global developmental delay, ID) are strongly linked neurodevelopmental conditions frequently comorbid with ASD, supporting "Existing." Additional support is indirect/biological: Kv1.2 interacts with CASPR2/CNTNAP2 (an autism gene) and with Shank3/ProSAP2 in the PSD, and PSD95–Kv1.2 condensates are implicated in a Fmr1 KO mouse autism model (PMIDs 30028556, 24211303, 40232934) — these are mechanistic/animal data supporting "Hypothesized" rather than human genetic association. The microdeletion burden study (PMID 25950944) implicates KCNA2 only within multigene CNVs and therefore cannot single out the gene. Weighing a plausible but non-primary ASD claim against strong mechanistic links, "Existing" is most probable with substantial mass on "Hypothesized."

Sequence-level (non-CNV) human evidence linking NR4A2 to ASD comes primarily from PMID 40564942, which reports 10 de novo indel/nonsense/splice and missense NR4A2 variants in 8 unrelated ASD probands from a single Saudi cohort, and from PMID 39126614, a Chinese ASD trio WGS study that nominated NR4A2 among 33 candidate risk genes; PMID 35813072 adds a rare NR4A2 variant in a Slovenian ASD cohort but at VUS level. Supporting but non-decisive evidence includes 2q24.1 deletions encompassing NR4A2 in patients with DD/ID/ASD (PMIDs 29770430, 27569545), which cannot isolate NR4A2 from neighbouring genes such as GPD2 (PMID 23554088). The broader NR4A2-related disorder literature (PMIDs 32366965, 38791237, 40497586, 35992907) firmly establishes NR4A2 haploinsufficiency as a cause of neurodevelopmental disorder with ID, language impairment and epilepsy—phenotypes overlapping and frequently comorbid with ASD—rather than of ASD per se. Because only one study (40564942) provides robust independent-proband, gene-specific variant evidence for ASD as the primary phenotype, replication is not yet convincing enough for "Established", so "Existing" is the best-supported category, with substantial residual probability for "Established".

The strongest human evidence is the candidate-gene association study (PMID 21750575), which reported association of XPO1 SNP rs6735330 with ASD across several family cohorts and with symptom severity — a credible but single, unreplicated association study. A recent report describes pathogenic XPO1 variants causing a dominant neurodevelopmental disorder (PMID 40819229), which supports gene-level causality for NDD but does not clearly establish ASD as a replicated outcome in the abstract. The remaining clinical reports (PMIDs 28573701, 24911659, 42315110) involve multigenic 2p15p16.1 deletions encompassing XPO1, USP34 and others, so they cannot single out XPO1 and in fact point to USP34 as the leading candidate. Mouse/in vitro Crm1 work (PMID 32008040) provides supportive biological plausibility (progenitor apoptosis, microcephaly) but is non-human. Several other papers are cancer/nuclear-export biology and are irrelevant homonym-free but non-ASD co-mentions.

The only available article (PMID: 38715938) is a molecular/functional study showing LMTK3 binds KCC2, promotes PP1-mediated dephosphorylation of S940, and thereby modulates neuronal Cl- extrusion and excitability — biology highly relevant to autism/epilepsy mechanisms but demonstrated in vitro and in neurons, not in patients. It states as background that LMTK3 "has been identified as a risk factor for autism and epilepsy," which is a citation of prior work rather than its own genetic evidence in human probands. No article here reports variants in independent probands or families, so Established cannot be supported. Existing retains some weight because the background claim implies at least one prior human genetic report, but since that evidence is not presented in the provided literature, the bulk of probability falls on Hypothesized.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report ITSN1 sequence-level variants in autism probands: the SPARK/large-cohort exome analysis reached exome-wide significance for ITSN1 as a new autism risk gene (PMID 35982159); a multi-family cohort described ten novel patients from eight families with truncating/missense ITSN1 variants, 90% with ASD (PMID 34707297); an additional independent de novo pathogenic variant case with autism was reported (PMID 38346866); and a Chinese NDD targeted-sequencing/integrative study prioritized ITSN1 as preferentially contributing to ASD (PMID 33994118). These are point/truncating variants rather than multigene CNVs, so the gene is uniquely implicated, and the findings replicate across independent probands and cohorts. Supporting mouse (Itsn1/2 KO ASD/OCD-like behavior, PMID 37603735) and mechanistic work reinforce biological plausibility but are not needed for the human evidence. Residual probability is given to "Existing" in case reviewers judge the case series and cohort statistics insufficiently definitive.

None of the provided articles addresses Autism Spectrum Disorder at all. Two papers (PMID 34968869, 26460951) concern PHF12/PF1's role in the SIN3A chromatin-repressor complex in triple negative breast cancer, and one (PMID 32246154) reports rare PHF12 coding variants in families with age-related macular degeneration — neither phenotype is a recognized precursor, subtype, or risk factor for ASD. There are no human genetic studies linking PHF12 variants to autism, so Established and Existing are unsupported. A small allowance for Hypothesized reflects the general biological plausibility that PHF12, as a chromatin-modifying SIN3A/KDM5A complex component, belongs to a gene class enriched in neurodevelopmental disorders, but no article here makes that connection explicitly.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo, intragenic SETD2 variants in probands with autism spectrum disorder as part of Luscan-Lumish/SETD2-related neurodevelopmental syndrome. Primary evidence with patient variants includes PMID 26084711 (de novo frameshift p.P677Lfs*19 in a girl with ASD, ID, epilepsy), PMID 29681085 (two new patients with de novo frameshift variants and ASD), PMID 31643139 (four new patients plus review, ASD in 89%), PMID 37372360 (18 new patients with SETD2 variants, mostly LLS with ASD), PMID 33766796 (two novel de novo variants identified in ASD individuals), and PMID 26637798 (recurrent deleterious SETD2 mutations in ASD postmortem brains). These are independent cohorts/probands with single-gene variants (not CNVs), satisfying replication. Supporting functional/mouse work (PMID 34014281) and reviews (PMID 37921122) reinforce, but the human genetic evidence alone supports Established.

Multiple independent human studies report single-nucleotide/indel disruptive NCKAP1 variants in patients with ASD phenotypes: PMID 33157009 assembled 21 affected individuals from 20 unrelated families with truncating, structural, and de novo missense variants showing ASD/autistic features and reported a de novo and ultra-rare variant burden; PMID 41462819 describes a de novo frameshift with autistic traits; PMID 40551827 reports an adult with a pathogenic NCKAP1 variant and ASD; PMID 41531171 documents a familial splice-site variant with autistic features in father and daughter; PMID 27632392 identified a mosaic NCKAP1 variant in an ASD proband. These are independent probands/families with gene-specific variants, satisfying replication rather than mere citation. Supporting functional work (mouse in utero electroporation, WRC structural analyses in PMID 39660913) reinforces biological plausibility. Some residual probability remains for "Existing" because much of the phenotype is broad NDD/ID with autistic features rather than strictly defined ASD, and the primary cohort itself notes the burden "needs further replication."

Two articles (PMID 37292950, the preprint, and PMID 38412861, the peer-reviewed version) report their own patient-level results: 41–42 individuals with protein-truncating variants or deletions of ZFHX3 presenting with syndromic intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder, supported by methylation signatures, ChIP-seq of neurodevelopmental targets, and Drosophila modeling. These provide human, single-gene-resolution LoF evidence in many independent probands, which argues for a strong causal role in the neurodevelopmental phenotype. However, they appear to represent the same international cohort rather than two independent replications, and ASD is described as a variable feature within a broader syndromic ID presentation rather than the primary ascertained phenotype. Remaining articles concern circadian/sleep biology, retinal function, BMI, atrial fibrillation, ataxia, or cell fitness and contribute only supportive or incidental biology. I therefore weight Existing slightly above Established, with modest residual probability for Hypothesized.

Several human studies report ASD directly among patients carrying pathogenic CACNA1A single-nucleotide/frameshift variants: PMID 35722745 describes 47 individuals with 33 unique likely pathogenic/pathogenic variants, of whom 23% had ASD, and PMID 25735478 reports 16 affected individuals from four unrelated families with point mutations, a stop-gain, a frameshift and a splice variant presenting with autism, ADHD and intellectual disability. PMID 37555011 adds an independent case series with genotype–phenotype correlation for CACNA1A-related NDD including ASD, and PMID 26566276 provides a family-based association study in 553 Chinese Han trios with nominally associated SNPs (not surviving correction). Additional case reports (PMIDs 36494636, 42038079) and reviews (33737904, 36592223, 32571372) reiterate ASD within the CACNA1A phenotypic spectrum, though these are largely background citations. Because ASD is generally a component of a broader neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than an isolated outcome, and some supporting evidence is nominal or review-level, substantial weight remains on "Existing," but the replicated variant-level human data across independent probands supports "Established."

No article in this set reports its own cohort of ASD probands with de novo ARID1A variants; the human genetic data here concern Coffin-Siris syndrome/BAFopathies (PMIDs 34205270, 25169878, 39355979, 40962111), where ARID1A variants cause intellectual disability and a neurodevelopmental syndrome that frequently includes autistic features, and reviews merely restate as background that germline SWI/SNF mutations have been linked to ASD (PMID 28124119). ARID1A also appears among the 893 SFARI ASD risk genes in a computational network study (PMID 41595671), which reflects prior human genetic evidence but is not primary proband data here. The strongest mechanistic support is a mouse study showing microglial Arid1a loss produces autism-like behaviors (PMID 35858990), which is animal, not human, evidence. Established is therefore excluded (no two independent human ASD proband reports cited), with probability split mainly between Existing (syndromic ND phenotype/SFARI listing) and Hypothesized (animal and chromatin-biology evidence).

The literature strongly establishes GNB1 de novo variants as a cause of a neurodevelopmental disorder (severe developmental delay, hypotonia, seizures, movement disorder; PMIDs 27108799, 28087732, 30194818), but ASD itself is only incidentally documented. Only one report explicitly lists autism spectrum disorder as part of the behavioral phenotype in a single patient with a novel GNB1 variant (PMID 34646230), which is not replicated across independent probands with ASD as the assessed phenotype. A human serum study measured GNB1 alongside GNAO1/GNAI1 in ASD (PMID 40873676) but reported significant dysregulation of the other subunits, providing only weak/biological support. Because GNB1 causes a severe NDD that is a recognized context for autistic features, and one human case explicitly reports ASD, "Existing" is the most appropriate category, with residual weight on "Hypothesized" given the pathway/biomarker-level evidence; "Established" cannot be supported since two or more independent ASD-focused proband reports are lacking.

None of the provided articles link RAB14 variants or biology to Autism Spectrum Disorder. The only autism-related paper (PMID 29244813) concerns multistable visual perception in Asperger observers and does not mention RAB14 at all. All RAB14 articles concern membrane trafficking, autophagosome maturation, epithelial polarity, cancer, bacterial infection, and SARS-CoV-2 gene expression eQTLs, with no neurodevelopmental or ASD phenotype. There are no human genetic association studies, probands, or families implicating RAB14 in ASD, and no relevant animal-model or pathway evidence connecting the two. This therefore represents an incidental co-mention rather than a substantive gene–phenotype relationship.

Neither provided article addresses Autism Spectrum Disorder. PMID 38789417 concerns telomere length GWAS validation, identifying KBTBD6 as a telomere length regulator, with no autism phenotype. PMID 30982432 mentions KBTBD6 only as an abbreviation in the context of Atg8/LC3-GABARAP autophagy protein specificity, again with no autism link. There are no human genetic variants, probands, families, expression, or animal-model data connecting KBTBD6 to ASD; the only tenuous biological thread (autophagy pathways broadly implicated in neurodevelopment) is incidental and not gene-phenotype specific. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel.

The strongest human evidence is the large multi-ancestry schizophrenia exome study (PMID 36914870), which explicitly reported PCLO as a gene shared between schizophrenia and autism based on rare protein-truncating variant burden, and a recent ASD whole-exome study (PMID 42589554) listing PCLO among the most frequently recurrent genes across probands, though without demonstrated pathogenicity. Supporting but weaker context includes PCLO's location in the 7q autism linkage region (PMID 12175852) and its role in presynaptic active-zone function, plus biallelic loss-of-function causing pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 3 with developmental delay (PMIDs 25832664, 40661989), a distinct neurodevelopmental phenotype. Against this, a candidate SNP study in 196 multiplex families found no linkage or association with autism (PMID 12707945). No study reports independent ASD probands or families with a demonstrated causal PCLO variant, so "Established" is untenable; the burden/recurrence signals in humans best support "Existing," with residual weight on "Hypothesized" given the largely biological/pathway-level nature of much of the evidence.

Multiple human genetic studies report de novo/inherited PSMC5 variants (e.g., p.Pro320Arg, R325W, Q160A, nonsense) in independent probands with syndromic neurodevelopmental disorders, with cohorts of 26–38 affected individuals and functional validation of impaired proteasome activity (PMIDs 38776958, 38293138, 41298377, 40650163). These constitute strong, replicated evidence for a causal role in neurodevelopmental proteasomopathies, and models show synaptic loss, impaired neuritogenesis, and reversal-learning deficits — biology directly relevant to autism. However, the abstracts describe the phenotype as syndromic NDD/developmental delay/intellectual disability rather than explicitly diagnosing Autism Spectrum Disorder, so the link to ASD specifically rests on ASD being a recognized subtype/component of these NDD presentations. This best fits "Existing" (association with a phenotype strongly linked to ASD), with meaningful residual probability for "Established" if the reported cohorts include formally diagnosed ASD probands. Remaining weight goes to Hypothesized, since supporting synaptic/behavioral evidence is largely from rodent, Drosophila, and in vitro models (PMIDs 38001534, 33658307).

No article reports PTK2 sequence variants segregating with or associated with ASD in human probands or families, so Established is not supportable. The strongest human data (PMID 21703394) show decreased FAK/integrin β1/Src protein expression and impaired migration/adhesion in B lymphoblasts of autistic subjects — a functional/expression finding rather than a genetic variant association, which supports a biological link but only weakly meets the "Existing" bar. Remaining supportive evidence is mechanistic or from animal models: Top3β/FMRP regulation of ptk2 in flies and mice (PMID 23912945), Tspan7 knockout rats with disrupted integrin β1/FAK/Src signaling (PMID 36625203), VPA-exposed rat offspring with altered FAK expression (PMID 35648200), and integrin β3 Pro33 knock-in mice where FAK inhibition rescues serotonin transporter function (PMID 29038237). An early speculative paper (PMID 9105973) proposes FAK as an autism candidate without data. Many other listed papers are cancer/bone/AML studies irrelevant to ASD. Therefore the relationship is best characterized as Hypothesized, with some weight to Existing given the human lymphoblast findings.

There is credible human genetic evidence linking NRXN3 to ASD: a case–control association study in a Chinese cohort found rs12879016 associated with ASD susceptibility (PMID 29045040), a monoallelic frameshift (p.Gln54AlafsTer50) in the NRXN3 beta isoform was reported in a girl with ASD and developmental delay (PMID 37372397), and a novel NRXN3 missense variant (c.3889C>T) was reported in a neurodevelopmental disorder patient (PMID 38739110). Additional support comes from exonic deletions of NRXN3 in ASD probands (PMID 22209245) and a segregating exonic deletion in a three-generation family (PMID 30076746), but per the rules these copy-number changes cannot isolate NRXN3 from neighboring sequence and do not count toward "Established". Reported variants show incomplete penetrance (inherited from unaffected carriers), and biallelic NRXN3 variants (PMID 36898513) produce a broader syndromic phenotype rather than definitive ASD causation. Thus the evidence is real but not definitively replicated at the single-gene sequence-variant level, favoring "Existing".

Most of the listed papers concern the mTOR signaling pathway as a mechanism in ASD-associated conditions (TSC1/TSC2, PTEN, DEPDC5), not variants in the MTOR gene itself; these are reviews or studies of upstream regulators (PMID 29490194, 29338461, 35963265, 35429726, 31433956), plus mouse work (Pten deletion, PMID 16675393) — all supporting a strong biological/pathway rationale, i.e., Hypothesized. The one paper with primary human variant data implicating MTOR itself is the de novo mutation screen in epileptic encephalopathies (PMID 23934111), where MTOR appears among genes with de novo mutations in a phenotype (DEE/infantile spasms) that is a well-recognized comorbidity and risk phenotype for ASD; this supports at most Existing. No article in this list reports MTOR variants in independent ASD probands or families with their own results, so Established cannot be supported (no two qualifying PMIDs can be named). Points are therefore split mainly between Hypothesized and Existing, with a small residual for Established given known Smith–Kingsmore/megalencephaly literature not represented here.

KANSL1 haploinsufficiency (intragenic loss-of-function variants and 17q21.31 deletions) causes Koolen-de Vries syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder in which autistic features are commonly described, and one case series reports a de novo KANSL1 variant in a child with infection-provoked autistic regression (PMID 39985218). Human genetic association data also support a link: eQTL colocalization with the largest ASD GWAS implicates KANSL1 (PMID 37907504), and common-variant analysis found KANSL1 nominally associated with ASD in 18,382 cases/27,969 controls (PMID 35052433). However, the strongest gene-level clinical papers (PMIDs 26424144, 26293599, 28211987) focus on the KdVS phenotype broadly rather than demonstrating ASD as a replicated primary outcome in independent probands, and much of the deletion evidence spans multiple genes, so causal specificity for ASD is not definitive. Mechanistic work on chromatin modifiers and dendritic spine/synapse pathology (PMID 36743289) provides supportive biology but is not itself variant-level human evidence. Therefore "Existing" is the best fit, with meaningful probability for "Established."

Several human studies report CHD7 variants in individuals with ASD: a recurrent inherited intronic CHD7 variant in a Chinese ASD cohort with functional validation in human stem cell–derived neurons (PMID 33948885), a deleterious CHD7 variant found by WGS in an ASD family cohort (PMID 23849776), potentially pathogenic CHD7 variants in an East African familial ASD cohort (PMID 37492102), CHD7 as a credible autism-related gene in a family pedigree WES study (PMID 34368859), and reports of pathogenic CHD7 variants in individuals with isolated autism or atypical CHARGE presentations (PMIDs 26590800, 38790272). Additionally, ASD is frequently observed in CHD7-related CHARGE syndrome (PMIDs 32493418, 24172694), and CHD7 mutation carriers show ASD-associated sleep phenotypes (PMID 34088660). However, most single-gene ASD-specific findings are individual probands or small cohorts without strong, replicated statistical gene-level association specifically for idiopathic ASD, so the evidence is credible but not fully definitive. Supporting mechanistic work (zebrafish chd7, Drosophila kismet) is non-human and only reinforces biological plausibility.

SMARCB1 is firmly established as a cause of Coffin-Siris syndrome and Kleefstra syndrome spectrum, neurodevelopmental disorders in which intellectual disability and autistic features co-occur, which supports at least an "Existing" relationship with ASD through a strongly linked syndromic phenotype (PMIDs 25169878, 34205270, 42206491, 29069077). Direct ASD-specific human genetic evidence is thinner: a Bulgarian ASD exome cohort listed a SMARCB1 variant among candidate genes (PMID 40558542), and a case with ASD carried a multigene 22q11.2 deletion encompassing SMARCB1 (PMID 25018128), but the latter cannot isolate the gene. Supporting mechanistic work showing that SMARCB1 loss produces hyperactive neuronal networks shared with other ID/ASD genes is in vitro (PMID 31914384) and therefore only supports the hypothesized tier. Because I cannot cite two independent primary reports of SMARCB1 point variants in probands ascertained for ASD itself, "Established" is not warranted, though residual probability is retained given the syndromic ASD overlap.

The original report (PMID 24076603) described four unrelated individuals with truncating paternal MAGEL2 point mutations, all of whom had autism spectrum disorder, and this has been replicated in independent human cohorts: a large international series of 78 patients with nonsense/frameshift MAGEL2 variants in which ASD was one of the most consistent features (PMID 30302899), a systematically phenotyped cohort of 9 molecularly confirmed patients showing elevated rates of ASD relative to Prader-Willi syndrome (PMID 30343463), and further independent cohorts/case series (PMIDs 37404980, 36836222, 31397880). These are single-gene truncating variants, not multigene copy-number changes, so the gene can be singled out. Additional supporting human work includes caregiver-burden and phenotype-expansion studies, plus mechanistic mTOR/autophagy data in patient-derived cells that provide biological plausibility (PMID 31685878). The evidence therefore meets the bar for Established, with only slight residual uncertainty since ASD is one feature of the broader Schaaf-Yang syndrome phenotype.

Human genetic evidence links YY1 variants to neurodevelopmental disease: de novo/germline YY1 variants cause Gabriele-de Vries syndrome, a syndrome of developmental delay, intellectual disability and behavioural abnormalities (PMIDs 35027293, 37658636, 35829845, 39586716), and one trio-based whole-exome study of Chinese ASD probands reported a de novo damaging YY1 SNV, listing YY1 among reported ASD candidate genes (PMID 31838722). However, only the latter is an ASD-ascertained cohort, and it is a single proband with the paper's own conclusions centred on JAK2/MAPK7; the GADEVS reports emphasise ID/DD rather than explicitly replicating an autism diagnosis, so I cannot cite two independent ASD-proband studies required for "Established". Additional support is mechanistic or non-human: DNM burden analysis in developmental disorders placing YY1 as a network hub (PMID 33777337), rodent BPA/YY1-Matr3 splicing work (PMID 40790242), rat NEAT1-YY1-UBE3A models (PMID 38922486), and regulatory roles at the ASD gene PTCHD1 (PMID 37990104). Overall this fits "Existing" (ID/NDD is a well-recognised phenotype strongly linked to ASD, plus one ASD proband), with meaningful probability for Established and residual weight on Hypothesized.

None of the provided articles report an association between CGREF1 variants and Autism Spectrum Disorder in any cohort of ASD probands or families. The strongest signal is the schizophrenia whole-exome study (PMID 40753099), which implicates rare coding variants in CGREF1 at FDR 5% and states the gene is also "enriched for rare coding variants in other developmental and psychiatric disorders" — an indirect, unspecified hint that could encompass neurodevelopmental phenotypes overlapping ASD, but it is not ASD-specific evidence. The risk-taking GWAS (PMID 30181555) highlights CGREF1 only as a candidate gene via brain expression for a behavioural trait linked to ADHD/bipolar/schizophrenia, and the antidepressant remission study (PMID 32664413) is unrelated to ASD. No PMIDs demonstrate causal ASD variants in independent probands, so Established is essentially excluded; the balance falls between Novel (no ASD-specific evidence) and Hypothesized/Existing (shared neuropsychiatric/neurodevelopmental rare-variant burden).

Two independent human reports describe intragenic (non-CNV) NFIB variants in probands whose phenotype includes autism spectrum disorder: the haploinsufficiency cohort (PMID 30388402), which included five premature-termination and three functionally inactivating single-nucleotide variants with ASD among the neurodevelopmental features, and a separate patient with the nonsense variant c.265C>T p.(Arg89*) presenting with ASD level 2, ACC, ADHD and ID (PMID 33130023); a further familial missense case adds neurodevelopmental disorder support (PMID 36756855). This satisfies replication with point variants in independent probands, favoring Established. However, ASD in these reports is a variable feature within a broader ID/macrocephaly syndrome rather than the primary, consistently segregating phenotype, so substantial weight remains on Existing. Additional support is mechanistic/human-cell based only (NFIB as cofactor of FOXP2 and as mediator of the EN2 ASD-associated haplotype, PMIDs 31067457, 22180456), which would only justify Hypothesized on its own; other listed papers concern sciatica, BMD, clozapine metabolism, or cancer and are irrelevant.

The only article linking LEMD3 to autism is the 12q14 microdeletion series (PMID 21267005), in which two of six children with multigene deletions spanning 12q13.3-q14.1 had autism; because these are contiguous gene deletions including HMGA2 and other genes, they cannot implicate LEMD3 specifically. All other LEMD3 literature concerns Buschke-Ollendorff syndrome, osteopoikilosis and melorheostosis (PMIDs 32519343, 29465813, 17223882, 28434888, 42166119), TGF-β/SMAD signalling at the inner nuclear membrane (PMIDs 30321401, 16211582, 25665639), chromatin architecture in smooth muscle (PMID 41044070), or incidental findings in unrelated cohorts (PMID 35022528), none of which address ASD. There are no point mutations in LEMD3 reported in autism probands, and no neurodevelopmental animal model data. Thus the relationship is essentially unsupported, with only a weak, non-gene-specific CNV co-occurrence keeping a small probability on Existing/Hypothesized.

SYT1 de novo missense variants clearly cause Baker-Gordon syndrome, a severe neurodevelopmental disorder with behavioral disturbances, stereotypies and developmental delay (PMIDs 30107533, 35101335, 39049490), but these reports emphasize intellectual disability, hyperkinetic movement disorder and EEG abnormalities rather than a formal ASD diagnosis. The most direct human ASD evidence is a single de novo P401L proband with developmental delay and autistic symptoms (PMID 38321119), and a computational multi-omics network study nominating SYT1 as a central regulator of ASD common- and rare-variant risk (PMIDs 40470234, 41651809). This constitutes credible but limited/non-replicated evidence for ASD specifically, and much of the mechanistic support (mouse and hiPSC neuron models, dominant-negative synaptic transmission deficits: PMIDs 32362337, 41475766) is non-human/in vitro, which supports Hypothesized rather than Established. Because I cannot cite two independent clinical reports of ASD-diagnosed probands with SYT1 point variants, Established is capped low and most weight goes to Existing.

The GALA Consortium sequencing study (PMID 39830258 preprint and PMID 41912808 published version) is a single large human study that identifies GSE1 among genome-wide significant, "emerging" autism genes based on deleterious coding variation in >15,000 Latin American individuals, with reported overlap with European cohorts. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence of association, but the two records represent the same dataset rather than independent replication, and the paper describes GSE1 as "emerging" rather than firmly established. The remaining articles (medulloepithelioma, medulloblastoma NES cell models, intraventricular meningioma, congenital scoliosis methylation, Alzheimer eQTL) involve somatic/tumor or unrelated phenotypes and do not support an ASD causal role. Therefore "Existing" is the most probable category, with some weight to "Established" given the genome-wide significance and cross-ancestry consistency.

Two human genetic studies provide direct variant-level evidence: a deep resequencing study reporting significant excess of rare missense variants in MAP1A in ASD (and schizophrenia) cohorts (PMID 21383861), and a large exome study identifying MAP1A as exome-wide significant for childhood psychiatric disorders in a combined ASD/ADHD analysis (PMID 31768057). However, the exome-wide signal was driven by a combined ASD+ADHD phenotype rather than ASD alone, and the strongest replication (PMID 41224997) is for ADHD, a closely related neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than ASD itself; a single case report of a MAP1A nonsense variant occurs in a 22q11.2DS/schizophrenia context (PMID 39189429). Supporting biology comes from mouse Map1a knockouts with Purkinje degeneration and dendritic/synaptic phenotypes (PMID 25788676), a rat VPA ASD model with elevated MAP1A (PMID 42192792), and mouse dendritic spine/SNP analyses (PMID 34616277), which are non-human and only support the hypothesized tier. Given credible but not independently replicated ASD-specific proband evidence, "Existing" is most appropriate, with some probability that the exome-wide significant finding plus resequencing constitutes established causality.

Direct human evidence exists: PMID 28130356 reports a de novo CAMK2A E183V variant in a proband diagnosed with ASD, with extensive functional and knock-in mouse validation showing ASD-related synaptic and behavioral phenotypes. Additional human cohorts (PMID 29100089, 29560374, 37510258) establish de novo CAMK2A variants as causal for intellectual disability/neurodevelopmental disorders in which autism spectrum features, aggressive behavior and hyperactivity are part of the phenotypic spectrum, and PMID 29147782 reports a nominally replicated common CAMK2A variant (rs2241694) associated with non-verbal communication in ASD cohorts. However, most of these studies frame the core phenotype as ID/NDD rather than ASD per se, and only one report identifies an ASD-ascertained proband, so replicated ASD-specific causal evidence in independent probands is not clearly met. Mouse Camk2a-Cre papers (34349780, 31427534, 29133437, 40799750) are driver-line/tool usages, not CAMK2A variant evidence. Therefore "Existing" is the best fit, with meaningful weight on "Established" given the NDD-spectrum causality.

GABBR2 is firmly established as a neurodevelopmental disorder gene (Rett-like NDPLHS, DEE59; PMIDs 28856709, 29100083, 29369404, 35414446), but the ASD-specific evidence is narrower. Direct human evidence linking GABBR2 variants to ASD comes from a de novo variant characterized in an ASD proband (PMID 38076211) and de novo GABBR1/GABBR2 missense variants in individuals ascertained with ASD/ID/ADHD with functional validation (PMID 41803176), plus suggestive statistical signals: GABBR2 as a top locus in a Middle Eastern family GWAS (PMID 34069769), a cluster-based GWAS hit (PMID 32807774), and a trend toward male-specific de novo enrichment in >41,000 ASD trios (PMIDs 41646820, 42032772). These are largely single/small case reports plus sub-threshold association signals, and much of the remaining literature is background citation (PMIDs 40756990, 35850019) or non-human/mechanistic work (PMID 22994563). This supports at least Existing with a reasonable but not decisive case for Established, since ASD is often a co-feature of the broader GABBR2 NDD phenotype rather than a replicated primary diagnosis across independent probands.

The only ASD-relevant article (PMID 24895325) is a mouse knockin study showing that catalytic inactivation of PTPRT alters social approach behavior — this is animal-model/functional evidence, which supports "Hypothesized" rather than human genetic evidence. That paper cites a prior GWAS naming PTPRT as an ASD candidate, but that is background citation, not primary human data presented here, so it cannot establish or fully substantiate an "Existing" classification (though it raises the possibility, hence non-trivial weight). The other papers are irrelevant to ASD: one concerns cancer-derived mutations affecting cell–cell aggregation in vitro (PMID 20230342), and one lists PTPRT polymorphisms in relation to glatiramer acetate response in multiple sclerosis (PMID 34683173). No article in this list reports ASD-causing variants in independent probands or families, so "Established" is effectively excluded.

Only one article in this set explicitly links EFTUD2 to autism spectrum disorder: a single adult case with a de novo pathogenic EFTUD2 variant (c.1705C>T) diagnosed with ASD, intellectual disability, and MFDM features (PMID 40439473). All other papers robustly establish EFTUD2 haploinsufficiency as the cause of mandibulofacial dysostosis with microcephaly, a syndrome consistently involving developmental disability/intellectual disability and other neurodevelopmental features (PMIDs 26507355, 33247512, 23879989), which is a neurodevelopmental context strongly related to but not equivalent to ASD. Since only a single human proband with ASD is reported and no replication across independent probands specific to ASD exists, the Established threshold (≥2 independent single-gene probands with the phenotype) is not met. Therefore "Existing" is most probable, with residual weight on "Hypothesized" given the plausible spliceosome/neurodevelopment mechanism.

Multiple independent human studies report de novo single-nucleotide/truncating CHAMP1 variants in probands who were prospectively assessed for autism: PMID 35271727 deep-phenotyped 11 individuals with CHAMP1 mutations and diagnosed ASD in 33%, PMID 37454340 prospectively evaluated 16 mutation-carrying individuals with neurobehavioral phenotyping, PMID 34021018 reported 14 individuals with de novo loss-of-function variants including behavioral problems/ASD, and PMID 36797464 described new point-variant probands and concluded that CHAMP1 loss-of-function produces a homogeneous phenotype of severe ID with ASD. Independently, an ancestrally diverse ASD exome cohort (PMID 39632905) identified CHAMP1 among genes with potentially pathogenic variants in individuals ascertained for ASD. These are human, gene-level (not multigene CNV) findings in independent probands, satisfying replication; the 13q33-q34 microdeletion series (PMID 31321490) is supportive but not counted. Remaining uncertainty reflects that autism is a variable feature of a broader syndromic NDD rather than an isolated ASD phenotype, which some would score as "Existing".

The strongest human genetic evidence comes from the Chinese ASD whole-genome sequencing cohort (PMID 42463903), which nominates/strengthens ADGRB1 as an ASD risk gene through de novo mutational burden, constraint, and functional assays; a unified SNV/CNV analysis of neurodevelopmental disorders (PMID 35468861) provides additional, but less gene-specific, support. Beyond this, most supporting literature is animal or in vitro: Adgrb1 knockout mice show social deficits and seizure susceptibility (PMID 35114205), astrocyte phagocytosis deficits (PMID 40930306), and synaptic/scaffold interactions relevant to ASD biology (PMIDs 26881134, 36157580, 30604775), with reviews restating the ASD link as background rather than presenting new patient variants. Because I cannot cite two independent human studies each reporting single-gene ADGRB1 variants in distinct probands/families with replication, "Established" is not warranted; the evidence best fits "Existing" with a residual chance that the association is only biologically hypothesized. Papers on cervical cancer neoantigens and Alport syndrome podocytes are irrelevant to ASD.

Two independent human clinical studies report de novo/heterozygous UBR5 variants in probands with autism and neurodevelopmental disease: PMID 39721588 describes 29 individuals with UBR5 variants presenting with developmental delay, autism, intellectual disability and epilepsy, with functional support from autoubiquitination assays and C. elegans; PMID 41318701 independently reports three unrelated individuals with de novo loss-of-function UBR5 variants presenting with ASD and intellectual disability and reviews 11 additional de novo LoF variants in ASD/DD probands. These are separate cohorts with single-gene point/LoF variants (not multigene CNVs), satisfying replication in humans. Supporting but non-decisive evidence includes a de novo UBR5 variant in a developmental epileptic encephalopathy genome-sequencing cohort (PMID 34622207) and UBR family/Notch pathway involvement in neurodevelopmental syndromes (PMID 33340455). Remaining probability reflects the recency of the second cohort and modest proband numbers.

Only one article in the list directly concerns Autism Spectrum Disorder: the whole-exome trio study of 79 Chinese autistic children with intellectual disability (PMID 36320054), which reports de novo mutations in candidate genes; if TLE3 is among them, this constitutes a single, limited, unreplicated human genetic observation, consistent with "Existing" rather than "Established" (no second independent proband/family series is present). No article in the list demonstrates a replicated causal link between TLE3 variants and ASD. The remaining literature concerns TLE3 as a Groucho/TLE transcriptional corepressor in cancer (FOXA1, FOXC1/RUNX1, WNT/β-catenin), pituitary development, islet cell specification, and Six3-dependent eye/forebrain patterning in zebrafish — biologically plausible neurodevelopmental relevance supporting a "Hypothesized" designation, plus an incidental Lewy body GWAS hit that did not replicate. Because the ASD abstract does not explicitly name TLE3, some probability remains for "Novel."

Two independent human case series report intragenic/sequence-level JARID2 loss-of-function variants (not merely multigene deletions) in probands with a neurodevelopmental syndrome that consistently includes autism/autistic features: PMID 33077894 (16 patients, mostly de novo) and PMID 35533077 (7 individuals from 5 families, including inherited variants showing variable expressivity), with further support from a partial de novo intragenic duplication (PMID 35979655) and molecular confirmation via a JARID2-specific DNA methylation episignature (PMIDs 35887345, 37762546). Independent candidate-gene and GWAS association studies in ASD cohorts add supporting human genetic evidence (PMIDs 22681640, 29216786, 26314684, 21308764). Multigene 6p22-p24 deletion reports (PMIDs 22480366, 23324214) are consistent but cannot isolate JARID2. The main reservation is that ASD is described as an associated feature of a broader JARID2 neurodevelopmental syndrome rather than isolated ASD, which keeps meaningful weight on "Existing."

No article reports EGR3-specific sequence variants in ASD probands or families; the only human genetic data (PMID 33683518) is a rare multi-gene 8p21.3 deletion in which EGR3 is merely one of six candidate genes in the minimal region, which by definition cannot single out EGR3, and PMID 19204725 is a review listing 8p genes as background. Supporting evidence is mechanistic: human snMultiome profiling of ASD putamen identified EGR3 as a key regulatory driver of altered D1 MSN programs (PMID 41279076), and mouse work shows Egr3 upregulation accompanying resveratrol rescue of social deficits in Oxtr-KO and VPA ASD models (PMID 32698690). Additional Egr3 biology (immediate early gene downstream of neuronal activity, seizure/DEE modulation in Kcna1-null mice, schizophrenia association) provides plausible pathway relevance but not ASD-specific variant evidence (PMIDs 40589545, 38327141, 26474411). This pattern best fits Hypothesized, with meaningful weight on Existing owing to the CNV/candidate-gene human report.

The strongest human data are a de novo 1.9-Mb 7q31.33q32.1 microdeletion spanning LRRC4, GRM8 and 11 other genes in a child with severe ID and autistic features (PMID 28224041) — a multigene CNV that cannot implicate LRRC4 specifically — and MPRA screens of proband-derived 5'UTR variants that identified LRRC4 5'UTR mutations from autism/NDD families altering translation and protein production (PMIDs 37961498, 41344325). These constitute credible but limited, non-definitive human variant-level evidence, i.e., "Existing," but fall short of replicated, single-gene causal proof in independent probands required for "Established." Substantial supporting evidence is non-human or mechanistic: Lrrc4/NGL-2 knockout mice show autistic-like behaviors rescued by NMDAR activation (PMID 29949768), NGL-2 is a postsynaptic adhesion molecule regulating excitatory synapse development (PMIDs 19467332, 36780420), and its partner NTNG2 causes a developmental disorder with autistic features (PMID 31372774). Several other listed papers concern gliomas, pituitary adenoma, rosacea, or cancer methylation markers and are not relevant to ASD.

Multiple independent human studies report loss-of-function CAPRIN1 variants in probands with a neurodevelopmental phenotype that prominently includes ASD: PMID 35979925 describes 12 unrelated cases with LoF variants of whom 67% had ASD, PMID 41859620 reports an additional independent proband with a novel de novo nonsense variant (p.Q349*) and ASD, and PMID 23849776 identified a deleterious CAPRIN1 variant in an ASD family by whole-genome sequencing. PMID 35977029 further implicates de novo CAPRIN1 variants disrupting stress-granule assembly in NDD cohorts, and functional work in patient-derived iPSC neurons (PMID 35979925, 40112765) plus the Rng105/Caprin1 heterozygous mouse showing reduced sociality (PMID 26865403) supports biological plausibility. Because at least two human studies with independent single-gene point variants in probands exist, Established is favored, though some weight remains on Existing since ASD is one component of a broader NDD phenotype and cohort sizes are modest. Remaining papers (stress-granule biology, SOD1/G3BP1 biophysics, Caprin-2 structure) are mechanistic co-mentions only.

The strongest primary human evidence is the Chinese ASD cohort sequencing study (PMID 27824329), which reports DSCAM among the most prevalent genes for recurrent de novo likely gene-disruptive mutations in ASD probands, and the iPSC study of an ASD patient carrying a heterozygous DSCAM point mutation with functional validation (PMID 34253863). Additional human genomic work (PMIDs 26749308, 38565598) treats DSCAM as a dosage-sensitive gene with recurrent disruptive de novo protein-coding mutations in autism, though largely as background or in other phenotypes. Much of the remaining support is mouse/mechanistic (PMIDs 34848499, 39294095, 35672151, 42119898), which would only sustain a "Hypothesized" call, and one mouse study even failed to find ASD-relevant social phenotypes in heterozygotes. Because within-list independent replication of patient-level single-gene variants is thin (essentially one large cohort plus one single-patient study), points are split between Established and Existing, with Established favored given DSCAM's recognized status as a high-confidence ASD risk gene from large-scale sequencing.

The TRIM8 literature provided is dominated by de novo truncating variants causing a neuro-renal syndrome comprising epileptic encephalopathy, developmental delay, intellectual disability and FSGS (PMIDs 33508234, 30244534, 39416667, 37061734, 32531461), plus non-neurological work on cancer, inflammation, and ischemia. None of these papers report a formal diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder in TRIM8 variant carriers; only nonspecific "behavioral anomalies" alongside global developmental delay are mentioned. Because severe developmental delay/ID with epilepsy is a broadly co-occurring neurodevelopmental context (a recognized risk background) rather than a direct autism association, the evidence best supports "Existing" at most, with substantial weight on "Hypothesized" (neurodevelopmental biology, nuclear-body localization defects in neuronal cells) and some on "Novel" since ASD is never explicitly assessed. The two autism-containing abstracts in the list (PMIDs 25502226, 24651380) concern VPS13B and general variant-prioritization methods, not TRIM8, and thus do not provide gene-specific evidence. No two independent studies report ASD probands with TRIM8 variants, so "Established" is excluded.

Several human studies report SCN8A variants in probands with autistic features: PMID 30615093 characterizes patients carrying R1620L and A1622D loss-of-function variants presenting with intellectual disability and autism without epilepsy (independent probands, with supporting electrophysiology), and PMID 27875746 specifically assessed SCN8A's contribution to ASD/ID cohorts in clinical genetic testing. PMID 22365152 describes a de novo N1768D proband whose phenotype included features of autism, and PMID 37498161 reports an ASD patient with a SCN8A variant, though that one is inherited from an unaffected mother and classified as VUS. Much of the remaining literature (PMIDs 37240836, 41162233, 34425903, 31904124) restates ASD association as background within reviews of sodium channelopathies rather than presenting new proband-level evidence, and in PMID 35348308 the SCN8A carrier had intellectual disability while the ASD phenotype belonged to the SCN2A carrier. Thus autism is a recurrent but often comorbid/secondary feature within the broader SCN8A neurodevelopmental spectrum, supporting at least "Existing" with a substantial chance of "Established".

KMT2D is the principal cause of Kabuki syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder in which autistic features are a recognized behavioral component (PMIDs 33805950, 36292647), which supports at least an "Existing" level of association through a strongly linked phenotype. Direct human evidence tying KMT2D variants specifically to ASD is limited: a case series of three children with Kabuki syndrome and ASD (26129805) lacks individual molecular detail, and a small Turkish ASD cohort reported only variants of uncertain significance in KMT2D (41420732); one KS/ASD case was ultimately attributed to KDM6A rather than KMT2D (37379880). Animal work (Kmt2d knockdown mice and zebrafish showing autistic-like behavior and E/I imbalance, PMID 40883562) provides strong mechanistic plausibility but is non-human and therefore supports "Hypothesized" rather than "Established". Because I cannot cite two independent human studies whose own results demonstrate pathogenic KMT2D variants causing ASD in distinct probands, "Established" is not warranted, though a modest probability is retained given the title "Linking KMT2D to ASD" (41028400) whose content is unavailable.

No human genetic study in this set reports HNRNPD variants in ASD probands or families; the only human variant-level report is a multi-gene 4q21.22 de novo deletion in a boy with cerebral palsy/ID/seizures (PMID 28371330), which cannot single out HNRNPD and does not describe ASD, so it cannot support Established or robust Existing. The strongest ASD-relevant data are mechanistic and non-human: a Drosophila DNMT3L–Sqd/HNRNPD–NCAM axis producing neurobehavioral and synaptic changes framed around ASD comorbid with Down syndrome (PMID 42320545), and mouse Fmr1 KO forebrain proteomics showing altered nuclear HNRNPD (PMID 30176067). Additional biology supports plausibility: HNRNPD/AUF1 is an RNA-stability regulator implicated in mRNA turnover, neurodegeneration-related hnRNP networks, and neurodevelopmentally relevant transcripts such as BDNF regulation (PMIDs 24687816, 36592411, 26526993). This pattern—biologically directly relevant but lacking human ASD genetic association—fits Hypothesized, with a small residual for Existing given the neurodevelopmental deletion region and BDNF/NCAM links.

Many of the listed articles use "MAF" as the acronym for minor allele frequency (e.g., PMIDs 33004838, 28503910, 24094742, 35773312, 31827489, 24002087) and are dismissed as homonym hits. The relevant human genetic evidence comes from Aymé-Gripp syndrome, a MAF-related disorder explicitly described as including autism spectrum disorder features, cataracts, deafness and intellectual disability; PMID 31390148 reports an original family with a maternally inherited MAF p.P69R variant and classical phenotype, and PMID 29314435 catalogues MAF variants causing Aymé-Gripp syndrome and ocular defects. However, only one primary report with ASD-relevant phenotyping in its own results is provided here, so replication across independent probands is not demonstrated within this set, precluding "Established". Additional support is biological/animal-based (Maf in cortical interneuron specification downstream of ARX, PMID 38895467; Maf transcription factors patterning neuronal synaptic properties, PMID 40482032; MAF mouse models, PMID 37895232), which reinforces plausibility but is non-human. Hence "Existing" is the most likely category, with some residual probability for "Established" given the well-recognized syndromic ASD association.

The strongest evidence comes from PMID 32853829, which reported a new de novo RALGAPB missense variant in an ASD proband and, by aggregating published de novo variants, found a genome-wide significant excess of de novo LGD variants in ASD/NDD, with functional confirmation of loss of function for a frameshift allele. PMID 30564305 (ACGC targeted sequencing) contributed proband-level mutation data for autism candidate genes including RALGAPB, but largely as part of a candidate panel rather than independent gene-specific replication. PMID 36553552 nominates RALGAPB from de novo CNVs in macrocephaly, but multigenic CNVs cannot single out the gene. Remaining papers (RalGAP structure, pancreatic cancer, adipose glucose uptake, cholesterol/LDLR, microexon perturbation, RALGAPA1 biallelic variants) provide biological plausibility or concern a different gene, supporting at most a hypothesized link. Because only one primary study convincingly reports patient variants specific to RALGAPB in ASD, "Existing" is the most appropriate designation, with some chance the aggregated de novo excess is judged as established.

Two human studies report intragenic (non-CNV) de novo MEIS2 variants in independent probands where autism spectrum disorder is explicitly part of the phenotype: PMID 25712757 (de novo in-frame p.Arg333del in the homeodomain, patient with ASD) and PMID 30055086 (four de novo homeodomain missense variants, with ASD listed among the observed features). Additional support comes from CNV cases (PMID 28736618, a 15q14 microdeletion patient with ASD), which cannot isolate MEIS2 from neighbouring genes, and from ADHD/behavioral phenotypes in other variant carriers (PMID 39776641), plus animal work framing Meis2 as "autism-associated" (PMID 36418415, mouse—only hypothesis-level). The dominant, replicated human phenotype is a syndromic triad of cleft palate, cardiac septal defects and intellectual disability (PMIDs 30291340, 27225850, 30735726), with ASD an inconsistent secondary feature, so the ASD-specific evidence is real but not the primary, well-powered association. Points are therefore split nearly evenly between Established (two qualifying sequence-variant probands/studies) and Existing (ASD as a limited, non-core syndromic feature).

No article in this set reports autism spectrum disorder itself as an outcome of ZBTB7A variants, so Established cannot be supported (the cohort paper PMID 34515416 and the de novo missense report PMID 31645653 describe intellectual disability, macrocephaly and sleep apnea, not ASD; the 19p13.3 deletion paper PMID 23610052 spans eight genes and cannot isolate ZBTB7A). However, there is robust human genetic evidence that de novo heterozygous ZBTB7A variants cause a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability in multiple independent probands, and PMID 40836029 identifies a likely pathogenic de novo ZBTB7A variant in developmental stuttering while explicitly linking the gene to neurodevelopmental disorders. Because ID/NDD is a phenotype domain strongly linked to and frequently comorbid with ASD, this best fits "Existing" rather than "Established." Supporting biology (ZBTB7A as a regulator of neural development, PMID 20336405; astrocyte-mediated stress susceptibility in psychiatric disease, PMID 40516534) provides mechanistic plausibility, keeping meaningful weight on Hypothesized. Novel is unlikely given the consistent neurodevelopmental phenotype.

Human evidence linking TOP3B to ASD is largely from 22q11.22 microdeletions/duplications (PMIDs 32028044, 27880953, 38674362, 24315824), which cannot isolate TOP3B from neighboring sequence, and from the Finnish isolate study associating TOP3B deletion with schizophrenia/cognitive impairment rather than ASD proper (PMID 23912948). A de novo autism-linked point mutation (C666R) is discussed, but the supporting paper (PMID 41189056) is a cell-based/biochemical functional study rather than an independent clinical proband report, and the review (PMID 40754336) restates the association as background. Mouse knockout and Tdrd3-null work (PMIDs 32561719, 38216113) provide strong mechanistic/animal support but are not human variant evidence. Thus the evidence best fits "Existing": at least one credible human report implicates TOP3B in ASD-related neurodevelopmental phenotypes, but definitive gene-specific replication in independent probands is lacking.

None of the provided articles report any variants in SLTM in autism probands or families, nor any association testing with autism spectrum disorder phenotypes. The available literature concerns rare loss-of-function variants and adult BMI in men (PMID 37601970), SHH/GLI transcriptional regulation with a mouse knockout showing neural tube phenotypes (PMID 30782847), male infertility eQTL/MR analyses (PMID 40700968), and RNA nuclear localization biology (PMID 33938020).
