The only indirect biological hook is that SLTM is a chromatin-associated transcriptional modulator with a role in SHH-dependent ventral neural tube development, a class of function often relevant to neurodevelopment—this supports at most a weak "Hypothesized" reading, and it derives from mouse/in vitro work rather than human genetics. Since no human genetic evidence tying SLTM variants to ASD or a recognized ASD precursor phenotype is present, Established and Existing are effectively unsupported.

The only ASD-relevant human genetic evidence comes from a single whole-genome sequencing study of 1,033 Chinese ASD families (PMID 42463903), which nominates SPPL3 as a candidate risk gene through de novo variant burden, constraint, recurrent missense sites, and functional assays. This is a credible but singular, not independently replicated, human report, so Established cannot be supported (no two independent proband/family studies demonstrating causation). The remaining articles concern SPPL3 biology (intramembrane proteolysis, regulation of N-glycosylation, CLN5 processing, immune/NK cell function, CAR-T engineering, breast cancer methylation, inflammation GWAS), which provide plausible neurodevelopmental relevance (e.g., glycosylation of neuronal surface proteins, CLN5/neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis link) but no direct ASD variant evidence, supporting a residual Hypothesized weight. Novel is nearly excluded because the ASD cohort study explicitly nominates SPPL3.

Human patient-variant evidence exists: PMID 33473207 delineates a cohort of individuals with de novo GNAI1 variants presenting a neurodevelopmental syndrome in which autism spectrum features are part of the described phenotype, and PMID 34819662 reports a novel de novo GNAI1 variant in probands with severe intellectual disability where autistic features are cited as part of the syndrome; GeneReviews (PMID 39083633) and further case reports (PMID 41235373, 38441201) reinforce a GNAI1-related NDD. However, the core, consistently replicated phenotype is developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia and epilepsy, with ASD as a variable accompanying feature rather than an independently replicated ASD-specific association, so full "Established" status for ASD is not clearly met. The one directly ASD-focused human study (PMID 40873676) measures serum GNAI1 protein levels, not variants, supporting association but not causation. Substantial mechanistic work is non-human/in vitro (C. elegans, Xenopus oocytes, cell lines; PMIDs 41052774, 40894620, 41329793, 34685729), which supports biological plausibility rather than genetic causation, keeping some weight on "Hypothesized". Several other papers (angiogenesis, Alzheimer's, cancer, T lymphopoiesis) are irrelevant to ASD.

The strongest evidence is PMID 35395208, which reports 35 individuals with de novo and inherited FBXW7 monoallelic variants (nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, missense) causing a neurodevelopmental syndrome with global developmental delay, intellectual disability and hypotonia, supported by functional assays and a Drosophila knockdown; however, autism spectrum disorder is not explicitly the reported phenotype. PMID 38114583 independently identifies a de novo FBXW7 variant in an Indian syndromic intellectual disability cohort, providing human replication for the NDD phenotype but again not ASD specifically. Because intellectual disability/neurodevelopmental disorder is a phenotype strongly linked to and frequently comorbid with ASD, but no study here directly demonstrates ASD causation in multiple independent probands, "Existing" is the best fit rather than "Established." The remaining papers concern FBXW7 in cancer biology, ubiquitination, or unrelated autism topics (e.g., CHD8, SHANK3, folate) and do not contribute direct gene–ASD evidence, though the ubiquitin-proteasome/NOTCH/presenilin biology gives mechanistic plausibility supporting some weight on "Hypothesized."

PSMD12 haploinsufficiency causes Stankiewicz-Isidor syndrome (STISS), a neurodevelopmental disorder in which intellectual disability with autism spectrum features is a core component. Direct patient-level evidence with single-gene point variants comes from PMID 30421579 (inherited nonsense p.R123X in a multiplex family with ID and autistic features, plus a de novo p.R201X in an unrelated simplex case) and PMID 28132691 (multiple de novo point mutations and deletions in unrelated syndromic NDD probands), with further independent cohorts in PMID 34906456 and PMID 39641441 (novel p.Tyr111* and known p.Arg289* families) explicitly listing ASD within the STISS phenotype. These are human genetic studies in independent probands/families, supporting an established causal role for syndromic ASD, though the phenotype is ASD features within a broader NDD rather than isolated idiopathic autism, which tempers full confidence. Functional/animal work (zebrafish CRISPR model, proteasome assays, PSMD11 comparison) provides supportive mechanistic plausibility but is not itself human genetic evidence; the CNV/deletion reports (PMID 28465847) cannot isolate PSMD12.

Most listed articles use "BCR" as a homonym: BCR-ABL fusion in leukemia (PMID 26588464, 34108312) and B-cell receptor signaling pathway in a transcriptomic ASD study (PMID 37139330), none of which implicate the BCR gene in ASD. The only directly relevant article (PMID 34190380) reports loss-of-function of Bcr causing gastrointestinal dysmotility and brain developmental defects, findings consistent with ASD-related biology (BCR enrichment in CNS, GI comorbidity), but this is an animal/functional study, not human genetic evidence. No paper reports ASD-associated BCR variants in human probands or families, so Established and Existing cannot be supported. The biological plausibility from the murine Bcr loss-of-function model places most weight on Hypothesized, with residual probability for Novel given the weak, indirect nature of the link.

The only human genetic evidence in this set is PMID 37071997, which reports 17 individuals with mostly de novo heterozygous SRSF1 loss-of-function and missense variants causing a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability, hypotonia, and neurobehavioral problems, supported by Drosophila splicing assays and DNA methylation episignatures. This is a single (though multi-proband) study, and the phenotype described is NDD/ID with behavioral features rather than ASD per se, so it supports "Existing" (a well-recognized neurodevelopmental phenotype strongly linked to ASD) rather than "Established," which would require at least two independent single-gene variant reports specifically for ASD. All other listed articles concern SRSF1 in cancer biology, splicing mechanics, angiogenesis, aging, or ALS/Alzheimer models and are irrelevant to ASD; PMID 38450720 mentions autism only as background for synaptic adhesion molecules, not SRSF1. Some residual weight goes to "Hypothesized" because the ASD-specific human evidence is indirect and much supporting functional work is non-human.

The strongest evidence is PMID 39472663, which reports a genome-sequencing burden analysis of de novo potential splicing-disrupting variants in ASD cohorts and assembles 15 unrelated individuals with GSK3B variants showing developmental delay, ASD, sleep disturbance and aggression, supported by single-cell expression and mouse knockdown functional work. This is a single (though multicenter, multi-proband) publication, so under the stated rule I cannot cite a second independent human study demonstrating causal variants in probands, capping the classification at "Existing" while acknowledging substantial support for "Established". Other papers are pathway/mechanistic or review in nature (PMID 26881141 Wnt/GSK3β hub in autism; PMID 41310868 UBE3A/GSK3β in Angelman; PMID 26576547 PPP2R5D where GSK3β is only background biology), and several are homonym-irrelevant or about schizophrenia, Alzheimer's, depression, or breast cancer. These provide biological plausibility (hypothesized-level) rather than additional human variant evidence for ASD.

The evidence linking ACTG1 to autism is suggestive but not replicated in dedicated ASD cohorts. PMID 35190550 is a human whole-genome study of consanguineous ASD families that identified a putative brain-specific regulatory (promoter/enhancer) variant at ACTG1 and treats it as a known ASD/neurodevelopmental gene, but this is a single, non-coding, candidate-level finding. Individual ACTG1-related Baraitser-Winter syndrome case reports describe autistic features or a question of ASD (PMID 28496999, PMID 36205783), which places ACTG1 variants within a syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype strongly overlapping ASD, supporting "Existing" rather than "Established." The remaining literature (PMIDs 25052316, 27240540, 26188271, 32028042, 31231230, 41529692) documents robust human causal evidence for cortical malformation, intellectual disability, and deafness—strongly relevant neurodevelopmental biology—but does not test or demonstrate ASD as a replicated outcome. No two independent studies report ACTG1 coding variants causing ASD per se, so Established is disfavored.

One human study directly tests DIP2C polymorphisms for association with ASD susceptibility and clinical phenotypes (PMID 35987071), and references a prior GWAS signal, which provides credible but limited, non-definitive evidence — the hallmark of "Existing". The largest variant series (PMID 38421105) reports 23 individuals with de novo/inherited loss-of-function DIP2C variants, but the delineated phenotype is expressive speech delay and neurocognitive impairment rather than ASD itself, so it supports a neurodevelopmental role and only indirectly an ASD link. Other reports concern focal infantile epilepsy (PMID 34617658), 10p15.3 microdeletion syndrome (PMIDs 40915331, 34818214) where contiguous genes such as ZMYND11 confound gene-level attribution, or non-human models (PMIDs 41054236, 33813174), which cannot establish causation for ASD. No two independent single-gene human studies demonstrate DIP2C variants causing ASD, so Established is not warranted.

None of the provided abstracts explicitly report autism spectrum disorder in TRAF7 variant carriers; the consistently described human phenotype is TRAF7-related CAFDADD (cardiac, facial, digital anomalies with developmental delay/intellectual disability), established by de novo missense variants in independent probands (PMID 29961569, 32376980, 38569228, 34513876, 37067385). Because this is a well-characterized multisystem neurodevelopmental disorder with developmental delay and ID—phenotypes strongly linked to and frequently co-occurring with ASD—an "Existing" (indirect/related-phenotype) classification is most defensible. "Established" cannot be supported because no cited article reports ASD diagnoses as a primary result in TRAF7 patients. Supporting biological plausibility (E3 ligase, MAPK/ERK signaling, ciliary and neural crest development, zebrafish/Xenopus models) keeps some weight on "Hypothesized," while the complete absence of any autism-specific mention leaves residual probability on "Novel."

Human genetic evidence for NACC1 is strong but for a specific neurodevelopmental syndrome (NECFM: profound developmental delay/intellectual disability, infantile epilepsy, cataracts, delayed myelination, stereotypies) rather than for Autism Spectrum Disorder per se: PMID 28132692 reports seven independent probands with the recurrent de novo c.892C>T variant reaching genome-wide significance, replicated in additional independent patients (PMIDs 34869110, 39421062, 38698576, 38763882). Autistic features (stereotypic hand movements, episodic irritability, severe ID) are described, and the mouse model paper explicitly states it "simulates a rare form of autism" (PMID 38388424), but the ASD diagnosis itself is not the primary reported human phenotype in these cohorts. Because the human variants cause a phenotype (severe NDD/ID with epilepsy and stereotypies) strongly linked to and overlapping ASD, "Existing" best fits, with some probability for "Established" if the syndromic ASD features are counted. Mechanistic support (impaired glutamatergic transmission, SynGAP1/GluK2A interaction, ESC-derived neuron synaptic transcript changes) is largely animal/in vitro and supports the "Hypothesized" tier.

Nearly all provided articles concern RANBP2 missense variants (e.g., p.Thr585Met) causing autosomal dominant acute necrotizing encephalopathy, with no autism phenotype reported (PMIDs 37090838, 33777149, 39710814, 35108406, 25522933). The only article referencing autism is the 2q12.3–q13 CNV study (PMID 35837682), but this is a multigene copy number region encompassing several genes and cannot single out RANBP2 as the driver of neurodevelopmental/autistic phenotypes; per the rules it cannot support Established or strongly support Existing. Reviews of RANBP2 biology (PMIDs 37795679, 40976348, 35058867) describe nucleocytoplasmic transport, SUMOylation, and neurological disease, giving a plausible but indirect biological rationale for neurodevelopmental involvement, supporting a Hypothesized weighting. No study reports RANBP2 point variants in autism probands, so Established is effectively excluded, and a substantial probability remains that co-mention is incidental (Novel).

Multiple human genetic association studies report common-variant association of GABRA4 with autism, including the original family-based study with gene–gene interaction with GABRB1 (16080114), replication across Caucasian and African-American families (16770606), and an independent Argentinean case–control dataset (26239769); this supports at least "Existing." However, these are association signals, not demonstrations of causation, and a targeted resequencing effort found no rare-variant association (29151244). De novo GABRA4 missense variants (35152403, 38565639) cause a neurodevelopmental/epilepsy phenotype with autistic features in only a subset, so ASD is not the established monogenic outcome, and the supportive CNV reports (32028044, 18163449) span multiple GABA receptor genes and cannot implicate GABRA4 specifically. Supporting biology comes from the Gabra4 knockout mouse showing autistic-like behavior (32033586) and altered GABRA4 expression in autistic brain/LCLs (20066485, 35743705), which would only sustain "Hypothesized" on their own. Overall the weight of human evidence is credible but not definitive, favoring "Existing."

The human genetic evidence for ZBTB18 is strong for intellectual disability/neurodevelopmental disorder (MRD22, 1q43q44 syndrome) with multiple de novo point variants in independent probands (PMIDs 24193349, 27598823, 28283832, 38215144, 42183389), but these reports describe ID, corpus callosum anomalies, microcephaly and seizures rather than diagnosed ASD. The strongest ASD-relevant human data come from large-scale targeted sequencing of NDD/autism cohorts including thousands of autism trios, where ZBTB18 emerged as a significant risk gene with genotype-phenotype correlation (PMID 33004838), supporting an "Existing" level of evidence via a broad NDD/ASD phenotype. Other papers referencing autism (PMIDs 40475427, 41851468, 40666864) cite the ID/autism link as background while their own results are mouse/cross-species regulatory biology, and the multi-omic ASD data are from a Cntnap2 mouse model (PMID 42502111), which supports only "Hypothesized." Because no two independent human studies report ASD-diagnosed probands with single-gene ZBTB18 variants, "Established" is not warranted; most weight goes to Existing with substantial residual probability on Hypothesized.

None of the provided articles examine autism spectrum disorder. The nicotine dependence GWAS (PMID 22377092) and the cerebral small vessel disease GWAS (PMID 31430377) implicate ZCCHC14 in unrelated phenotypes, and neither is a recognized precursor or subtype of ASD. The only neurodevelopmentally relevant report (PMID 22407726) describes a 265 kb contiguous multigene deletion at 16q24.3 including ZCCHC14 in a single proband with microcephaly and mild intellectual impairment — a CNV that cannot single out ZCCHC14 from neighbouring genes (C16ORF95, FBXO31, MAP1LC3B, FOXC2 regulatory elements), and autism is not reported. This leaves at most weak, indirect biological plausibility (a brain-expressed gene in a neurodevelopmental deletion region), supporting mainly a Novel classification with some weight for Hypothesized.

No article reports HSF2 variants in autism probands or families. The only ASD-specific paper (PMID 30670685) implicates HSF2 as a trans-acting regulator binding the risk allele of a ZNF804A promoter SNP — the variant is in ZNF804A, not HSF2, so it supports a mechanistic/biological role rather than HSF2 genetic association. Human neurodevelopmental relevance is supported by a single de novo deleterious HSF2 variant in an Angelman-syndrome-like cohort (PMID 34653234, candidate gene status only) and by HSF2's role in cortical development and Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome biology (PMID 36385105), which are related neurodevelopmental phenotypes but not ASD per se. This combination of strong biological plausibility with, at best, a single indirect human variant observation places the weight on Hypothesized, with meaningful probability for Existing; Established is untenable since no two independent proband/family studies of HSF2 variants in ASD exist.

Multiple independent human clinical studies report de novo truncating variants in PPM1D exons 5/6 (Jansen-de Vries syndrome) with autism spectrum disorder/autistic behavior as a recurrent phenotypic feature. PMID 28343630 identified 14 individuals with de novo PPM1D truncating mutations and deep phenotyping documenting ASD, ADHD and anxiety; PMID 37183572 independently expanded the phenotype across 34 families with pathogenic PPM1D variants; PMID 30795918 reported two unrelated girls with novel de novo exon 5 frameshift variants and autistic behavior; PMID 40630121 adds a further proband with a novel truncating variant and ASD/ADHD. These are single-gene point/frameshift variants (not multigene CNVs) in independent probands, satisfying replication criteria. Some uncertainty remains because ASD here is one component of a broader syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than isolated ASD, and much of the remaining literature (clonal hematopoiesis, cancer, in vitro/mouse work) is irrelevant to the phenotype.

The human genetic evidence for CERT1 is strong but is framed around intellectual disability/neurodevelopmental disorder (CerTra syndrome) rather than Autism Spectrum Disorder specifically: 31 individuals with de novo missense variants (PMID 36976648), additional ID probands with S132L/G243R and S135P gain-of-function variants (PMIDs 34688657, 33347465), and a de novo mutation screen in moderate/severe ID listing COL4A3BP/CERT1 (PMID 25356899). None of the provided abstracts reports ASD as an ascertained diagnosis or an autism cohort association, so "Established" for ASD cannot be supported. However, ID and syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder are well-recognized co-occurring/related phenotypes strongly linked to ASD, and disrupted sphingolipid homeostasis affecting neural differentiation and synaptic transmission provides a plausible mechanism, which supports "Existing" with substantial weight also on "Hypothesized." Remaining papers are biochemical/structural or animal-model work (PMIDs 28652409, 29848549, 14685229, 42051775) that supports mechanism but not a direct ASD variant association.

The only autism-relevant evidence comes from a single study (reported as a preprint, PMID 37961498, and its published version, PMID 41344325) that screened 997 patient-derived 5'UTR variants from neurodevelopmental disorder/autism families and identified a ZNF644 5'UTR mutation altering translational activity, including in neurons in vivo. This is human proband-derived variant evidence with functional support, satisfying "Existing," but it is one study reported twice rather than independent replication in separate probands or families, so "Established" cannot be supported. All remaining papers (PMIDs 22539872, 24991186, 25525168, 31560770, 36964802, 23379998, 23024268) concern ZNF644 in high myopia, an unrelated phenotype that is not a recognized precursor or subtype of ASD, and therefore contribute nothing to the ASD link. Some weight is retained for "Hypothesized" because the ASD evidence rests largely on reporter/translation assays (partly in vivo mouse neurons) rather than a clinical genetic association study, and a small residual for "Novel" given the single-source nature of the evidence.

Several human case reports describe de novo heterozygous KIF1A missense variants in independent probands with autism spectrum disorder: p.R13H with ASD, spasticity and axonal neuropathy (PMID 28834584), a distinct p.R13C proband with autism, hyperactivity and spastic paraplegia (PMID 31813911), a pathogenic KIF1A mutation in an ASD/ID participant additionally carrying a 22q11.2 duplication (PMID 29589274), an ASD family trio with a harmful missense variant (PMID 34247363), and a comorbidity-free ASD proband with de novo p.N222H (PMID 41868953). Large-scale de novo mutation analyses of developmental delay/autism cohorts also implicate KIF1A with an excess of missense DNMs (PMID 30559488). These are single-gene point variants in independent human probands, supporting more than a single-study association, but the ASD phenotype is generally embedded within the broader syndromic KIF1A-associated neurological disorder spectrum (PMIDs 33880452, 34487232), and no formal replicated ASD-specific gene-level association study is presented. Evidence therefore sits between Existing and Established, leaning slightly toward Existing.

No article in this set reports PLXNA1 variants identified in ASD probands or families; the only human genetic reports concern developmental encephalopathy/epilepsy, Dworschak-Punetha neurodevelopmental disorder, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and Parkinson's disease (PMIDs 28464511, 34054129, 41424197, 28334861), where autism is not the assessed outcome. The imaging-genetics paper (PMID 25518740) is human and links PLXNA polymorphisms to corpus callosum microstructure while merely citing autism as known background, so it is supportive of neurodevelopmental relevance rather than direct ASD-variant evidence. The strongest mechanistic support is non-human: PlxnA1 knockout mice show increased self-grooming and reduced prepulse inhibition with interneuron deficits (PMID 36451778), and semaphorin–plexin axon-guidance biology is highly relevant to ASD pathways. Some credit goes to "Existing" because PLXNA1-related neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability and syndromic features in humans is a phenotype adjacent to ASD, but no ASD-specific human association is demonstrated, so "Hypothesized" is most appropriate.

No article reports point mutations or single-gene variants in BRD1 in independent autistic probands, so Established is excluded. The strongest human data are a CNV/gene-network prioritization study in an ASD cohort that highlighted BRD1 among copy-number changes (PMID 19492091) and Phelan-McDermid syndrome studies where BRD1 lies within multigene 22q13 deletions and is prioritized computationally as a contributor to the ASD/ID/seizure phenotype (PMIDs 38002941, 35328081, 42192297, 38414139); these are contiguous-gene deletions and cannot isolate BRD1, so evidence is suggestive rather than definitive. Additional support is indirect and biology-based: BRD1 variants are associated with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder in humans (PMIDs 16924267, 19693800, with negative replication in Chinese Han, 29794561), and BRD1 functions in histone H3K14 acetylation, brain development, and neurodevelopmental gene networks, with mouse behavioral/neurotransmission phenotypes (PMIDs 27837920, 27142060). Thus points split mainly between Existing (human CNV/deletion-level association with ASD phenotypes) and Hypothesized (mechanistic, animal, and related-psychiatric-phenotype evidence).

Human evidence linking GNAO1 to ASD exists but is limited: a SNP-based diagnostic classifier study found GNAO1 among the three genes contributing most to ASD prediction (PMID 22965006), and a case-control serum study reported decreased GNAO1 protein levels in individuals with ASD (PMID 40873676), which is expression rather than variant evidence. A report on "mild forms in epilepsy and autism" (PMID 38724739) suggests autism-like presentations among GNAO1 variant carriers, but this is a single, non-replicated source and the broader GNAO1 literature (PMIDs 40225165, 37142469, 37548038) characterizes the gene primarily as causing developmental and epileptic encephalopathy and movement disorders, with autism at most as a comorbid feature of global neurodevelopmental impairment. The 16q12.1q21 deletion cases (PMID 32045705) include ASD but span multiple genes and cannot implicate GNAO1 specifically. Since I cannot cite two independent variant-level proband studies demonstrating GNAO1 causation of ASD, Established is not supportable; Existing best fits, with residual weight on Hypothesized given the gene's Gαo neuronal signaling biology.

Only one article (PMID 40966122) provides primary human genetic evidence, reporting 23 families with monoallelic likely gene-disruptive or de novo missense INTS6 variants, with autism, intellectual disability, language/motor delay, and sleep problems as shared features, supported by a conditional KO mouse showing social novelty deficits and hyperactivity. This is compelling and internally replicated across many probands, but it is a single publication, so the two-independent-publication requirement for "Established" is not met, capping the assessment at "Existing". The remaining articles concern INTS6/Integrator biology in cancer, adipogenesis, mRNA 3' processing, zebrafish dorsoventral patterning, yeast, and Arabidopsis, or involve the unrelated INT6/eIF3e homonym, and provide only background or non-human functional context. Those support at most a "Hypothesized" biological rationale, which retains a modest share of probability.

None of the provided articles mentions autism spectrum disorder, neurodevelopmental phenotypes, or brain/neuronal function for CXXC1. The literature set is entirely about CXXC1/CFP1 as an epigenetic regulator (Setd1 complex, H3K4me3, DNA methylation), meiotic recombination with PRDM9, hematopoiesis, Treg homeostasis, oocyte development, and skin disease regulatory variants (PMIDs 19951360, 15923607, 25470594, 27932493, 28768200, 40183773, 40998781). No human genetic variant study links CXXC1 to ASD, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. A modest Hypothesized weight is warranted only because CXXC1 is a chromatin/H3K4-methylation regulator, a pathway class (SETD1/KMT2, CHD8-like chromatin machinery) broadly implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders, and it is essential for embryonic development and differentiation—but this is an indirect, generic inference rather than a documented ASD-specific link in these papers.

The strongest evidence is PMID 35904126, which reports eight individuals with de novo putative loss-of-function variants in TAF4 and a neurodevelopmental disorder phenotype including intellectual disability, abnormal behavior, and dysmorphism ("TAF4-related NDD"). This is human genetic evidence for a broad NDD phenotype strongly linked to autism spectrum disorder, but ASD is not explicitly diagnosed or replicated in an independent ASD cohort, so "Established" for ASD specifically is not supported (no two independent ASD-proband studies can be cited). Supporting biological plausibility comes from human neural progenitor work showing TAF4/hTAF4-TAFH controls neuronal differentiation (PMID 24696168) and reviews of TAF involvement in nervous system development (PMID 38126142). Most other listed papers concern TAF4 biochemistry, yeast/plant/worm/fly biology, or unrelated diseases, contributing only mechanistic context. Hence, "Existing" is most probable, with substantial weight on "Hypothesized" if one requires direct ASD-labeled variant evidence.

No article in this set reports PHF2 variants in autism probands or families, so Established is untenable. The closest human genetic evidence is a deep-learning imaging-genetics study in ADHD children (PMID 40858546), where PHF2 appeared in a "shared" (non-ADHD-specific) gene–white matter association, and an IBS GWAS implicating a PHF2/FAM120A locus linked to mood/anxiety traits (PMID 34741163) — neither addresses ASD directly, though ADHD is a neurodevelopmental comorbidity, giving modest weight to Existing. Stronger support comes from biological plausibility: PHF2 (KDM7C) is a H3K9me2 histone demethylase in the same PHD/JmjC family as PHF8, whose mutations cause X-linked intellectual disability, and knockdown of family homologs causes brain defects in zebrafish (PMIDs 20818169, 37751140, 37696455); PHF2 also regulates neuroinflammatory genes and synaptic function in AD models (PMID 40849543), and clusters with chromatin regulators implicated in autism such as ASXL3 (PMID 25835095). Most remaining papers concern cancer, adipogenesis, or bone biology and are incidental to ASD, so a substantial share is also assigned to Novel.

No article reports pathogenic BAZ2A variants in ASD probands or families, so Established is effectively excluded. The strongest human evidence is the ELGAN placental multi-omic study (PMID 36938998), where BAZ2A mRNA expression predicted ASD diagnosis at age 10 in children born preterm — a human phenotype association, but based on expression rather than genetic variation, which the criteria place under Hypothesized (with some residual weight for Existing given the human clinical cohort design). Mechanistic support comes from the SETD5 haploinsufficiency work (PMID 32299058), where the ASD-related protein SETD5 acts via TIP5/BAZ2A-mediated rDNA repression, and TIP5 ablation rescues proliferation deficits — but this is mouse/cell-based. Remaining papers describe BAZ2A/TIP5 chromatin, rDNA silencing, prostate cancer, liver regeneration, or unrelated GWAS traits, providing biological plausibility (epigenetic regulator in the MBD/MECP2 family, PMID 40684532) but no ASD variant evidence.

The strongest human evidence comes from 18q12.2 microdeletion reports, including a familial 275 kb deletion involving CELF4 and KIAA1328 in a mother and daughter with intellectual disability and autism/autistic behavior (PMID 28407444), plus previously reported de novo 18q12.2 deletion carriers with autism. However, these are contiguous copy-number changes spanning more than one gene, so by the stated rule they cannot establish CELF4 specifically. The only cohort with intragenic sequence variants (PMID 40108438, 15 patients with heterozygous missense/LoF N-terminal variants) reports developmental delay/ID, seizures and obesity rather than ASD as the defining phenotype, so it supports a neurodevelopmental role but does not independently replicate an ASD causal link. Reviews (PMIDs 38729272, 42523702) and mechanistic work (CELF4 binding synaptic/autism-candidate mRNAs, ZNF804A–CELF3/4 interaction, PMID 30597088) plus the Celf4 mouse phenotype add biological plausibility. This profile fits "Existing": credible but limited/non-definitive human genetic evidence, with substantial supporting biology.

Human genetic evidence exists on two fronts: candidate-gene association studies of ATP2B2 polymorphisms with autism (PMID 21757185 in AGRE/Italian male subjects; PMID 23620727 in Chinese Han; PMID 33076578 in Pakistani cases, where significance was lost after adjustment), and de novo/dominant coding variants causing a neurodevelopmental syndrome in which autistic traits are part of the phenotype (PMID 37675773 case series; PMID 39367743 five additional families with autistic traits; PMID 42360223 single case with ASD and ID). These variant-level reports involve independent probands, but ASD is a comorbid feature of a broader dystonia/ataxia/ID syndrome rather than the primary indexed phenotype, and the common-variant associations are of modest, inconsistently replicated strength. Supporting biology (calcium extrusion, PMCA2 heterozygous mouse Purkinje dysfunction, astrocyte Ca2+ signaling, CNTNAP2-ecto/PMCA2 interaction, AUTS2-marked enhancer near ATP2B2) is compelling but non-human or indirect (PMIDs 34921780, 22789621, 36932889, 25180570). Overall the weight of evidence best fits "Existing" with a substantial chance of "Established."

The only article linking MKX to an autism-related phenotype is the monozygotic twin study discordant for Rett syndrome (PMID 23805272), in which differential DNA methylation upstream of MKX (with inverse correlation to expression) was observed in fibroblasts; this is an epigenetic, single-twin-pair observation rather than evidence that MKX sequence variants cause or associate with Autism Spectrum Disorder, and no independent probands or families are reported. The remaining articles concern MKX biology in tendon/ligament development and homeostasis (PMIDs 20696843, 29667905) or antibody response to smallpox vaccine (PMID 22542470), none of which involve ASD. Thus no study demonstrates a causal or replicated genetic association, excluding "Established." The suggestive human epigenomic finding in a neurodevelopmental disorder with autistic features gives modest support for "Existing," but because it involves methylation rather than genetic variants and is derived from a single twin pair, "Hypothesized" is the best fit, with some residual probability that the co-mention is incidental ("Novel").

The only human genetic evidence is a single report (PMID 12032595) describing two boys from separate families with hereditary multiple exostoses and autism/intellectual disability carrying novel EXT1 frameshift/truncating deletions; however, their fathers carried the same variants without autism, and the authors themselves state coincidental association could not be excluded. This is one study, not independent replication, so Established cannot be supported. Strong supporting biology comes from a mouse model in which conditional postnatal Ext1 inactivation and heparan sulfate loss produced a near-complete autism-like behavioral phenotype (PMID 22411800), plus pathway-level work linking heparan sulfate/glycosylation genes including EXT1 to ASD risk (PMID 39859496). The remaining articles concern osteochondroma/chondrosarcoma or non-ASD phenotypes and contribute no ASD evidence. Overall this fits "Existing" (limited human evidence) with substantial weight on "Hypothesized" given the animal/pathway nature of most support.

The only human-variant evidence is PMID 41029903, which reports compound heterozygous BCAT1 variants in a single patient with a severe progressive neurodevelopmental syndrome and supports pathogenicity with hiPSC neuronal and mitochondrial models; this is a candidate neurometabolic disorder rather than a replicated Autism Spectrum Disorder association, and there are no independent probands or families with ASD. Biologically, BCAT1 initiates branched-chain amino acid catabolism, a pathway (e.g., BCKDK, BCAA dysregulation) well recognized as relevant to autism and neurodevelopmental phenotypes, and animal/model data (Bcat2 ENU mouse MSUD model, PMID 14755340) reinforce the neurometabolic plausibility. Most remaining articles concern BCAT1 in cancer metabolism, atherosclerosis, aneurysm, or as a methylation biomarker and are irrelevant to ASD. Therefore the evidence best supports a Hypothesized relationship, with some weight to Existing given the human neurodevelopmental variant report, and Established is not supportable since no two independent ASD proband reports exist.

Human de novo and inherited MAPK8IP3 variants are firmly established as causing a neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability and brain anomalies (PMID 30612693, 30945334, 42027429, 40734308), and autism is listed among the associated features of the MAPK8IP3-related phenotype spectrum (PMID 40111412), while an OCD pedigree study cites MAPK8IP3 as previously implicated in OCD and autism (PMID 42078338). A human transcriptomic/machine-learning ASD study also nominated MAPK8IP3 as a candidate ASD biomarker (PMID 38153584), providing supportive but non-genetic, non-definitive human evidence. However, no paper here reports independent ASD-diagnosed probands whose autism is attributed to specific MAPK8IP3 variants in its own results, so "Established" for ASD specifically is not supported. Much of the remaining literature is mechanistic (axonal transport, lysosome trafficking, JNK scaffolding in C. elegans, Drosophila, mice, iPSC neurons), which supports biological plausibility (Hypothesized) rather than direct ASD genetic association. Overall the evidence best fits "Existing," with a substantial residual weight on "Hypothesized."

Most autism-relevant papers in this set concern PTCHD1, a distinct X-linked gene, and are explicitly shown to be functionally different from PTCH1 (PMIDs 36769003, 28416808, 32947579); these must be dismissed as gene-name confusion. The only direct human PTCH1–autism evidence is a single case report of a girl with autism and Gorlin syndrome carrying a 22-bp PTCH1 deletion (PMID 21190878), which is credible but isolated and cannot support "Established" (no second independent proband/family with a PTCH1-specific variant). Supporting biological plausibility comes from Ptch1+/- mice showing sex-specific social behavior and cortical/hippocampal/cerebellar changes (PMID 32113901), PTCH1-mutant human cerebellar organoids with altered neurodevelopment (PMID 38411252), and SHH/ciliopathy pathway links to autistic traits (PMID 30478281) — all animal/in vitro, hence Hypothesized-level. The remaining PTCH1 literature is oncologic (BCC, Gorlin syndrome, medulloblastoma) with no autism phenotype measurement, so evidence sits between Existing and Hypothesized, favoring Existing on the strength of the single human proband report.

The strongest human evidence is the exome-based burden study of kainate receptor channel genes (PMID 31844109), which reported a significant burden of damaging coding variants for ASD and specifically replicated GRIK3 S310A as a protective allele — a credible but single, non-definitive human association. Supporting but weaker evidence includes a 2.6-Mb 1p34.3 microdeletion involving GRIK3 in a child with severe developmental delay (PMID 24449200), which cannot implicate GRIK3 alone since multiple genes are deleted, and a GRIK-family review in Egyptian ASD children (PMID 41327126) that only genotyped GRIK1/intergenic variants and merely cites GRIK3 as background. Additional support is biological rather than variant-based: Grik3 upregulation in hippocampus of socially defeated mice (PMID 33659799), germline epigenetic Grik3 changes in a mouse thyroid model (PMID 30356120), and GluK3 pharmacology/structure work (PMID 23141068, 11124978). No two independent human studies report causal GRIK3 variants in ASD probands or families, so Established cannot be supported; the balance falls on Existing with residual weight on Hypothesized.

Human loss-of-function MAP1B variants clearly cause a neurodevelopmental syndrome (periventricular nodular heterotopia, intellectual disability, epilepsy, behavioural dysregulation, ADHD), and several reports list autism spectrum disorder within the phenotypic spectrum (PMID 40869917, 40874586, 33772511, 31317654, 30150678); however, in these series ASD is largely cited as known background rather than demonstrated in the authors' own probands, so replication for ASD specifically is lacking. The strongest ASD-specific human data come from PMID 37365192, where MAP1B triplication in ASD patient-derived neurons and MAP1B elevation downstream of FMRP loss impair neuronal maturation — a CNV plus functional work, supportive but not definitive. Considerable additional support is mechanistic/animal (FMRP–MAP1B in mouse migration, VPA and Tsc2 rat/mouse models, Cntnap2 S-nitrosylation of MAP1B, KIRREL3 interaction), which fits Hypothesized rather than Existing. A TWAS/Mendelian randomization analysis explicitly found no causal association between MAP1B and ASD (PMID 39514479), tempering the evidence. Overall, evidence is best described as Existing with substantial weight on Hypothesized.
